articles.title: ‘Ebenezer’ Review: Johnny Depp Blissfully Goes All Scrooge In Ti West’s New Horror-Flavored Take On Dickens Christmas Classic
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete ‘Ebenezer’ Review: Johnny Depp Blissfully Goes All Scrooge In Ti West’s New Horror-Flavored Take On Dickens Christmas Classic Robert Pattinson To Receive 40th Annual American Cinematheque Award ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Review: Oscar Winner Takashi Yamazaki’s Vision Of Japan’s Most Iconic Monster Is Back Bigger Than Ever Battling An Even Deadlier Foe View All November 12, 2026 9:04am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Johnny Depp in Ebenezer from Paramount Pictures. Paramount Pictures There have been countless iterations on the Charles Dickens yuletide classic, “A Christmas Carol” which was first birthed to the world as a novella in 1843, but has been a favorite of Hollywood for nearly a century. Actors have warmed to the bah humbug of it all in various takes beginning with Reginald Owen in 1938’s A Christmas Carol to perhaps still the best, Alastair Sim in the 1951 version. George C. Scott and Patrick Stewart did well-regarded TV movies. Bill Murray did a contemporary comedic version with Scrooged. Albert Finney turned it all into a big screen musical in 1970. Even Kermit and Miss Piggy jumped on board with The Muppet Christmas Carol, and no less than Mr. Magoo in the evergreen (and personal favorite) Mr. Magoo’s Christmas Carol. In 2017 Christopher Plummer even took a whirl with Scrooge in the clever and wonderful biopic, The Man Who Invented Christmas which was all about Dickens writing the time honored tale. Related Stories News Daisy Ridley, Darren Criss, Travis Fimmel & Judy Greer Join Catherine Zeta-Jones In Tate Taylor's Marriage Counselor Thriller 'Cupid'; Filming Underway -- AFM News Johnny Depp & Ti West Land In A Chilly London For 'Ebenezer' Global Premiere It seems inevitable though that modern day master of all disguises, Johnny Depp would get a turn at bat, and in the latest version, Ebenezer , he has done just that. To say it is a perfect fit for Depp would be an understatement as he finds his own unique way into the role, but in a bit of a twist manages to unearth more humanity in Ebenezer Scrooge than previous versions that saved all that for the inevitable happy ending. Here, insufferable as he can be, this Scrooge allows us to have more empathy for the man as his own past is revealed as the source of his discontent. The other wrinkle with this version is brought by its director, Ti West , previously known as a horrormeister with the trilogy of X, Pearl, and MaXXXine , but it turns out he is a lifelong fan of the Dickens tale and found it ripe for more emphasis on its horror aspects built in with the infamous ghosts so crucial to the story. After all, the original title of the novella was “A Christmas Carol. In Prose. Being A Ghost Story At Christmas”. Paramount’s campaign for the movie also leans into this with the ad line: “If You Think You Know His Story, Think Again”. Fear not though, we do know the story and this is still all very PG13 and not as bloodletting as the filmmaker’s past filmography. West , and his screenwriter Nathaniel Halpern, have too much reverance for what Dickens hath wrought to mess around with the bones of the tale we know all too well. Paramount’s marketing department wants us to believe this is all new but it really isn’t for the most part, just an excuse for Depp to play in the sandbox. Watch on Deadline Ebenezer, with fine period production design by Eve Stewart and darkly lit cinematography from Checco Varese, perfectly sets the tone as we meet Ebenezer Scrooge and his even more greedy business partner Jacob Marley (an ideal Ian McKellen ), just before Marley succumbs to a heart attack. It is Christmas Eve and neither owner was all too swell to loyal but beaten-down employee Bob Cratchit (an effective Rupert Grint ) who is anxious to spend time with his family including wife Clara ( Daisy Ridley ) and young son Tiny Tim (Freddie Lee Grey). There is also a visit from Christmas-loving nephew Fred (Sam Claflin) who can’t understand his uncle’s disdain for the holiday and what it really means. As Scrooge retires for the night, the fireworks begin, first with a view from down under from the late not-so-great Marley with a foreboding warning. Then we have a visit from the Ghost Of Christmas Past (a spirited Andrea Riseborough ) who takes him back (Arthur Conti is the younger Ebenezer) to his roots growing up, to his own family life, and most notably to his one and only true love Belle (Ellie Bamber) in a relationship doomed to failure as his early inclination for money over love seems to take hold. Here we see the human being, flawed but recognizable, taking his first wrong turn. Cue the Ghost Of Christmas Present (a dynamic turn from Severance Emmy winner Tramell Tillman ) who really turns on the gas to show Scrooge a miserable world, including for the Cratchit clan involving death and despair. West finds his deepest dive into the tropes of horror with this sequence, about as dark as any version of A Christmas Carol can get. And then it gets even darker with the Ghost Of Christmas Future (creature actor Robert Strange) who is so imposing he needs to say nothing, just show what will become of Ebenezer – and it is not pretty. It is no spoiler to reveal how it all works out and Depp clearly is having a blast playing it to the hilt. Fortunately the audience will walk out with their Christmas spirit (if not the spirits) intact. I am not sure the world needed yet another dance with Dickens and Scrooge. As mentioned at the top of this review there is plenty to savor from the cinema of Christmases Past that hold up quite nicely to revisit year after year after year, but I have to say it is satisfying to see Depp give it a go. After a very rough patch in his life and career, just like Ebenezer Scrooge, this gifted actor is seeing the light again. Producer is Emma Watts. Title: Ebenezer Distributor: Paramount Release Date: November 13, 2026 Director: Ti West Screenwriter: Nathaniel Halpern Cast: Johnny Depp, Rupert Grint, Daisy Ridley, Andrea Riseborough, Sam Claflin, Ian McKellen, Tramell Tillman, Robert Strange, Ellie Bamber, Arthur Conti, Freddie Lee Grey Rating: PG13 Running Time: 1 hr 56 mins Jensen Huang Is Out As Nvidia CEO Amid Affair Scandal; Successor Sought Eddie Murphy & Ama Qamata Voicing Animated Fantasy Movie ‘M’Tali’ Helmer Denis Villeneuve Says He Is “Pushing The Gas” On Casting ‘Focker-In-Law’ Premiere Pics: Grande, De Niro, Feldstein & More Read More About: Comments

articles.title: Mind the Gap: British Producer-Financier Phil Hunt Is Bringing Head Gear Stateside
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All November 11, 2026 5:43am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Head Gear Co-founder and CEO Phil Hunt Phil Hunt, Hana Holmes The AFM got a welcome boost ahead of this year’s market when British producer-financier Head Gear unveiled plans to launch a U.S. operation, promising to invest $120 million in production in its first year of operation. Head Gear COO Samantha Allwinton will run the U.S. division as director of operations. For Phil Hunt , who launched Head Gear in 2002 with film financier (and oil industry exec) Compton Ross, setting up stateside has been a dream “for 25 years.” In the U.K., Head Gear has developed a reputation as the “producer’s producer,” working at every stage of financing and production — from presales and packaging to gap and bridge funding — to support about 30 films a year, including Talk to Me , Danny and Michael Philippou’s Australian horror breakthrough that grossed more than $90 million worldwide; Ali Abbasi’s Oscar-nominated “reality horror” film The Apprentice , about the making of Donald Trump ; and Molly Manning Walker’s art house crossover hit How to Have Sex. Related Stories Movies 'Exotic' Takes Us to Polish Pole Dance Camp to Tell a Female Story of Self-Discovery and Body Confidence Movies Producers Push for Year-End Passage of Trump-Backed Federal Film Incentive: AFM Head Gear also is active on the sales side through its international operation, Bankside Films, whose AFM slate this year includes the AI-themed sci-fi comedy Almost You , starring Juno Temple, Joey King and James McAvoy from Ted Lasso director Matt Lipsey. Bankside is selling the project, now shooting in Scotland, worldwide, co-repping the U.K. and North America with UTA Independent Film Group. Speaking with THR ahead of the market, Hunt explains why he’s bullish about the U.S., with or without a federal tax credit, the impact of the creator economy on indie film and what he’s learned from taking on Trump – and Julie Andrews . Why Head Gear USA, and how will it work? I’ve wanted a U.S. business for about 25 years. It took that long to find the right person to run it. Now the timing is right as well: more U.S. producers need financing, and a federal tax credit could bring a lot more production into the country. We’re putting about $120 million into U.S. film and TV in the first year. We’re not just a lender. We help producers package the project, build the financing plan, handle the business affairs and collect the money after release. We behave like a small studio. We decide whether a film goes into production, and we deliver about 35 films a year to our regular sales agents and buyers. Whether we like it or not, the U.S. leads the rest of the world on global distribution of English-speaking movies. Being there is often not an option. But we’re a British company with the culture we have built over the past quarter of a century, and that means we uphold key principles. We’re transparent and do what we say we’re going to do — while bringing a great punk rock style. ‘Talk to Me,’ which Head Gear backed, was a breakout hit, earning more than $90 million worldwide. Matthew Thorne/A24 How does the federal tax credit fit into your U.S. expansion plans, and what if it doesn’t pass? If it passes, a U.S. production gets cheaper to make and lenders can borrow against the credit, the way we already do in the U.K. and Europe. That’s why we’re setting up now, so we’re ready the day it lands. If it doesn’t pass, we’re still going to be investing heavily in U.S. movies. Nothing much changes that desire to open up there for the past 25 years. What are the biggest lessons you take from the past year’s indie successes and failures? The films that worked were made for a price that makes sense; good cast, clear idea, a budget the market can pay back. The ones that failed mostly cost too much for what they were. People priced the film on hope, not on what buyers actually pay. Second lesson: The old safety nets are gone. Revenue is down and costs are up. If your plan only works when everything goes right, it won’t work. Third: Be honest early. When a producer tells us the problem on day one, we can usually solve it together. Those are the people we make films with again and again. What has been the biggest disruption in traditional indie financing, and how has that changed how you put projects together? Presales stopped covering what they used to. Streamers buy fewer films from independents and pay less for the ones they do buy. So there’s a bigger gap between what a film costs and what’s guaranteed up front. Gap is the new equity. Investors like us now fill part of what used to be covered by sales. That means we build the film around the money from the start. We look at cast, genre and budget together, before the script is locked. We stay with low-cost, high-concept projects: action, thriller, horror. We also watch how much we have riding on any one genre or sales agent at a time. Head Gear scored a cross-over arthouse hit with ‘How to Have Sex’ from Molly Manning Walker Courtesy MUBI mk2 Films/Nikos Nikolopoulos How was Almost You financed? It’s a mix. Tax credit money from the U.K., a lender borrowing against it [us], some money from sales to territories, and equity from the producers and partners. Bankside came on early with the cast, which helped make the sales numbers believable. How is the creator economy affecting indie film? Creators have something indie films have always struggled to buy: an audience that already knows them. That matters more than ever because marketing a small film is hard and expensive. A creator with millions of followers brings people before the film is released. But a big following doesn’t automatically turn into cinema tickets. Watching a free video is very different from paying to see a film. The ones who will make it work are the creators who treat a film like a real production: proper script, proper budget, proper distribution plan. I’m interested in that. I’m not interested in a follower count on its own. But most of all it’s about great storytellers, whether they are from the creator economy or not. What’s been the biggest surprise for you, and which title (whatever the commercial success) are you most proud of? There’s a lot that I’m surprised that failed so badly, but on a more positive note: from a commercial perspective, it’s got to be Talk to Me . No one knew that it was going to do the incredible business it did. It changed global strategies for many distribution companies. On a more controversial note, it’s got to be The Apprentice , which talked to me in many ways. I’m always fascinated at the power movies can have globally. It was really the story of Frankenstein, how a monster was made. It’s the original horror — Trump is Frankenstein. It was almost “reality horror.” We got a cease and desist from Trump on the day of the film’s world premiere in Cannes, and of course we threw it in the bin … The way all the filmmakers went about making and releasing it is truly punk rock. Sebastian Stan as Donald Trump in ‘The Apprentice.’ Pief Weyman/Rich Spirit What project did you learn the most from, in terms of your approach to the business? It’s got to be my second feature, Chunky Monkey , which I made in 2000 in the early days of my producing career. The great Greg Cruttwell wrote and directed it, and I was the sole producer — in the days when there was only one producer credit. Some folk called it a cult movie, others were disgusted by it. [The comedy features, among other things, a Julie Andrews-lookalike prostitute and the obscene use of Chunky Monkey ice cream.] Particularly offended were Rogers & Hammerstein, EMI, Julie Andrews, Unilever and the original creator of the Chunky Monkey comic strip [Pauline Comanor], all of whom tried to sue us and totally failed. [Comanor] claimed Ben & Jerry stole the name from her. Unilever, who bought the ice cream manufacturers, were incensed about the nature of our depiction of “finding another pleasurable” use for the ice cream. EMI was being forced by the very conservative Rogers and Hammerstein [estate] to withdraw its signed agreement with us. We rerecorded “The Hills Are Alive With the Sound of Music” with our Black Jesus singing and the pink panther playing the bongos. Julie Andrews just didn’t get our love note to her … I got more column inches over the period of a month than any studio movie. It was a David and Goliath story that stole the front page of many newspapers. The film was harmless, and it just shows you how people react without really reviewing the facts. While the film made no money, it was pirated a lot and got a cult following and put me on the map as a producer. I made sure everyone in the industry knew me after that. I realized then this business is all about marketing.” THR

articles.title: ‘Tangled’ Takes Ciudad de la Luz From Up-and-Coming Studio to Production Must-Stop
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All November 11, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source The morning sun hits Studio Ciudad de la Luz. Publicity For the team at Studio Ciudad de la Luz, 2026 is the year it went from an up-and-coming shoot destination to a top-tier must-stop for major international productions. In Alicante, this large-scale film and TV hub was born from the vision of Spanish filmmaker and screenwriter Luis García Berlanga, who in 2005 set out to reindustrialize the Spanish audiovisual sector. That initial seven-year phase culminated in 63 projects, including J.A. Bayona’s The Impossible and Francis Ford Coppola’s Tetro . Studio Ciudad de la Luz reopened in 2023 with a renewed intention to set itself apart from its rivals. Boasting state-of-the-art facilities, it has six climate-controlled stages, interconnected in pairs, and two indoor, floodable pits that come in at over three metres deep. Among its signature draws is the outdoor water tank, a 100-by-80-meter facility with wave-generation systems, water cannons, slides, a seawater pumping system and partial fill-and-drain capability. The backlot totals 14.8 hectares of space with natural horizon, power, water and telecommunications, over 4,000 square meters of workshop space and 7,000 square meters of storage space, with three production support buildings hosting dressing rooms, make-up, hair, offices and services. Related Stories Movies 'Exotic' Takes Us to Polish Pole Dance Camp to Tell a Female Story of Self-Discovery and Body Confidence Movies Producers Push for Year-End Passage of Trump-Backed Federal Film Incentive: AFM And from 2023 to 2025, this production eden was a well-kept secret. Among some of their projects during that time period were Venom: The Last Dance with Tom Hardy, generating 35 million euros and 570 contracts, as well as The Walking Dead: Daryl Dixon , which shot in the aforementioned water tank, the French Netflix shows Nero and Under Paris , as well as Alberto Rodriguez’ Los Tigres and Alejandro Amenabar’s El Cautivo , which had an estimated economic impact of eight million Euros. But the word is officially out. This year, the studio has found industry consolidation in two projects of significant scale: Disney’s live-action Tangled and the permanent establishment of The Good Film Studios Spain , helping Ciudad de la Luz absorb some of the most technically and logistically demanding shoots with newfound confidence. Ciudad de la Luz is currently the only facility in Europe that allows indoor, outdoor and aquatic filming on the same site. That kind of versatility — paired with a warm-weather climate, competitive incentives and an experienced local crew — is attracting the eyeballs of producers across the globe. A shot from the outdoor water tank at Studio Ciudad de la Luz. Publicity Michael Gracey’s Tangled , produced by Kristin Burr, has emerged as a case-in-point example of what’s possible at this production behemoth. The original 2010 animation, following Rapunzel’s team-up with a local outlaw, the devilish Flynn Rider, was a smash hit that swiftly accrued nearly $600 million at the global box office. Set for a 2028 theatrical release and starring Teagan Croft, Milo Manheim and Kathryn Hahn, the new era of Tangled was shot at Studio Ciudad de la Luz over 10 months from February to October this year and involved the intensive use of stages, on-site exteriors and locations across the region of Valencia. Its direct economic impact on Ciudad de la Luz is currently over 40 million euros, with more than 1,000 professionals mobilized on the project. A whopping 2,500 local contracts were generated by the arrival of this Hollywood production, lending help to the studio’s 90 percent occupancy in 2026. Gracey argues that fellow U.S. execs should consider booking that flight to Alicante. “There’s an extraordinary level of passion and dedication here,” he says ahead of the American Film Market. “That energy comes across on screen.” The filmmaker, best known for his work on The Greatest Showman (2017) and Better Man (2024), said his crew was able to combine exterior and interior stages, “and it feels real,” he adds. “You don’t notice the transition.” He sings the praises of the local crews and scenery here in southeast Spain. The region certainly gives Los Angeles a run for its money, attracting more than 300 days of sunshine a year and diverse landscapes such as beaches, mountains, salt flats and protected natural areas. With the bustling Spanish town of Alicante, an international airport, and hotel capacity of over 70,000 beds in the surrounding area, Gracey lauds the no-fuss environment: “The people, the locations and the spaces have been fantastic. Having the city only 15 minutes away is a real advantage.” Burr even hails it as her “favorite location.” She explains: “The stages are among the most spectacular I’ve ever worked on [and] I’m extremely impressed by the level of dedication we’ve seen on the sets. I’m very demanding when it comes to production design, and I think this is some of the best I’ve seen in my career.” As vocal advocates of Studio Ciudad de la Luz, Gracey and Burr are in good company. Top producer Miriam Segal founded the Good Films Collective in 2007, established to develop and finance “intelligent, inclusive and commercially ambitious independent films.” Now, her joint venture with the Spanish government and Canadian-U.S. outfit Orogen Media, The Good Films Studios Spain has set up a permanent home at Studio Ciudad de la Luz, bringing with it an investment of 19.8 million Euros from the Spanish Society for Technological Transformation (SETT) and private partners. With the arrival of Segal’s Spanish branch here in Alicante — a long-term commitment eyeing 20 international features over the next 10 years — her company has evolved from rising production outfit to integrated studio business. “It’s the best crew I’ve worked with anywhere in the world,” says Segal, known for The Infiltrator (2016) with Bryan Cranston and The Postcard Killings (2020) with Jeffrey Dean Morgan. The Good Films Studios Spain have set their first film out of the Alicante hub: People of the Book , directed by Michael Haussman and based on the novel of the same name written by Pulitzer Prize-winning author Geraldine Brooks. The cast includes Ziad Bakri, Rania Ben Fattoum, Ankido Hussen, Luca Ferrini, Giorgia Sinicorni, Pasquale Esposito and Jose Luis Ferrier, who filmed in the studio’s outdoor water tank, as well as on their stages and workshops. It isn’t just the expansive facilities drawing the industry’s most prolific producers and crews, but the territory’s expertly trained ecosystem of graduates. The Film Trades School initiative, developed in collaboration with the country’s leading film school, Escola Superior de Cinema i Audiovisuals de Catalunya (ESCAC), has upskilled thousands of students across more than 30 specialisms, including set construction, lighting, camera, sound, VFX, green filming, costume, production, who are able to come and hone their craft at Studio Ciudad de la Luz. Regional and national tax incentives continue to be a real weapon in the team’s arsenal. A non-repayable grant of 25 percent on production and post-production expenditure is available in Valencia for a maximum relief of 1.5 million Euros per project. At the country-wide level, Spanish productions and co-productions can claim 30 percent of the first million and 25 percent on the remainder back, capped at 20 million Euros per production. For foreign shoots in Spain, it’s the exact same, but the minimum spend in the country must total at least one million Euros. Ciudad de la Luz and the region of Valencia are hopeful they’ve consolidated their position as a real and competitive option in the league of Europe’s most demanding production destinations. And the knock-on effect so far is palpable: “When the Region of Valencia believes in itself,” begins Marián Cano, the regional minister for industry, tourism, innovation and trade, “it can compete with anyone to attract top-level projects.” THR

articles.title: ‘How to Rob a Bank’ Review: Nicholas Hoult Delivers Adrenalized Big Finance Payback That Entertains Despite Its Tonal Mishmash
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All November 11, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Nicholas Hoult in 'How to Rob a Bank.' Megan Schoenbachler/Amazon MGM Studios If the midterm elections were not indication enough that Americans are feeling the pinch and hitting back at a system heavily rigged to favor obscene wealth and unchecked power, high-octane action specialist David Leitch ’s How to Rob a Bank offers further evidence. A kinetic heist thriller in which we root for the thieves — Mark Bianculli’s script name-checks Point Break , swapping Ex-Presidents for animal masks — the good-looking movie doesn’t reconcile its twin identities as a crime caper with a satirical edge and a poignant social justice fantasy. But a strong ensemble keeps things moving. Related Stories Movies David Leitch's 'How to Rob a Bank': First Reactions Movies How David Leitch Made 'How to Rob a Bank' on a Budget -- and Around Nicholas Hoult's Torn ACL Following up on the breezy insouciance of The Fall Guy , Leitch directs with his foot planted firmly on the accelerator, reassembling his trusty core team of DP Jonathan Sela, production designer David Scheunemann, composer Dom Lewis and editor Elísabet Ronaldsdóttir. If the early action overloads on YouTube interface and quippy content creation, that’s amply justified in the script, though it’s a relief when the movie takes time to breathe and allow the characters some depth. How to Rob a Bank The Bottom Line Now is the winter of our collective discontent. Release date : Friday, Nov. 13 Cast : Nicholas Hoult, Zoë Kravitz, Anna Sawai, Rhenzy Feliz, Pete Davidson, John C. Reilly, Christian Slater, Paul Sparks, Tati Gabrielle, Young Mazino, Alessandra Frugoli Director : David Leitch Screenwriter : Mark Bianculli Rated R, 2 hours 2 minutes Nicholas Hoult plays underdog antihero Ryan, aka “The Wolf,” who leads a close-knit crew of Pittsburgh bank robbers and fronts their popular online videos in a furry lupine mask. “Content is king,” he says in voiceover narration, explaining that an audience is more powerful than a gun. Their YouTube show is widely known by the acronym HTRAB and the catchphrase, “Who’s hungry?” It plays not only tightly edited footage of their daring bank escapades, providing tips for a growing number of copycat robbers across the country, but also their “pay it forward” philosophy of tossing cash at bank employees and customers, distributing larger sums to charities like schools, churches and hospitals. At a time when the American Dream is accessible only to the top wealth bracket, these bad guys are good guys, and they make it look easy. Says Ryan: “You’re more likely to live your entire life under the poverty line than get caught stealing your way out from under it.” The HTRAB crew includes Ryan’s partner Emi ( Anna Sawai ), the getaway driver and strategist, an expert at creating diversions to keep law enforcement occupied; combat vet Vince ( Pete Davidson ), who found that after he fought for his country in Afghanistan, his VA health insurance was not prepared to fight for him the same way; and tech wizard Hugo (Rhenzy Feliz), who shapes the YouTube content. Like many of their millions of followers — burdened by student debt and shrinking job opportunities, the goal of home ownership and medical coverage remaining out of reach — Ryan & Co. share a common bond of having run out of options. Bankrupted by medical bills and predatory money-lending policies, he and Emi struggle to accept tragedy that might have been forestalled with more available means. Hugo and Vince, who’s up against a ticking clock, are just desperate to provide for their families. While the robberies are diverting enough and the YouTube inserts splashed with pop-up graphics, the fun wears a bit thin, which makes the shift into trauma and pathos a welcome one, even if the transition might have been smoother. Basically, it turns into a different movie. The cast compensates for any shortage of fluidity, however, notably Hoult and Sawai, whose sexy body language counters the lacerating sorrow and anger left by a devastating loss; and Davidson, who curbs his comedy instincts to show uncustomary shadings. His final scene in the movie is intensely moving, in what’s arguably the actor’s best performance since The King of Staten Island . Feliz, best known for Marvel’s Runaways and HBO’s The Penguin , is given less to do, but his sparky personality makes him a magnetic presence. Having pulled off 15 bank robberies over three months and triggered a 400 percent increase in similar operations nationwide, the HTRAB bandits remain frustratingly elusive to the FBI. Nearing retirement and unwilling to go out on a failure, veteran agent John West ( John C. Reilly ) refuses to accept his team’s lack of leads. He recruits coding genius Reagan (Zoë Kravitz) to examine the hours of YouTube material for clues and patterns. An associate professor at Carnegie Mellon, Reagan is now serving time under house arrest on a hacking charge. She’s resistant at first, reluctant to break her routine of bong hits and junk food, not to mention sympathetic to the robbers’ cause. But West wins her over with an exchange that will wipe her slate clean. Reagan is a very cool character who gives Kravitz plenty of room to inject sly humor and irreverent attitude, even just via the low-key running joke of her constant eating in every scene. Initially looking to hunt down a deadbeat ex-boyfriend, she developed a tracking program called FYPOS (“Fuck You Piece of Shit”) designed to locate people via their social media activity. That becomes an essential tool in the FBI investigation. But after giving Reagan an intriguing setup, Bianculli’s script runs out of ideas for the character, relegating her to observer status for much of the climactic stretch. Reilly is put to better use as an old-school agency man set on doing his job, but with enough misfortune behind him to understand what drives Ryan and his crew. The chaotically plotted penultimate act involves West closing in during the “big finish” that the HTRAB team have been carefully plotting for months. That involves their agenda getting personal as they hit heavyweight financial institution Vitality Trust. That monolith is run by David Walton (Christian Slater), an arrogant asshole whose merciless loan scheme was designed to reap huge profits once the borrowers had been bled dry. The volatile mob of HTRAB followers gathered in the blocks surrounding VT inevitably recalls the wealth inequality protests of 2011 that began near Wall Street and spread to cities across the country, including Chicago, Boston, Los Angeles and Seattle. That brings a stirring “power to the people” sentiment, even as Ryan’s determination to complete their plan seems doomed once the Feds know their identities. But the movie keeps a few tricks up its sleeve for a satisfying coda. The narrative’s plot holes and contrivances don’t reward close inspection, but as an avenging underdog fairy tale pieced together from the shards of the American Dream, it’s fast-paced, entertaining and surprisingly emotional. That’s due in no small part to the soulful qualities the principals bring to their roles. Sela’s muscular camerawork, Lewis’ pulse-racing score and Ronaldsdóttir’s punchy editing all play vital parts, as do the energizing needle drops. These range from the pounding dubstep beats of “Victory Lap,” by Fred Again, Skepta and PlaqueBoyMax through the garage revival of The Hives, the alternative rock of Jane’s Addiction and the gorgeous, whispery vocals of Billie Eilish. The use of Radiohead’s haunting anti-corporate anthem “Karma Police” over one heartbreaking scene is a master stroke. How to Rob a Bank is not without flaws; there are times in the early action when it risks repeating the far-too-pleased-with-itself flashiness of Leitch’s numbing 2022 assault on the senses, Bullet Train . But there’s unexpected heart and a finger on the zeitgeist here that at least ensure it’s never dull — a mainstream commercial anti-capitalist movie in these rollercoaster times is a rare thing. Full credits Release date: Friday, Nov. 13 Production companies: 87North Productions, Imagine Entertainment, Amazon MGM Studios Distribution: Amazon MGM Cast: Nicholas Hoult, Zoë Kravitz, Anna Sawai, Rhenzy Feliz, Pete Davidson, John C. Reilly, Christian Slater, Paul Sparks, Tati Gabrielle, Young Mazino, Alessandra Frugoli Director: David Leitch Screenwriter: Mark Bianculli Producers: Brian Grazer, Jeb Brody, Allan Mandelbaum, Kelly McCormick, David Leitch Executive producers: Ben Ormand, Mark Bianculli Director of photography: Jonathan Sela Production designer: David Scheunemann Costume designer: Jocelyn Pierce Music: Dom Lewis Editor: Elísabet Ronaldsdóttir Sound designers: Pat Haskill, Ryan Nowak, Gregorio Gomez Stunt designer: Greg Rementer Casting: Mary Vernieu, Lindsay Graham Ahanonu Rated R, 2 hours 2 minutes THR

articles.title: ‘GTA 6’ vs. Hollywood: Industry Braces for “Biggest Entertainment Launch in History”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All November 11, 2026 6:16am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Amazon MGM’s new season of 'Rings of Power' and Lionsgate's latest 'Hunger Games' installment are bowing right as 'Grand Theft Auto VI' is poised to dominate the entertainment landscape. Illustrated by Cat Sims Logo text Are gamers who have waited 13 years to return to Vice City really going to spend their time in Panem, Middle-earth, and the Underworld instead? The massively anticipated release of Grand Theft Auto VI , coming Nov. 19, will land amid a slew of expensive and high-profile movies and returning TV shows dropping within several days of each other. Most of them offer their own escapist fantasy worlds that will compete in the attention economy with a title that’s expected to be the biggest video game launch in history. Season three of Amazon-MGM’s The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power is rolling out episodes over three weeks beginning Nov. 11 and Johnny Depp’s comeback vehicle Ebenezer lands Nov. 13. Lionsgate’s The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opens the day after GTA 6 launches on Nov. 20 along with the fourth season of the studio’s Paramount+ hit Yellowjackets . The same day, Disney rolls out the third season of Percy Jackson and the Olympians . Five days down the road comes Amazon MGM’s limited series Blade Runner 2099 . “It’s going to be a watershed moment for not only the gaming industry but also all the folks in the media and entertainment industry who are going to have to deal with the fact that eyeballs are going to be leaving their environments to go play GTA 6 ,” said Bart Spiegel, global media, entertainment, gaming and sports leader at PricewaterhouseCoopers. It’s indeed tough to overstate the earthquake GTA6 is expected to create in terms of entertainment spending, distraction hours and pop culture noise. The Rockstar Games project has a first-year sales forecast of 45 million copies and $3.2 billion in sales — a figure which would top all-time box office champ Avengers: Endgame . A whopping 29 percent of U.S. gamers expect to purchase the title and one economist suggested, rather wildly, that the game would cost the U.S. economy $1 billion in lost productivity due to PTO requests. Other video game publishers have run for the hills and surrendered November to Rockstar’s sun-drenched, pastel-colored 800-pound gorilla. “I think GTA 6 will be the biggest entertainment launch in history,” predicts Geoff Keighley, gaming industry producer and entrepreneur behind The Game Awards . “Not just as a game in terms of dollars it will make — this will easily trump Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part Three — but how much it will impact moviegoing, streaming, and the way people spend their time. Hollywood should look at the hours as closely as the dollars because GTA 6 is going to be some people’s entertainment plan for the rest of the year, basically. The entertainment industry has never really seen something like this before.” While the game’s core mission will likely take around 80 hours to complete — which alone is a massive amount of hours for one title — the title is also an open world environment where players tend to return again and again, and insiders assume the game will allow some kind of online multiplayer mode as well. “So this is not just about opening weekend,” Keighley says. But for Hollywood, which is accustomed to largely owning the entertainment attention economy, particularly around the holidays, the impact of GTA 6 seems almost certainly to be felt — if difficult to measure. Spiegel noted streaming is likely to take the biggest hit because a console game directly competes for viewing hours on living room TVs. Last year’s fourth quarter streaming numbers were rather strong, he noted, but he suspects GTA 6 could put a real dent in the year-over-year comps. The live urgency of sports viewing, however, will be safer from erosion than entertainment programming. “But trust me, if that game gets boring, GTA 6 is going on pretty soon,” he quipped. Behind the scenes, streamers are increasingly aware GTA 6 is coming and that Jason and Lucia might rob some of their viewers. “Everybody is rumbling about how big this game is going to be,” says a representative working with one potentially impacted streaming title. On the film side, a major exhibitor executive said it’s “tough to know” the effect on films like Ebenezer and Sunrise on the Reaping. “ It’s hardly come up in internal discussions, but anyone in the industry who’s ever been a gamer — or who lives with someone who is — knows it’ll have some impact,” he said. “Hunger Games presales are strong, which might point to it being solid counter programming. Ebenezer presales are dire, but I doubt GTA6 is the main reason. We’ll have to see how walkup sales go.” Future box office heavy hitters like Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part Three , which open “Dunesday” Dec. 18. Such titles would seem to fall outside the game’s blast radius, but perhaps not. Spiegel has noted the game’s “pull could last through December.” While hardcore gamers will rush out and play GTA 6 the first few weeks, others will hold off until they have more free time during the December holidays, while some kids (with rather permissive parents) won’t even be unwrapping the presumably Mature-rated game until Christmas. Music will be disrupted, too, with the game’s 34-song soundtrack already at 26 million monthly listens on Spotify and a 30-track original score by Justice coming Dec. 11. One as-yet-unappreciated aspect of the game’s gravitational pull will be on social media, where you’re already starting to see anticipatory videos (such as a boyfriend getting his girlfriend a kitten so she won’t bother him while playing the game, or another boyfriend who seemingly wrote up a contract pledging a list of compromises if his girlfriend doesn’t, yes, bother him while playing the game). But social media is also massive part of entertainment marketing — not just direct advertising but fan-generated content that helps programs generate buzz and become part of the cultural conversation. But what happens if GTA 6 becomes all anybody is talking about? “It’s going to take over live streaming and clips and content creators,” Keighley says. “Barbenheimer worked because you could go see Barbie and Oppenheimer , and you only needed five or six hours. People will still go see other things, but I think the entertainment value has to be extremely high.” This story appeared in the Nov. 12 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

articles.title: Next Gen 2026: 35 Rising Hollywood Executives Under 35
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content The Next Gen execs were photographed Oct. 26 and Oct. 30 at PMC Studios in Los Angeles. Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Nobody ever said that Hollywood careers come easy. But right now, with consolidation and layoffs decimating the middle rungs of entertainment’s steep corporate ladder and studio remits changing with each earnings report, dream jobs have never been more difficult to land, much less retain. Such trends aren’t slowing the ascent of THR ’s Next Gen class of 2026, who join such illustrious alumni as Donna Langley, Ari Emanuel, Kevin Feige and Peter Rice. In fact, this group is too busy forging new paths through the chaos — whether that’s bringing Gen Z back to cinemas (as indie producer Christian Vazquez did with both Primetime and You Can See Everything ) or fortifying the streaming ecosystem amid endless churn (see Claudia Shin and Louie Hayes, behind the Apple TV Emmy darling Widow’s Bay and the Prime Video breakout Sterling Point , respectively.) Meet the 35 executives and reps, each of them 35 years old or younger, who should be atop your call list, if they aren’t already. Alyssa Altman, 35 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion RK Films, senior vp LOGLINE Championing rom-coms like Anyone But You and Netflix’s upcoming 13 Going on 30 update. THE ARC Altman got a unique view of the industry when she would join her father, Steve, who rented out lighting, camera and grip equipment: “I grew up doing my homework in grip trucks, and I just loved being on set.” Her dad’s rom-com adoration rubbed off during their weekly trips to the movies, where films like Love Actually made an early impression. Altman studied journalism at Emerson but caught the producing bug while moonlighting on college TV projects. After time at Gersh, she became then-Universal exec Jeff Kirschenbaum’s assistant and followed him to RK Films. While the company focused on bigger IP plays, she endorsed the script for Anyone But You (“That was my baby”), Sony’s Sydney Sweeney-Glen Powell feature that became a rare theatrical comedy hit. Up next: Amazon MGM’s tennis rom-com Love Love and Netflix’s Millie Bobby Brown-led Just Picture It . PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Andy Cohen. My favorite way to de-stress after a long day is to watch and listen to the soothing sound of people fighting on Bravo.” WHY ISN’T HOLLYWOOD TALKING ABOUT … “The fact that movies geared towards women do great theatrically. Every time it happens, people act like it’s an anomaly. Women are starved for content and it’s not a coincidence.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “When I was an assistant at Universal, we set up a screening for an A-list star who specifically requested popcorn from the Universal Studios theme park. I had to sneak into the park through the back lot and bring it back before he arrived.” FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Sally Albright from When Harry Met Sally . She isn’t afraid to speak her mind, is a hopeless romantic, and has strong opinions on how she orders her food.” Jenna Berger, 35 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Marvel Studios, director of production development LOGLINE Berger is serving as co-producer, and Kevin Feige’s right hand, on Avengers: Doomsday and Avengers: Secret Wars . ’Nuff said. THE ARC An L.A. native with industry parents, Berger grew up wanting to make movies. “I had this theory that everybody who didn’t want to make movies was lying to themselves and secretly did,” she says. So, shortly after graduating from University of Pennsylvania with a double major in English and film, she landed a gig at The Mark Gordon Co. Still, it was Marvel that was making some of her favorite films — she saw Spider-Man: Homecoming four times in the theater — but the company felt impenetrable … until it wasn’t. In 2019, Berger scored a position, rising to junior exec before finding herself the solo exec on the Marvel TV series Ms. Marvel , where she earned a supervising producer credit and honed her creative leadership, talent development and production expertise. “It was the best crash course in figuring out how this company worked and making something worthy of the Marvel name,” she says. The higher-ups took note, which is why Berger now oversees some of the studio’s most ambitious films. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Kermit the Frog. Because my job is to bring amazingly talented people together to make something special amid total chaos … which sometimes means convincing everyone the show must go on before the set falls down around us.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH “David Heyman. To get to work on Bond and Harry Potter?! A dream. Would love to trade places for a day … or forever.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “Having a sneeze attack while leaving a voicemail for Aaron Sorkin on behalf of my boss.” Natalie Berkus, 35 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion LuckyChap, senior vp TV LOGLINE Developing (and producing) your future TV obsessions, including Andrew Garfield’s Wild Things . THE ARC Rather than follow her agent dad and comedy writer mom into the business, Berkus arrived at University of Michigan eager to be a lawyer. “Then I rushed the law fraternity and didn’t get in,” she says. “I mean, I whiffed it and was like, ‘Shit, now what do I do?’ ” The answer, it turns out, was to parlay her love of TV into a series of PA gigs on shows like The Mindy Project before talking her way into a job as the writers assistant on Girls and, later, with Lena Dunham and Jenni Konner’s company. From there, she logged six years at Imagine Entertainment, where she was intimately involved in a slate that included The ’Burbs and the upcoming Siegfried and Roy series starring Garfield and Jude Law for Apple TV. But LuckyChap came calling a year ago, and the L.A. native and new mom to daughter Roonie jumped at the opportunity to work at the Margot Robbie-led hit factory. In that time, she has built a roster of 10 to 15 projects, including a Life Is Strange series for Amazon Prime Video. Still, Berkus doesn’t take herself too seriously. “If I had to brand myself, I’d say I like to bring a levity to this business,” she says, “because I think sometimes, especially now, things can get really stressful and we lose sight of the fact that ultimately this is just one big party.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Nina Rosenstein, who does all of the HBO comedy specials. We’ve never met, but Nina, girl, if you’re reading this, let’s link and get our Freaky Friday moment started!” WORST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “That having unapproachable girlboss ‘I’m smarter than you’ energy is cool. It’s not, it’s lame! Normalize the quiet power in validating others and having a fun vibe.” THE BEST PLACE FOR A COFFEE MEETING IS “Nowhere are you crazy!! No more of these!!” Mandi Brooksbank, 34 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Netflix, senior manager, business affairs, scripted series LOGLINE Helps mold Netflix’s scripted slate, brokering deals with top talent like Ryan Coogler’s Proximity Media. THE ARC As a kid in Reno, Nevada, Brooksbank figured she was destined for Broadway. While most her age were on the playground, she was busy with casino shows, doing dinner theater (and playing the harp) in vintage Hollywood glam. “It was entertainment or bust,” she recalls with a laugh. Later, she’d speedrun undergrad at USC and law school at Southwestern, finishing both in five years. Since then, she’s built a Hollywood résumé that includes stints at CAA, Donaldson Callif Perez and eOne. Now in her fifth year at Netflix, Brooksbank helps steer the streamer’s scripted series unit, striking deal after deal with TV’s biggest names. It’s a high volume affair, with Brooksbank managing a slate that includes The Altruists , Ransom Canyon and Sirens , among many others. “I’m the third child in a family of six,” she says of her negotiating chops. “They all have big personalities, so they prepared me well for Hollywood.” TALENT I’M DYING TO WORK WITH “Miss Piggy.” WHY ISN’T HOLLYWOOD TALKING ABOUT … “Women directors’ second and third films. We talk about breaking through, but what about career longevity?” BEST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “When I was considering law school, Patti Felker encouraged me to see being a woman as an advantage in negotiations, particularly the ability to read people, adapt and adjust your approach to the person across the table without losing sight of what you’re there to accomplish.” Barry Buren, 35 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion CAA, TV talent agent LOGLINE Makes deals for A-listers including Pedro Pascal, Matthew Rhys, Steven Yeun and Eddie Redmayne. THE ARC Hollywood has Orlando’s Central Florida Talent agency to thank for putting Buren on his path. After the New Jersey native graduated a semester early from nearby Rollins College, he picked up a gig at the model/talent agency to stay near friends who were still in school. Though he imagined he might become an engineer someday, he accepted an L.A.-based relative’s offer to live with her while giving Hollywood a try. As luck would have it, agenting stuck, and after a stint at Gersh, the avid golfer joined CAA in 2014. Today, the married rep is entrusted by actors including Josh Hartnett, Charlie Hunnam and Hannah Waddingham. Earlier this fall, client (and double Emmy winner) Rhys gave Buren a shout-out from the Emmy stage. MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Serving coffee to people in an order determined by seniority and annual earnings. It was my first introduction to the Hollywood hierarchy, and I learned very quickly that even caffeine has a pecking order.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “Being on a call with 15 people to schedule another call with 15 people, only to discover that the one person who actually needed to be there wasn’t invited.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Lorne Michaels. To have spent five decades at the intersection of comedy, culture, and discovering talent is pretty remarkable.” Winnie Carrillo Montiel, 35 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Amazon MGM, film executive, production & development LOGLINE Oversees films that range from bro-y actioners ( The Wrecking Crew ) to weepy love stories ( Honeymoon With Harry ). THE ARC Carrillo Montiel’s career in entertainment began with a clerical error. As an Emerson undergrad, she was mistakenly admitted as a screenwriting major instead of the literature and publishing program she had applied to. She ended up staying the course, eventually doubling down by attending graduate school at USC’s famed Peter Stark Producing Program. While there, she landed a temp job in MGM’s film group, which she did by day, leaving classes for night. Ultimately, it was the studio’s then-president Jonathan Glickman who helped push through the Guatemala City native’s visa sponsorship to land her her first full-time Hollywood gig. “He just made me promise that I wouldn’t get my green card and leave,” she remembers. “This was almost a decade ago and I’m still here. So, I really kept my promise.” Carrillo Montiel has since survived several regime changes, not to mention an acquisition, to land at her current spot on Amazon MGM’s film team, where she has overseen such films as The Sheep Detectives and an upcoming slate with projects from Dan Fogelman ( Honeymoon ) and Michael Showalter (a Serendipity reimagining). One of her proudest accomplishments is shepherding Angel Manuel Soto’s The Wrecking Crew , explaining, “Latinos are often put in a very specific box, and we are only hired to tell Latino-specific stories. I’m always looking for opportunities to elevate talent that I think are just great filmmakers.” IF I HAD A ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH FOR … “Unlimited budgets.” WORST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “I was advised to look for an American husband as I was told it would be impossible for me to earn a work visa in this industry.” MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Cold calling very specific animal experts in Russia and Brazil to attempt to track down recent sightings of extremely large species of bears and snakes.” Margaret Clark, 32 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion 20th Television, director of development LOGLINE Manages a roster of overall deals (Liz Meriwether, Drew Goddard) and development projects, including the Hulu hit Furious . THE ARC Technically speaking, Clark was discovered at the Panera on South Beverly Drive. At least, that’s where a guy from APA overheard her during an informational coffee with a fellow University of Virginia alum and offered to pass along her résumé to his agency mailroom. She was hired the following week. “I treated it like my grad school,” Clark says of her agency stint. By late 2017, the Virginia native and onetime theater kid had jumped to 20th Television, where she eventually found her way to Dana Walden’s desk for three pivotal years. In that time, she gained both a high-level education and a top-tier mentor. These days, Clark’s back on the 20th team, punching above her weight as she manages a slate of projects and the studio’s IP pipeline. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Jennifer Lopez in The Wedding Planner .” MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Buying a single old-fashioned donut for the CEO on Friday mornings. It had to be from Winchell’s. I wasn’t his assistant.” THE BEST PLACE FOR A COFFEE MEETING IS “The National Theater in London. Or the ABC Riverside Starbucks.” Sarah Colvin, 30 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Neon, VP acquisitions LOGLINE Keeps Neon supplied with art house favorites and horror standouts, including The Secret Agent , Leviticus and All of a Sudden . THE ARC Colvin spends a good chunk of her year traveling to Sundance, Berlin, SXSW, Cannes and beyond in the name of supplying Neon’s film slate with titles that will soon be Letterboxd’s new obsession (see: Oliver Laxe’s Sirāt and the long-awaited doc Once Upon a Time in Harlem ). Raised in New Mexico by artist parents, young Colvin would spend whatever free time she had with friends at Santa Fe’s one art house cinema. She laughs, “We thought we were so highbrow.” But she took that passion to NYU, where her professor, indie producer David Hinojosa, helped her land an internship at Neon, right as the then-upstart distributor was releasing its first success, I, Tonya . “There was no formal end date to the internship,” she says. “Eventually, Tom [Quinn] was like, ‘You should probably have a job here, then.’ ” FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “A blend of PeeWee Herman and Griffin Mill from The Player .” THE TALENT I’D KILL TO WORK WITH IS “Wile E Coyote.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “The great equalizer that is the valet stand after the Academy Awards.” Dylan Conklin, 34 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Entertainment 360, manager LOGLINE Guides the careers of clients like Kaia Gerber and Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story star Ella Beatty. THE ARC Conklin was studying international business in China for a summer when he realized the path wasn’t for him. Fortunately, a TV class with guests from Breaking Bad and Mad Men opened his eyes to a career in the entertainment field instead. Following a stint as an assistant to producer Tripp Vinson and some good advice from mentor attorney Howard Weitzman, he landed at 360 in 2016. A decade later, the dad of two has an impressive roster of talent clients, including Costa D’Angelo, for whom he’s lined up back-to-back shows ( East of Eden , The Sticks , We Were Liars ), and Ji-young Yoo, whose post- KPop Demon Hunters path includes a Paramount movie and Presumed Innocent season two. BEST ADVICE ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “Don’t chase hits. Champion exceptional artists, nurture their talent, and the hits will follow.” IT WAS FROM… “Mo Ostin.” THE TALENT I’D KILL TO WORK WITH IS “Danny DeVito.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “Making PB&J sandwiches in the office kitchen with Jennifer Garner.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH “Jerry Bruckheimer.” Kai Dolbashian, 33 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion 1.21, Film & TV development head LOGLINE Identified filmmaker Michael Shanks and helped develop Together from script to splashy Sundance sale. THE ARC While attending Chapman’s film school, Dolbashian landed an internship at MGM TV. The problem: The job was an hour away on a good day, and he had no car. Though he racked up credit card bills renting Zipcars, the bet paid off. He scored a post-grad gig and found a mentor in producer Andrew Mittman. And when Mittman launched his own banner in 2020, he was there on day one. Now, as the company’s head of film and TV development, Dolbashian has a slew of projects in development, including Warner Bros.’ remake of Attack of the 50 Foot Woman with Margot Robbie and Tim Burton. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Arno from Uncut Gems . We’re both impatient Armenians and both desperately want to do business with Adam Sandler.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “The first time I had lunch with Christoph Waltz, he cut and ate his strudel exactly the way his infamous character Hans Landa does in Inglourious Basterds . Thankfully, unlike Hans, Christoph is one of the nicest human beings.” TALENT I’M DYING TO WORK WITH “Bill Hader. There is literally no one else who could write and direct that epic motorcycle chase and shootout from season three of Barry , yet also perfectly embody the unhinged role of Officer Slater in Superbad. ” Carly Elter, 32 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Hidden Pictures, senior vp film and TV LOGLINE The architect behind The Housemaid is also behind lit-centric packages based on best-sellers from Rebecca Yarros and V. E. Schwab. THE ARC When Elter first walked into the house at the center of her 2025 movie The Housemaid , she cried. “It was such a surreal moment,” she says. “In my apartment, I read a book that I thought was a good idea for a movie, and now we have 100 people-plus employed making that movie.” Elter sold the film adaptation when it was self-published by author Freida McFadden; it would later land a publishing deal and sell 6 million copies, while the movie earned more than $400 million and quickly scored a sequel, which is in production. It’s not the married New Jersey native’s only claim to fame. While still an assistant — with stints at WME, Pascal Pictures and Mandeville — she also founded Women Wednesdays (now The Real Champions), where she’d screen films from women and nonbinary filmmakers for fellow assistants with the goal of getting the directors studio jobs. Later, Elter — who lives in Playa Vista with her husband and mutt Archie and also counts TV as a part of her remit with MGM+’s Robin Hood — started a mentorship program that’s helped place over 150 people into jobs. MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “Being approached by a famous actor on a red carpet who told me he was a huge fan of mine. Turns out he thought I was Alana Haim.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Amanda Seyfried. She has built a life where she makes incredible movies and TV shows and then goes home to her farm to hang out with goats and emus. She’s cracked the code.” BEST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “You have to work hard to build the version of Hollywood you want to be a part of.” IT WAS FROM “Sara Scott.” Anna Flickinger, 34 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion UTA, motion picture lit agent LOGLINE From Mary Beth Barone to Sterling Point producer Raffi Donatich, she gets funny women’s work to screen. THE ARC “I read these goddamn think pieces like, ‘Comedy’s dead,’ ” says Flickinger, whose response is often: “Really?! There’s always going to be a big theatrical comedy that gets people back in the seats.” She saw it happen firsthand when writer client Ilana Wolpert’s Anyone But You made over $200 million at the box office. Initially, the Chicago native and oldest of eight thought she’d pursue a career in politics, but after interning in the office of Sen. Dick Durbin (“loveliest man in America”) and a DC lobbying firm (“fucking depressing”), she realized her love of The West Wing was more about an interest in entertainment than government. After temping her way around L.A., she landed at UTA, where she ultimately found a home in the motion picture lit group. Now, Flickinger, who lives with her husband and their Rottweiler and Chihuahua, guides clients like Sammi Cohen ( You Are So Not Invited to My Bar Mitzvah ) and Barone, who’s writing and starring in her own rom-com. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “C.J. Cregg sun, Josh Lyman rising, Toby Ziegler moon.” IF I HAD A ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH FOR … “The public transit infrastructure of New York in L.A.” WHY ISN’T HOLLYWOOD TALKING ABOUT … “Why it takes women making their first, second, third and fourth movie to get the compensation and resources that men get to make their second movie.” Carly Frankel, 32 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion WME, digital agent LOGLINE Brokers deals for top podcasts, including Giggly Squad’s nine-figure pact with SiriusXM. THE ARC An L.A. native, Frankel got an early taste of agency life while booking comedy shows, including Chelsea Peretti’s, as an undergrad at UC Berkeley. It led to an assistant gig in UTA’s comedy touring department, then another at then-podcasting startup Wondery. But after greenlighting Wondery shows including Baby, This Is Keke Palmer , Frankel was called back to the agency side at WME, where she’s helped Maria Sharapova launch a podcast with Vox Media and brokered Tinx’s deal with SiriusXM and Dr. Mary Claire Haver’s deal with Audacy. As more and more people consider starting a podcast, Frankel advises talent about the hard work required, including recording a minimum of 45 episodes a year. “I think the number one thing is someone who is genuinely enthusiastic about it,” she said. MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Chasing comedians down Melrose to introduce myself after their stand-up sets. Saying hi on behalf of the agency was my cardio.” THE BEST PLACE FOR A COFFEE MEETING IS “Truly anywhere that offers a 16-ounce cup. The ‘default 10-ounce latte’ trend is killing me.” BEST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “Your reputation is your greatest currency. Work hard and be kind.” Katie Giarla, 35 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Cut To, founding member/partner LOGLINE Building a slate of hot projects, including the upcoming Elle Fanning-Nicole Kidman legal thriller Discretion , for the A24-based company. THE ARC Raised by a psychologist and a lawyer in Pittsburgh, Giarla’s only link to the entertainment business was her childhood birthday parties at the local movie theater. “I thought I’d be a lawyer,” she says, “and then I did some internships in law and realized I could make money and I would hate my life.” Upon graduating from University of Pennsylvania, Giarla parlayed her love of reading into a gig in the books department at WME. The trouble, she’d soon learn, was that she was more interested in the books than the dealmaking. So, she shifted groups before segueing to Endeavor Content (later, Fifth Season), where she championed projects including East of Eden as a series for Netflix. Giarla would later jump with boss Joe Hipps to Cut To, a red-hot company that will soon have more shows than executives. Among its recent sales, all of which prompted frenzied bidding wars: the Joel Edgerton-led crime drama Trigger Point and a two-season order for a Gwyneth Paltrow drama. At press time, however, Giarla was more focused on her other major project, her newborn son, with whom she’s now home on maternity leave. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Lady Olenna Tyrell. I’ve been rewatching GoT on maternity leave. She’s inquisitive, sharp-tongued and loyal to a fault.“ MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “When I realized there was a typo on a deck that my boss was en route to present to Obama — at the White House. That was a crazy two hours.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH “Andy Cohen. The writers’ strike was in full swing when Scandoval hit, which gave me way too much downtime to stumble into the Bravoverse.” Jordan Gorelick, 34 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion UTA, talent agent LOGLINE Steers the career of rising stars Odessa A’zion and Alien: Earth lead Sydney Chandler. THE ARC As an undergrad at Colgate, Gorelick had his sights set on a career in screenwriting. The dream shifted, however, once he stumbled upon HBO’s Hollywood show Entourage and David Rensin’s book The Mailroom: Hollywood History From the Bottom Up . Suddenly, agenting was the goal, which led to an early gig in UTA’s mailroom. It was everything Gorelick had hoped for: “Watching the agents, the intensity, being a 21-year-old kid and driving around Hollywood and seeing the billboards on the Sunset Strip — I loved being in it.” Eleven years on, he’s constructing a list of rising stars (Nicholas Braun, Ray Nicholson, Lili Reinhart) and helping craft the next stage for established actors (Lizzy Caplan, Adam Scott, Timothy Olyphant, Paul Bettany). He feels his abandoned writing ambitions are actually key to his success. “The way I analyze and interpret and discuss material, that comes from a writer’s perspective and has set me apart in the way I work with actors.” FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Kevin McCallister eating that cheese pizza in the stretch limo.” TALENT I’M DYING TO WORK WITH “Buddy from Air Bud .” MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Driving a young Chalamet to general meetings.” Angie Haney, 31 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Netflix, director, film LOGLINE Supplies Netflix with rom-com hits like Voicemails From Isabelle and People We Meet on Vacation . THE ARC Haney was outside the Vatican on vacation when she saw two girls filming themselves doing a choreographed dance featured in her latest movie, Voicemails for Isabelle. “I was like, ‘There’s no way that’s what they’re doing!’” She approached the girls in St. Peter’s Square and that was exactly what they were doing. While Haney is now Netflix’s romantic comedy whisperer, she grew up envisioning a career in politics. In high school, the L.A. native and future Columbia poli-sci major was a congressional intern for outgoing L.A. Mayor Karen Bass. But a series of entertainment internships — not to mention a childhood watching classics like Singin’ in the Rain with her voiceover actress mom, theater director dad and screenwriter twin brother — prompted a change of heart. After a cold email led to a stint at Disney, she landed a job as the assistant to then-Lucasfilm head Kathleen Kennedy as the Star Wars series were starting to populate Disney+. She’d later jump to Netflix, where she has found success with rom-coms and coming-of-age films. Up next: a reimagining of 13 Going on 30 . “I’ve heard it said before that we should all make movies for our 12-year-old self,” she says, “And that is very true for me.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE EVER HAD “Watching George Lucas meet Grogu on the set of The Mandalorian .” IF I HAD A ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH FOR “Nora Ephron to have written 20 more movies.” Louie Hayes, 35 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion LuckyChap, vp TV LOGLINE The on-set producer for the summer smash Sterling Point . THE ARC Hayes’ family moved half a dozen times before he left for college. The constant in his home growing up was TV, which he claims he watched “an unhealthy amount of.” Eager to put down roots after graduating from Northwestern, he settled in L.A. with some college buddies. “At the time, everyone started at a talent agency,” he says, so he dutifully lined up a gig at Gersh. And while agenting wasn’t Hayes’ calling, it was there that he’d meet his future wife (and fellow Next Gen honoree), Samantha Militante, who’d later follow him to FX. But after nearly a decade as a buyer — working on hits like Dave and Alien: Earth — he jumped to LuckyChap, where he’s built an impressive roster. In fact, one of Hayes’ very first projects at the uber-successful Margot Robbie outfit was the runaway hit Sterling Point, which he was intimately involved with every step of the way. Up next: series Sex Criminals , from Kumail Nanjiani and Emily Gordon, and an adaptation of The Retrievals from Molly Smith Metzler. PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Jeff Probst. I consider Survivor America’s fifth major sport, and I have some ideas.” FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Arnold from Hey Arnold! An idealist with an oversized head and a compulsive need to help.” WORST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “Don’t date anyone in the industry. My wife is on this list.” Julia Iglesias, 34 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Focus Features, VP LOGLINE Shepherds artistic films including Sense and Sensibility and Nosferatu , along with the upcoming Werwulf and the adaptation of The Bell Jar . THE ARC Growing up in South Florida, Iglesias would regularly make her little sister act in her home movies. It wasn’t until she landed at Boston University that she learned how to turn her passion for storytelling into a career. “I did tons of internships,” she says, “and took all of the screenwriting and production classes I could get my hands on.” After a brief, post-grad stint as an unscripted postproduction coordinator at Relativity Media, she landed at NBCUniversal. A job working for then-Universal Filmed Entertainment Group chairman Jeff Shell turned into a gig at Focus Features, where Iglesias has been ever since. Now, the newly engaged exec — her fiancé proposed at this year’s Sundance Film Festival — cherishes seeing projects through to the end with auteurs like Sarah Polley and Robert Eggers. BEST ADVICE ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “Pick your boss, not your job.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “The dog handler on Sense and Sensibility .” THE BEST PLACE FOR A COFFEE MEETING IS “Somewhere neither person has to valet.” Ben Iguchi, 32 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Netflix, manager, original series, live-action comedy LOGLINE Champions buzzy comedies including Cobra Kai and Doozer Productions’ upcoming I Suck at Girls and Nick Kroll’s A Hundred Percent for Netflix. THE ARC Iguchi can’t remember a time when comedy wasn’t a central focus in his life. As he tells it, his Ph.D. dad had proposed to his dancer mom during an episode of The Golden Girls , and every memory in his childhood home seems to feature a sitcom of some kind. In fact, by the time Iguchi turned 13, Jewish comedy became his bar mitzvah theme. “It definitely was not cool,” he jokes as he recounts the Groucho Marx glasses with the mustache that adorned every table. Still, the L.A. native turned up at Georgetown thinking finance would be his path, a plan he swiftly abandoned once a career in comedy presented itself as a viable option. An early gig at APA led to a brief stint at Mosaic and, later, to Netflix, where he’s risen over the past eight years. In that time, he’s become known for his ingenuity, with more than one producer sharing projects that began as Iguchi ideas. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Ronnie from ‘Summer Loving.’ I’m just here for the zipline.” TALENT I’D DIE TO WORK WITH “Tyler the Creator, Matt Stone & Trey Parker, and Carlos Alcaraz (my backhand could really use some help).” WHY ISN’T HOLLYWOOD TALKING ABOUT … “Picking up and moving to Santa Monica. It’s time we stop pretending the Eastside is better than the West.” Kendall Jackson, 34 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion JSSK, associate LOGLINE Assists with Oscar winners like Michael B. Jordan and Daniel Kaluuya, while dealmaking for up-and-comers like PinkPantheress. THE ARC While Jackson helps shepherd big deals for A-list talent (see: Jordan directing The Thomas Crown Affair remake or Yahya Abdul-Mateen II’s Emmy-nominated turn in Wonder Man ), she jokes that she’s recognized in Hollywood circles almost as frequently for her Philadelphia Eagles fandom. “It’s a huge part of my personality,” she says of her hometown team, which she recently flew to London to see, a fact that has gotten brought up in a negotiation or two. Back in L.A., the Columbia Law School grad has been busy building out her own client list, which now includes pop star PinkPantheress, who will make her acting debut in the Daniels’ Universal event film, and negoitating Kaluuya’s return the big screen in A24 and Chris Rock’s Misty Green . PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Law Roach.” FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Joan from Girlfriends or Molly from Insecure . Not only because they are Black female lawyers in L.A., but because they are the ‘responsible friend’ but still going through it in their personal lives.” MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Getting a client out of jury duty, which now feels like such small potatoes.” TALENT I’M DYING TO WORK WITH “Teyana Taylor. She’s amazing, multi-talented, stylish, funny, and her star is only going up! I’ve been following her since My Super Sweet 16 .” Adam Klein, 34 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Untitled, manager LOGLINE Genre whisperer who counts Smile ’s Parker Finn as an early client. THE ARC When Klein shifted from WME assistant to a gig at upstart Grandview, he focused on finding hot genre short filmmakers ready for the next step. After getting promoted to manager, one of the Michigan native’s first signings was Finn, whom he helped sell what would blossom into the Smile franchise ($350 million globally). He also guided Finn to a first-look at Paramount, where the director is now in post on his Possession remake. Other clients signed by Klein, who’s engaged to a manager at Range, include Together ’s Michael Shanks (in post on the Daniel Kaluuya starrer Hotel Hotel Hotel Hotel ), emerging YouTube horror filmmaker Sam Evenson, Argentinian filmmaker Demián Rugna ( When Evil Lurks ) and David Bruckner, who was recently tapped to helm Smile 3 . FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “I think I oscillate between Josh Lyman and Toby Ziegler from The West Wing .” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “I’d take Mike De Luca for a spin.” TALENT I’D DIE TO WORK WITH “Tom Cruise.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE EVER HAD “Meeting my fiancée, Lauren, at the CAA Sundance Party.” IF I HAD A ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH FOR “Detroit Lions Super Bowl. I’m not sure if Curry can deliver that.” Tim Kressman, 35 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Gersh, motion picture lit and production agent LOGLINE Reps Oscar-winning below-the-line talent and international directors. THE ARC In high school, Kressman was known as both a marching band drum major and a major film buff who devoured the Blu-ray special features for Peter Jackson’s Lord of the Rings movies. These taught him that behind the glitz and glamor of Hollywood were craftspeople who made it all happen. After Yale, where he was president of the film society and conducted the pops orchestra, he found his way to Gersh as David Gersh’s assistant. There, he has carved out a niche repping Oscar-worthy below-the-line talent, meaning the film geek in him gets to have 20 conversations a day about different aspects of production. He’s now a perennial Oscar and Emmy attendee, with clients including production designer Shona Heath (Oscar winner for Poor Things ), Charles Wood (in the race for designing Project Hail Mary ) and visual effects supervisor Michael Ralla (nominated for Sinners ). He also signs international directors and brings them to Hollywood, as he did with Kenji Tanigaki, director of the acclaimed action hit The Furious, and Venice Golden Lion winner Tran Anh Hung ( The Taste of Things ). PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Joe Hisaishi, so I could conduct the world’s best orchestras with his incredible music.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE EVER HAD “Going backstage at the Oscars when Shona Heath won for her extraordinary production design in Poor Things and later introducing her to LeBron James with Oscar in hand.” BEST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “Always listen to advice with an open mind, but make your experiences your own and find out for yourself.” IT WAS FROM … “My mom, who has never worked in Hollywood.” IF I HAD A ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH FOR … “Costume designer Shawna Trpcic to have seen the moment when she posthumously won the Emmy for Ahsoka , which was a lifelong dream of hers.” Albert Lee, 35 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion CAA, motion picture lit agent LOGLINE Train Dreams and Sing Sing filmmakers Clint Bentley and Greg Kwedar and Heated Rivalry breakout Connor Storrie look to Lee for their filmmaking deals. THE ARC Growing up in a working-class neighborhood of L.A., Lee’s early exposure to film was strictly via VHS tapes at his grandmother’s — or what he borrowed from the library. Ironically, it wasn’t until he arrived at Harvard, where he was studying biology, that he got serious about filmmaking as a potential profession. At first, he was taking film electives in between science courses because, he reasoned, they’d be easier than reading textbooks. “Spoiler alert: They weren’t,” says Lee. He did, however, get the bug, which led him to production work on everything from car commercials to a Kurt Cobain documentary. By 2015, Lee started at CAA as an intern the week of the Sundance Film Festival, where he’s now a regular. These days, he works on the agency’s biggest lit clients, from Chloé Zhao to LuckyChap, but he’s really made a name for himself moving indie directors to bigger projects that let them retain their artistic sensibilities, as he did recently with Georgia Oakley, who went from Venice standout Blue Jean to Focus’ Sense and Sensibility . FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Depending on the day, Remy from Ratatouille , Lucille Bluth or Maya Ishii-Peters.” MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Getting an early read of Drive as it headed into production. Not a bad start for an unpaid intern at an international sales company.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE EVER HAD “Belting karaoke in the wee hours of a party to an empty room … empty except for Madonna trying to have a quiet conversation and, I can only assume, wishing we’d stop.” Jeremy Lowe, 34 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Dick Clark Productions, vp talent and partnerships LOGLINE Books talent (for the red carpet and the stage) at major TV events and award shows. THE ARC For more than a decade, Lowe has worked New Year’s Eve, though he’s doing so from a prime seat — at the center of the action in Times Square. Through his role at DCP, the Boston University grad has helped book major performers, including Sabrina Carpenter on the heels of Taylor Swift’s Eras tour and Druski as the Chicago co-host for this year, for the iconic holiday celebration. During his 12 years, the onetime intern has had a keen eye for artists on the rise (he booked Raye for the 50th anniversary special of the American Music Awards).
