He’s also continued to work on social and digital strategies, including revitalizing the red carpet for major events like the Golden Globes, where he’s booked Chicken Shop ’s Amelia Dimoldenberg and Recess Therapy ’s Julian Shapiro-Barnum. “I very much feel a responsibility as somebody who works at a company that’s been around for 50-plus years to bring these younger, very of the moment, creator-driven talent to our shows and to meaningfully involve them,” says Lowe. MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE EVER HAD “Answering the phone and it’s Diana Ross, asking me a question about her New Year’s Rockin’ Eve performance.” MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Live posting on the American Music Awards Twitter account in 2009, on my first-generation iPhone, from a seat in the auditorium.” TALENT I’D DIE TO WORK WITH “Rihanna.” Mitch Mason, 34 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Untitled, manager LOGLINE Guides the careers of stars like Hunter Schafer and The White Lotus ’ Charlie Hall. THE ARC The Pittsburgh native had his sights on a career in broadcast news until a chance meeting with a manager during an internship at the American Pavilion at the Cannes Film Festival put him on a different path. After a successful PowerPoint presentation convinced Mason’s very skeptical father to let him move to L.A. — yes, one slide had his face on the Hollywood sign — he began with an internship at Untitled, where he’s largely remained for 12 years. In 2023, Mason relocated to New York, where he’s busy navigating the careers of talent like Schafer, who will star in Blade Runner 2099 and an untitled A24 horror movie, and Poorna Jagannathan, who became a key player on HBO’s Lanterns . FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH … “Jimmy LuSaque Jr. from Hacks .” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Mariska Hargitay.” IF I HAD A ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH FOR … “The Lizzie McGuire reboot but made just for adults.” WHY ISN’T HOLLYWOOD TALKING ABOUT … “Making comedies funny again.” Andrea Massaro, 33 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Goddard Textiles, VP LOGLINE Produces High Potential , Phony and the upcoming Pagans at Drew Goddard’s prolific production company. THE ARC “I feel like my whole story is just a lot of people telling me that I’d be good at this until I believed them,” says Massaro, who admits she needed the boost. First, it was a digital video teacher at her arts vocational high school on the Jersey Shore who saw talent and encouraged her to study film. Then a professor at Johns Hopkins said she’d make a great producer. To Massaro’s credit, she listened, which led her to UCLA’s Producers Program and eventually to a gig as If Beale Street Could Talk producer Sarah Esberg’s assistant at Plan B. Seven years later, the duo is still together, now at Goddard Textiles, where Massaro is making her mark. In fact, she was the first person to send the French format that inspired ABC’s hit series High Potential to Goddard, who went on to direct the pilot (Massaro produces). Now, she’s working on Pagans , the Steven Yeun-led supernatural drama series that sparked a major bidding war won by Netflix. When she’s off the clock, Massaro’s often either walking her golden retriever or baking. TALENT I’D DIE TO WORK WITH “Zach Cregger or Megan Park.” FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Carl from Up , for many reasons but most importantly because I also have an adopted golden retriever obsessed with squirrels like Dug.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE EVER HAD “Bringing my dad to the Porject Hail Mary premiere and getting a photo of him standing next to the back of Ryan Gosling’s head.” WHY ISN’T HOLLYWOOD TALKING ABOUT … “How female executives throughout both film and TV are being pushed out of decision-making roles.” Erick Mendoza, 33 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Untitled, manager LOGLINE In early on writers and filmmakers like Primetime ’s Ajon Singh and Lurker ’s Alex Russell. THE ARC In high school, Mendoza spent an hour on the 405 each way from his home in Inglewood to Brentwood School as part of the Young Eisner Scholars program that helps place talented kids from around L.A. at elite private schools. There, he learned Hollywood was a career path, as many of the school’s parents were agents, lawyers and execs, including Dawn Ostroff, then head of The CW, where he interned. USC and the UTA mailroom came next before he settled at management firm Grandview. “My first day, I’m building my desk from an Amazon box, but also got to attend the big staff meeting,” he recalls. Lurker ’s Russell was an early client (he won two Indie Spirits this year). His list also includes Kalos Chu, a former DreamWorks Animation assistant who sold the elite university pitch Imposter to HBO in a bidding war. Mendoza was also behind The Waffle House Index ’s splashy sale to Apple from Andrew Nunnelly, with Inde Navarrette starring. And Ajon Singh hit it big with his spec Primetime , which became the A24 movie starring Robert Pattinson. MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE EVER HAD “ Curb Your Enthusiasm , season nine, episode nine. I’m somewhere in the background.” TALENT I’D DIE TO WORK WITH “Alex Garland.” MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Sorting through fan mail for the Vampire Diaries cast. People sent some gnarly stuff.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D LOVE TO TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “CEO of LEGO … my nephews would find that very cool.” Samantha Militante, 34 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion FX, vp current series LOGLINE Guides FX series including Adults to a bigger and far buzzier season two. THE ARC Militante’s love of TV began with Filipino soap operas, which she spent her Orange County childhood devouring with her mom and grandma. Initially, it was a way to learn their language. “Then I just fell in love with the bonkers storytelling,” she says, following that passion all the way to Chapman, where she got her film school degree in three years and managed to squeeze in roughly 10 internships in the process. “It was aggressive,” she jokes, but it set her on a path, ultimately landing at Gersh, where she’d meet her future husband (and fellow Next Gen honoree) Louie Hayes. In fact, it was Hayes who first jumped to FX and later put Militante, then just his friend, up for a job. In the decade since, she’s been intimately involved in projects like Reservation Dogs , What We Do in the Shadows and the zoomer hit Adults . Despite her “current” executive title, the self-proclaimed foodie has also, at various points, been deployed to develop new shows, oversee a doc slate and work with short-form content. MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “When the stand-in on a Wendy’s shoot called in sick, I was the only brown person on set, so naturally I got promoted from PA. Ate a lot of hamburgers that day. No spit bucket.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE EVER HAD “Riding a private jet for the first time to go to a film festival. Also, getting on this list with my husband.” WORST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “There is such a thing as stupid questions.” IT WAS FROM … “My internship supervisor when I asked about my pay.” Sam Rabinowitz, 33 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion WME, talent agent LOGLINE Confidant of A-listers Teyana Taylor, Austin Butler, Nicolas Cage and Dwayne Johnson. THE ARC Rabinowitz’s early education in the art of the cold call came from a college-era internship selling life insurance for Northwestern Mutual. “It was amazing prep for this whole business because it’s just rejection every day,” says the Cornell grad, who entered Hollywood via another internship (at Paradigm) before ultimately landing in the WME mailroom and working his way up to assistant, going into the office seven days a week. In those days, the Rochester, New York, native lived so cheaply that he didn’t have Wi-Fi at his apartment, and would go to a nearby Starbucks for Wi-Fi so that he could stream shows like Dwayne Johnson’s Ballers . Now, Rabinowitz is on Johnson’s team, as he is for Taylor (who just directed her first movie, Paramount’s Get Lite ), Butler (filming Joe Kosinski’s Miami Vice ’85 ) and Cage (starring in the next season of True Detective ). In recent years, he also signed Dave Bautista, now starring in Amazon’s God of War , and helped Will Poulter go from well-regarded actor to TV producer on Apple’s Beat the Reaper . His roster also includes Lukas Gage, who just wrapped on the Prison Break revival , and Michael Gandolfini , who just shot a role in Daniels’ untitled Universal movie. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “George Costanza.” MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Getting a Vitamin D deficiency from spending every hour of daylight in the mailroom.” THE BEST PLACE FOR A COFFEE MEETING IS “The Fountain Room.” BEST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “It’s a relationship business.” Claudia Shin, 33 Image Credit: Courtesy of Subject Chum Films, senior vp film and TV LOGLINE Guides projects including Emmy darling Widow’s Bay for Hiro Murai’s busy production shingle. THE ARC How did a biomedical engineering major at Yale end up at one of Hollywood’s coolest production companies? For Shin, the story began with the Spike Jonze film Her . The 2013 movie inspired the Pasadena native to take a film class. Before long, she was taking on a second major in film and, later, landing a gig in UTA’s mailroom. “I thought I’d just start it off in Hollywood, and then really one job led to another and I never left,” she says. While working at Paramount TV Studios, she reconnected with Atlanta director-producer Murai, a client of a former UTA boss, and they hit it off. When Murai launched his first production company, Super Frog, Shin was his first hire. She’s worked with Murai ever since (now at his Chum Films), through season one of Amazon Prime’s Mr. & Mrs. Smith to FX’s The Bear and Apple’s Widow’s Bay , which Shin produced. When she’s not on set, you can find her taking coffee meetings at her climbing gym, doing karaoke in Koreatown or traveling the world with her partner. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Calvin from Calvin and Hobbes .” IF I HAD ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH FOR … “Teleportation powers, so that I can be on set and sleep in my own bed.” Alix Taylor, 33 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Gloria Sanchez, head of TV LOGLINE Oversees a slate of nearly a dozen upcoming projects, including adaptations of Dream State and Prep . THE ARC Raised two blocks from her public library in Atlanta, Taylor was a self-proclaimed “psychotic reader.” In fact, she says, “We’d joke that when my mom was working, she’d drop me there and that was my day care.” Fittingly, she became a comparative literature major at Brown, though Taylor thought she, like her mom, would ultimately pursue a career in the art world. There were a few internships and early gigs, but in the end, Hollywood proved more alluring. After a quick stint with producer Nathan Kahane, Taylor found her way to Amazon’s comedy team, where she worked on series like Undone , Modern Love and Overcompensating before jumping to Will Ferrell’s company to run the TV division three and a half years ago. She’s since built a considerable slate, with projects in various stages of development, including several adaptations and one idea loosely inspired by Taylor’s time interning at Christie’s. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Jane from Broadcast News — but not in a depressing way.” MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Spending every Friday afternoon at my boss’ house turning on and off all the lights to check for burned-out bulbs.” IF I HAD A ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH FOR … “Dramaturgically, this feels like a trap.” Christian Vazquez, 30 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Indie producer LOGLINE Lance Oppenheim’s right hand on You Can See Everything and Primetime . THE ARC If you were a firefighter in the mid-aughts and flashed your badge at Long Beach’s Regal movie theater, they’d usher you in for free. Such was the experience of Vazquez and his two siblings thanks to their firefighter dad, an immigrant from Mexico. Vazquez was a driven student and track athlete, and ultimately made his way to Harvard, where he met Oppenheim, who asked for his help producing his senior thesis film. That film became the Sundance darling Some Kind of Heaven , about the Villages retirement community in Florida. Spermworld and the HBO docuseries Ren Faire followed, but nothing compares to this year’s Elizabeth Holmes doc, a box office hit and an Oscar contender. The latter came just weeks after their first narrative feature, the Robert Pattinson starrer Primetime . Vazquez, a hands-on producer who never misses a day on set, has been out of town working on HBO’s Neighbors for the rollout of both films. His firefighter dad (now retired) has attended the premieres in his place, and has been introducing himself to talent, including Nathan Fielder. TALENT I’M DYING TO WORK WITH “Danny McBride.” BEST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “Never ask someone to do something you wouldn’t do yourself.” FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Shelley ‘The Machine’ Levene.” Allie Veneris, 34 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Brillstein, manager LOGLINE Navigating the careers of Cara Delevingne, whom she put in Club Kid , as well as Phil Dunster and Reacher spinoff star Maria Sten. THE ARC The Huntington Beach native grew up as a sports enthusiast who loved softball and golf. She studied film editing at Boulder before a friend suggested becoming a rep: “I was way too extroverted to be an editor,” she says with a laugh. The revelation led to an internship at Brillstein and then stints at Gersh, 360 and Authentic. Amid the strikes, she returned to Brillstein and has leaned into a personal passion for music and sports. The latter space fueled recent wins, like Sophie Nélisse booking Heated Rivalry a month after Veneris set up a general with creator Jacob Tierney. Ted Lasso breakout Dunster — Veneris’ frequent companion for Dodgers and Arsenal games — is not only joining the How to Train Your Dragon live-action franchise but has moved into writing and producing, as has longtime client Jessica Rothe, who leads the TIFF horror favorite River . Thanks to her obsession with online trends, Veneris jumped to work with gymnast-turned-content creator Livvy Dunne — making her acting debut on Fox’s Baywatch reboot — and would not rest until Cara Delevingne landed Club Kid , the Cannes sensation from former viral comedian Jordan Firstman. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “A mix of Liz Lemon ( 30 Rock ), Sutton Brady ( The Bold Type ) and Jimmy from Hacks .” IF I HAD ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH … “To have the attention span of someone who has never heard of TikTok.” TALENT I’M DYING TO WORK WITH “Kristen Stewart … and any or all members of Blackpink.” Paige Wandling, 33 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Range, manager LOGLINE Reps hot TV talent Shailene Woodley and Fallout ’s Ella Purnell. THE ARC A hostessing gig at a small Malibu restaurant gave Wandling her earliest brushes with Hollywood notables. “If I thought they could be someone, I would Google them,” she says. “Oh! That’s David Ellison. Oh my God, that’s Nicole Avant and Ted Sarandos.” The Pepperdine grad would have many more such brushes when she moved from ID PR to CAA, where she worked for David Bugliari, whom she’d later follow to Range. After getting a tip from an assistant friend that Woodley had parted ways with her manager, she spent the next year working sources for intel that could woo the actress. One such piece of intel paid off when she learned an actress had dropped out of Michael Mann’s Ferrari . Wandling helped coordinate a meeting between the actress and the filmmaker. Woodley got the part and signed with Range, with Wandling attending the Emmys this to watch her client win for Paradise . The Minneapolis native and former competitive dancer has also guided the careers of Purnell, Gabrielle Union and Furious star Lola Petticrew, who landed the co-lead in the upcoming Assassin’s Creed . MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Finding six dozen sunflowers the Saturday before Oscars Sunday for a client who wanted to decorate a fellow nominee’s hotel room with them.” BEST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “The most important thing about any job in representation is to ‘anticipate the need.'” IT WAS FROM … “Publicist Leah Chang.” Caroline Warner, 33 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Apple TV, domestic programming executive LOGLINE Supports some of the streamer’s most ambitious TV bets, from Ascension to Disclaimer . THE ARC “I’ve always been obsessed with TV,” says Warner, who received a script from Charmed for her 10th birthday. The New York native parlayed that passion into a series of internships — at Katie Couric’s short-lived talk show, Piers Morgan Live and at Showtime — while still at Yale and, later, a post-grad gig in the WME mailroom. But after a job at Chernin, she was debating a career pivot, beginning with business school. It was her dad who advised her to try one more gig before deciding. That job was at Apple TV+, where Warner was the fourth-ever hire. Rising through the ranks, she’s now working with Alfonso Cuarón for the second time on his upcoming series Ascension and, already mother to a rescue dog named Winston, is expecting her first child. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Dream: Rory Gilmore. Reality: Paris Geller.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “I feel like this is a cliche but I’d be lying if I said anyone other than Jeff Probst!” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “I had to babysit a puppet for four days on my first business trip. It was awesome.” This story appears in the Nov. 12 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

articles.title: Entertainment 360 Buys Influencer Firm Brigade As It Expands In Creator Economy
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All November 11, 2026 7:04am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'How Long Gone' podcasters Jason Stewart and Chris Black are among Brigade's clients. Roger Kisby/Getty Images Entertainment 360 has accelerated its drive into the creator economy by acquiring Brigade, the creative management firm focused on digital talent. Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but the acquisition brings elite digital tastemakers, including Substack writers, podcasters and influencers, to the Los Angeles-based talent management company run by a collective of partners as it moves beyond traditional film and TV representation. Brigade founder Max Stein will become a partner at Entertainment 360 and bring his team and clients with him to help the combined company tap a growing influencer universe and manage and monetize celebrity creators coveted by brand marketers. “The ways audiences discover and engage with entertainment have changed, and so have the needs of the talent building careers today,” the Entertainment 360 partners said in a statement. “Max recognized this evolution early and he and his exceptional team have built a remarkable business representing exactly the kind of original, forward-thinking talent we have always sought to work with. Bringing Brigade into 360 expands what we can offer our clients and strengthens our ability to create extraordinary opportunities for artists across an increasingly diverse entertainment landscape.” Entertainment 360 will look to Brigade to help sign digital talent fostered by Stein and others to brand deals and partnerships, and new business opportunities in publishing, podcasts and traditional media. “I’ve always been drawn to people with a singular point of view, whose work and ambitions don’t fit neatly into one category,” said Stein in his own statement. “Our clients have built remarkable careers by following their own taste and instincts, and our job has been to help them turn those ideas into lasting businesses. Entertainment 360 shares that philosophy and brings an extraordinary depth of experience, relationships, and resources. Joining forces gives our clients access to many more opportunities, while allowing us to preserve the personal approach that has always defined Brigade.” The Brigade acquisition comes as YouTube stars, podcasters and other digital creators increasingly rise to the fore in Hollywood and a fast-shifting entertainment ecosystem. Brigade’s clients include fashion writer Leandra Medine Cohen; Feed Me

articles.title: Peacock Overhauls Mobile App for Vertical Video Era in Effort to “Win Another Hour Per User, Per Month”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All November 11, 2026 8:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Peacock Peacock mobile users might want to check their app store for updates — the NBCUniversal streaming platform is undergoing its largest mobile revamp ever. Peacock mobile 2.0 (it’s probably well beyond 2.0, but stick with us here) is designed to, in part, “win another hour per user, per month,” Matt Strauss , chairman of NBCUniversal Media Group, told a small group of reporters including The Hollywood Reporter on Tuesday. Peacock has been profitable for two straight quarters now, and it’s part of Strauss’s job to keep it that way. To accomplish that reasonable-sounding goal, NBCU is overhauling Peacock’s smartphone display and functionality for the vertical video craze, which it boasts as having been early money on, as well as the Comcast entertainment brand’s fandoms and its sports content. Peacock users who use the app on both their TV and smartphone double the engagement of those who only sign in on their television. As John Jelley, the group’s senior vice president of product and UX (user experience), sees it, today’s opportunity is on the smaller of the two screens. “Every streamer today is really a sea of sameness on the homepage. Because they’ve taken a TV experience and largely ported it over, they are expecting the user to do the sorting,” Jelley said. “We see an opportunity to recognize what a fan is trying to accomplish in that session and make the next most useful action easier to find.” “We recognize that we have to start thinking of ourselves less as a streaming platform and more of an entertainment platform,” Strauss said. “How do we super serve our franchises and our fandoms where the best experience is on our app?” To those ends, “conversational AI search” will help users find what they want even if they don’t know how to directly express it. Short clips that lead to full episodes will expedite and elongate engagement, and franchise/fandom hubs can be a one-stop shop for fans of the Bravo-verse, for one standout example. There will also be games (like Law & Order: Clue Hunter and Public Eye ) and a membership program “giving eligible subscribers exclusive rewards, benefits and activities tied to the movies and shows they enjoy,” per the official announcement. One particularly cool idea is adaptive live viewing. Peacock plans to expand its live vertical video tests to The Voice live simulcasts, NCAA basketball games and, in a clear direct response to the rise of YouTube Golf, you guessed it: golf. A “dynamic video player” will switch between vertical and horizontal video playback automatically depending on the device orientation, keeping key action in frame. NBA games will soon get the same treatment, with “easy access to player stats” and “deeper game information sitting directly underneath the live feed in a dual screen view,” the executives say. Finally, these days, you cannot talk about vertical video without discussing microdramas . Jelley discusses them frankly, because he says that’s how his users speak about them. “When we talk to users about microdramas, they’re not embarrassed by them. They don’t feel that they’re something they’ll just do in private,” Jelley said. “They’re watching them at home at different moments of the day, they’re watching them on the commute. We are very committed to premium long-form content, and that has a massive place not only on the phone, but also on TV. But this is really another modality.” THR

articles.title: ‘The Good Daughter’ Review: Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy Elevate Peacock’s Overly Familiar Southern-Fried Thriller
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Daniel Fienberg Plus Icon Daniel Fienberg Chief Television Critic TheFienPrint Follow Sign Up View All November 11, 2026 8:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Meghann Fahy (left) and Rose Byrne in ‘The Good Daughter.' Mark Hill/PEACOCK Logo text We all have our television pet peeves and, for me, red flags abound in Peacock ‘s new limited series, The Good Daughter . Adapted by Karin Slaughter from her book of the same name, The Good Daughter is interchangeable, in terms of title, plot or structure, with a dozen recent limited series — most conspicuously, Amazon’s The Better Sister and Netflix’s His & Hers . The Good Daughter The Bottom Line A strong cast makes up for familiar irritations. Airdate: Thursday, November 12 (Peacock) Cast: Rose Byrne, Meghann Fahy, Brendan Gleeson, Olivia Williams, Harper Steele, Michael Dorman, Audrey Grace Marshall, Drew Cheek Creator: Karin Slaughter Director: Steph Green It’s a story set in and filmed in the Deep South, but its central cast is populated by actors from Australia, Ireland, Massachusetts and basically anywhere other than the Deep South, leading to a succotash of colorful and, to put it politely, inconsistent accents. Related Stories TV 'O.J.'s Accomplice' Has Its Own 'The Jinx' Hot Mic Moment TV Matthew Weiner Out as Showrunner of Eddie Murphy Peacock Series After Clash With Producers And it’s a story instigated by a school shooting and pushed forward by multiple instances of sexual violence, all propping up a mystery that’s barely mysterious — at least until the characters all sit down to explain everything in a series of weakly staged monologues. That The Good Daughter is so full of tropes I find tedious or annoying and yet somehow ends up being compulsively entertaining is a tribute to Slaughter’s gift for characterization and dialogue, the confident hand of series director Steph Green, and particularly the committed, emotionally exposed and often funny performances from leads Meghann Fahy , Rose Byrne and Brendan Gleeson . The Good Daughter begins with a double dose of trauma, the better to winnow away squeamish viewers. First, in flashback, devoted sisters Sam (Audrey Grace Marshall) and Charlie (Drew Cheek) witness a horrible act of violence perpetrated on their doting mother (Olivia Williams’ Gamma), perhaps the latest retaliation against their father (Gleeson’s Rusty), a defense attorney prone to rubbing people the wrong way. Their lives will never be the same. Jump to the present. Charlie (Fahy) has grown up to follow in her father’s footsteps, working out of his ramshackle office in the same Georgia town populated by people who still hate him and don’t feel too kindly toward her. She’s separated from hubby Ben (Michael Dorman, endearingly normal in a show populated by broad portrayals) and making various self-destructive choices, including a one-night stand with Huck (Jake McDorman), whose ponytail and scruff let you know he’s a bad idea. Charlie and Huck accidentally swap phones, which leads her to discover that he’s a high school teacher. In the process of returning his phone, she is present when Kelly (Shayna Benardo, an impressively grounding force) shows up and shoots and kills the well-liked principal and a freshman. Rusty, who has a bad cough and a history of heart problems, and likes to wear — for reasons that are never explained — a red clown nose, shows up to represent Kelly, whose cognitive issues haven’t stopped the local powerbrokers from eyeing the death penalty. Sensing everything is going astray, Rusty also calls elder daughter Sam (Byrne), now a patent lawyer in New York City and left with a permanent limp and partial blindness stemming from the incident with her mother. Sam hasn’t seen or talked to Charlie in 10 years, but she quickly finds herself back in Pikeville, caught up in the mystery of the shooting, as well as several additional mysteries from her family’s past. If you just look at the bones of the series, The Good Daughter is beyond rudimentary, with a crime in the present and a crime in the past that just coincidentally happen to be directly connected. The story can barely even decide what twists are supposed to be surprising and, as a result, nothing is really “guessable” or revelatory. Instead, The Good Daughter works best as a dirtied-up — though confusingly racially whitewashed — version of To Kill a Mockingbird , with Rusty as a lawyer doing noble things in a disreputable way, constantly looking like he slept at his desk, bottle in hand, eschewing Atticus Finch’s seersucker and moral rectitude. He stands up to threats from his adversaries that are violent and gory rather than ominous and insinuated, investigating cases in which the rape and persecution of the handicapped and impoverished play out on the surface rather than being buried in euphemism. It almost certainly works better on the page than on the screen, where we’ve seen too many versions of these generic rednecks in their generic pick-ups and these generic drawling, obfuscating lawmen to take them seriously. Green and the series’ cinematographers are able to embed in the rundown streets of Pikeville and take us into the “holler,” capturing this community within a community. But when every main cast member talks like the closest they’ve ever been to a holler was a quick drive-through during rehearsal, the verisimilitude suffers. What holds the show together is Slaughter’s grasp on the characters and their relationships. When Sam, Charlie and Rusty talk, it’s in a vernacular that mixes in-jokes, deeply felt family history, snooty literary references (lots of Flannery O’Connor and Emily Dickinson), amusingly unsnooty pop culture references (from Die Hard to Buffy the Vampire Slayer ), and an awareness of how to hurt or heal the people they know best. Byrne, Fahy and Gleeson don’t talk like they come from the same place, but the energy among them gives the series its energy and its authenticity. Sure, Fahy is doing a variation on her bad sister character from Netflix’s Sirens , but she’s tremendous at playing these open books of damage. A little too much of Byrne’s performance consists of actorly takes on disability, but she makes those notes of artificiality pay off. Everything Sam does is a put-on; her attire, hair and speech are defined in opposition to the place she left behind and hoped never to return to, with aspects of her natural self returning as she spends more time in Pikeville. It’s easy to buy them as sisters, in both the parts evoking pain and the parts where they bicker humorously. Plus, it’s easy to see the toll taken by trauma and time because Byrne and Fahy are well-matched by Marshall and Cheek. Gleeson isn’t as convincing in the flashback segments, and his Southern-ish intonations kept reminding me of somebody I couldn’t quite place, but he makes Rusty rascally and flawed. Like the actors, the characters are occupying roles — the city mouse, the bad girl, the folksy country lawyer — but when they’re together, they can be themselves. It’s a nice touch that one of the few characters who doesn’t have a public role to play, Rusty’s longtime assistant Lenore, is played by Harper Steele — you know her from the documentary Will & Harper — who isn’t an actor and comes across not as studied but as gentle and natural. For five episodes, Green maintains the flow between past and present smoothly, and is able to modulate most of the agonizing parts of the story so that they feel tense but not exploitative. Too bad the finale collapses under the weight of all its over-explaining. I never quite cared who did what and why, but Fahy, Byrne and Gleeson at least made it possible to care about the people to whom these things were happening. THR

articles.title: AI Audio Startup ElevenLabs Expands Nvidia Collaboration Amid CEO Jensen Huang’s Affair Scandal
articles.full_text: × Nov 11, 2026 8:00am PT AI Audio Startup ElevenLabs Expands Nvidia Collaboration Amid CEO Jensen Huang’s Affair Scandal By Corbin Bolies Plus Icon Corbin Bolies Latest Nvidia Stock and AI World Rocked by CEO Jensen Huang’s Affair With Alleged Chinese Spy 22 hours ago AI Takes Center Stage at Tech-Forward AFM With Innovation Hub and AFM House Expansion 1 day ago Elvis Music Owners, Eminem Publisher File Sprawling New Lawsuits Against AI Music Generator Suno: ‘The Next Elvis Won’t Pick Up a Guitar’ 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Getty Images ElevenLabs is keeping its yearslong Nvidia partnership strong, no matter the national-security chaos enveloping the chipmaker’s CEO . The AI audio startup said on Wednesday during its New York Summit it would expand its partnership with Nvidia to power its suite of voice agents, dubbed ElevenAgents, with the tech provider’s Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, its latest open model that helps power AI agents’ understanding of workflows and human reasoning. Some of the expanded features for the agents unveiled on Wednesday include memory features, routines and helping users architect new agents. Related Stories Invercine, Gema Films and Gaman Cine, Top Producers on Latin America’s Film-TV Scene, Bring to Market New Productions Alex de la Iglesia on His Upcoming Chilean Shoot ‘The Misunderstanding’: ‘Reality Has Become My Parallel World’ The company is also employing Nvidia’s Vera Rubin architecture to provide the compute required for the deployment of its AI agents, capacity the company said would help support large-scale demands from businesses. Some of those demands include powering the voice agents used for Centralna e-Rejestracja, the appointment-making platform within Poland’s national online health system, and the companies said they wanted to make more voice agents available to governments worldwide with Nvidia’s AI architecture. The two are also trying to bring such agents to robots. The expanded collaboration, CEO Mati Staniszewski said in a statement, was necessary as “voice agents become critical infrastructure.” “By combining our audio models and agents, with Nvidia’s LLMs, accelerated computing and security stack, we’re giving enterprises and governments the platform they need to deploy voice agents at massive scale,” Staniszewski said. “Nvidia has been a superb partner to us, and we’re excited to keep building together.” The two companies have been partners since 2022, with ElevenLabs using Nvidia’s GPUs to power its first text-to-speech model and Nvidia using ElevenLabs to create voiceovers for videos at company events. Nvidia last year became an ElevenLabs investor, complete with a splashy produced video posted to Staniszewski’s LinkedIn page. ElevenLabs completed a $300 million employee tender offer in September that valued the company at $22 billion, doubling the $11 billion valuation it reached in February after a funding round. But the expansion comes as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has become enveloped in a national-security scandal over his affair with a Chinese tech executive allegedly recruited by China to spy on Huang and learn more about the company’s AI technology. Huang, who pulled out of ElevenLabs’ summit this week, is currently under investigation by Nvidia’s board of directors and the FBI over the relationship. He will continue leading the company throughout the inquiries. “For decades we adapted to computers — keyboards, screens, menus. Now computers are learning to speak our language,” Huang said in a statement about the ElevenLabs partnership. “With Nvidia Nemotron reasoning inside ElevenAgents and Nvidia accelerated computing powering large-scale deployments, enterprises and governments can run voice agents securely at national scale — and make talking the fastest way to get things done.” ‘Logan’ Star Dafne Keen Says ‘I Was Offered Cocaine’ as an 11-Year-Old in Hollywood and Hugh Jackman ‘Made Sure No One Abused My Hours’ on Set Loading comments...

articles.title: Skydance Succession: As David Ellison Sets His Team, Heads Are Rolling as Hollywood Finds Out Who’s Really in Charge
articles.full_text: Illustration by Will Hooks Of all the things keeping David Ellison up at night, the countdown to 2028 may be the most pressing. At least that’s what many media observers and Hollywood insiders believe. Ellison’s anxiety, they say, isn’t fueled by the forthcoming presidential election or the Olympic Games that will descend on Los Angeles, where Ellison now owns two iconic studio lots. Instead, his agita is arising from the 8 movies he still needs to acquire or produce in 2028 to reach the magic number of 30 — that’s the benchmark Skydance pledged to meet annually in order to close the $111 billion acquisition that made his company a content behemoth. Related Stories Sanfic Mórbido Lab Lineup Ranges From an LGBTQ Alien Monster Comedy to a Mapuche Parable, Extreme Horror and Cold War Sci-Fi ‘The Cry of Serankwa,’ an Indigenous Eco-Thriller and Triple Sanfic Industria Award Winner, Strikes Distribution Deal for Latin America Between Paramount and Warner Bros. Pictures, 22 films have been dated for 2028 so far. A large number of those — like “Gremlins 3,” Baz Luhrmann’s rumored Joan of Arc biopic and an untitled movie from the Duffer brothers — have yet to start production. And, of course, Hollywood is keeping a close watch on how the new regime handles the urgent task of closing deals with Margot Robbie and Greta Gerwig for a “ Barbie ” follow-up. Zohar Lazar Despite Skydance’s other pledge — to streamline costs via cutting-edge technology — feature films remain one of the most expensive gambles in the business (and that’s if audiences respond). The challenge before Ellison and his team is to churn out hits fast — not just to prove their hotly debated merger will be viable in the long run but to generate the cash needed to pay down the combined company’s staggering $80 billion debt. Five weeks in, if Team Ellison is losing sleep about the operational challenges ahead, it’s not letting that on to the media. “People are viewing our $30 billion-plus content spend as an expense, but content is our asset,” Skydance chief financial officer Dennis Cinelli told Variety , speaking ahead of the company’s third-quarter earnings report. “Whether it’s for our theatrical or TV business, both of our streaming platforms, third-party sales, the networks portfolio — we’re investing in content because it has proved tremendously valuable. We’re confident we can drive growth and increase profitability and cash flow.” On Nov. 9, as Skydance unveiled its first quarterly earnings report as a combined company, leadership said a big push will come in early 2027 to offer consumers a bundle of the streaming services now under the Skydance roof: HBO Max and Paramount+. The price will come at a competitive discount designed to allow Skydance to gain market share among subscribers, one source says. Skydance plans to offer a fully integrated service that puts both brands on a single platform — which will make it easier for the company to keep viewers moving around its streaming universe — by 2029. There is much speculation that the company will eventually retire the Paramount+ moniker, given that HBO is the more powerful consumer brand. Meanwhile, Skydance is touting the power of its portfolio: A combined 205-million streaming subscribers in more than 100 global territories, a library of roughly 15,000 films and more than 100,000 hours of TV series. Hollywood’s new colossus has a content library larger than its studio rivals’ by a significant factor, even if its stewards change, as James Gunn and Peter Safran found out the hard way this week. (The DC Studios chiefs made it just five weeks into the Skydance regime before Ellison announced on earnings day that he would replace the pair with producer Jeremy Latcham, an early architect of Marvel Studios.) Superman, Batman and many other characters in the Skydance vault represent a treasure trove of the kind of IP that can yield new adaptations and spinoffs for decades. The chance to buy Warner Bros.’ vault was so attractive that last year even Netflix, the leader in global streaming, was driven to give up its build-not-buy philosophy regarding big acquisitions to chase Warner Bros. and HBO — until Ellison stuck his foot in the door and refused to leave without a deal. Streaming is the engine of the future for Skydance. But in the short term, the company’s fate will be determined by that of its linear cable channels. With the merger, Skydance hasn’t just doubled down on this sector — it has tripled down; Skydance has by far the industry’s collection of linear cable channels. Its TV portfolio is anchored by CBS and spans some 55 cable networks, including CNN, TNT, TBS, Cartoon Network, TCM, Nickelodeon, Comedy Central, BET, Discovery, TLC, Food Network and HGTV. But the traditional business of cable television is deteriorating; subscribers are slowly but surely giving up on linear cable services in favor of streaming platforms. The erosion of once-reliable cable TV profits has bedeviled Hollywood’s majors for more than a decade and has been a catalyst for the latest round of merger mania. As was the case for Paramount and WBD when they were separate companies, the enlarged Skydance remains heavily dependent on linear TV for cash flow and profits — and the cable and satellite biz remains a steadily melting iceberg. In the second quarter of this year, for example, Paramount’s TV business revenue slid 9% to $3.1 billion, but the segment still delivered all of the company’s adjusted $1.1 billion earnings for the quarter. Skydance’s ability to meet its post-merger financial targets hinges on whether the TV business crumbles faster than Ellison and his financial engineers have projected, and whether streaming sees commensurate growth to make up for it. That’s a lot to leave to fate. Here’s the quandary: Skydance must slash costs while investing in content and paying down its immense $80 billion in net debt. The numbers may not add up. “[W]e are concerned more aggressive cost-cutting measures in TV media could leave the segment vulnerable to a faster-than-expected rate of revenue declines,” MoffettNathanson analyst Robert Fishman wrote in an Oct. 23 research note. Industry veterans have watched the creation of Skydance with wonderment. More so than Disney’s acquisition of 21st Century Fox, the union of Paramount and Warner Bros. feels like a milestone transition for the motion picture business that emerged in the 1910s and ’20s around silent films. Both iconic studios were foundational brand names for entertainment back then, and there is great hope among the many industry insiders who have worked across both that those proud logos and studio lots will endure for another century. After finally closing the WBD acquisition, Skydance leadership opened themselves up to a media firing squad on the Paramount lot in early October. Ellison and team addressed burning questions about real estate, cash flow, layoffs and more. Yet inside the company, rank-and-file employees across both operations feel left in the dark. Conversations with staffers in many corners of the Skydance business yielded a feeling of “radio silence,” as one person put it, from the top as pink slips loom and anxiety around greenlights and general spending persists. On balance, another source inside the company deadpanned: “It’s been about a month” since the two entertainment giants combined (Skydance had no comment on the matter). Skydance’s CEO David Ellison, left, and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz, right, pose for a picture on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange on Oct. 8. AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura Who can blame them, as the town places bets on whether Ellison will have the cash to pay back his lenders. Skydance’s interest expenses are expected to be more than $6 billion next year. According to financial projections, the company intends to reduce that debt load from a figure that is seven times larger than its adjusted annual earnings to a number that is three times larger than adjusted net earnings, which is a more typical debt ratio for large companies. If that model doesn’t hold, Ellison will need to find additional sources of capital. Will his father, billionaire Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, whose Ellison Family trust committed $14 billion in equity financing for the WBD takeover, be willing to pump even more money into his son’s gambit to create one of Hollywood’s biggest conglomerates? That remains to be seen. There have also been rumors that David is hunting for more big-money backers to keep Skydance afloat — including Elon Musk. Cinelli told Variety that Skydance is not seeking any additional capital at this time. (Skydance and Musk declined to comment on the tech mogul’s possible involvement.) Skydance’s pledged $30 billion annual spend on new content towers over those of rivals Netflix ($20 billion annually) and Disney ($24 billion in 2026), but investment and prayer alone will not make a meaningful dent in the company’s tremendous liabilities. To that end, bloodletting will come in the form of layoffs (expected by the end of the year and extending into the first quarter of 2027) and ruthless efficiency targets. Insiders at Skydance say cost savings from the company’s acquisition of Paramount Global will blow past an anticipated $2 billion in cuts and approach $3 billion. That’s after only a year in control of the former Shari Redstone empire. Fat-trimming opportunities from the inherited Warner Bros. Discovery books also abound, three sources say. A recent team meeting on the Warner Bros. lot revealed that Skydance will be looking closely at its financial commitments to sporting events like the Olympics. Unexpected (and eyebrow-raising) expenses have been discovered, like trifling luxury costs that amount to “tens of millions” of dollars, per two sources, on hospitality hospitality splurges like dining, travel and gifts. The former WBD regime spent in ways big and small — like stacks of receipts for sandwiches and green juices from the gourmet grocery store Erewhon. There will also be “millions” saved by combining or reducing spends on outside vendors, studio services, redundant marketing budgets and more (one source even suggests press junkets will be revamped. Sorry, journalists: No more sushi at the Four Seasons. And Ellison’s executive table prides itself on its strong, effective characters. Co-CEO Ynon Kreiz, a respected operator and the former CEO of Mattel, has claimed daily operations as his purview. President Andy Gordon and CFO Cinelli will mind people and the purse, respectively. HBO golden child Casey Bloys sits atop the entire streaming operation with JB Perrette. Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein are now at the molten core of the movie business, controlling both Paramount, WB and DC Studios. Former CBS chief George Cheeks now runs all of linear TV and news. And what about David? “There’s a lot of talk about David Ellison. Not since Walt Disney have you had an owner-operator running a major Hollywood company,” says Cinelli. “David is uniquely well-positioned to lead. He’s someone who loves the creative aspect of the business, and wants to spend his time making films and shows with passion. But he also grew up in Silicon Valley. His mentors and most valuable lessons come from that place, and that’s exactly what Skydance needs to succeed in the future.” As any Hollywood executive knows, all the strength in the world cannot account for the exercise in pain that is managing creative budgets. Take the juicy fallout around “Barbie 2” as a case study. As Ellison toiled for almost a year to win WBD, that company was stuck in tense negotiations for a sequel to Warner Bros.’ highest-grossing movie ever: “Barbie.” Director Gerwig and co-screenwriter Noah Baumbach dangled a concept for a sequel in front of now-axed WB film chiefs Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy. They would not, however, allow a new movie into development until new deals were struck for themselves, producer-star Robbie and her A-list Ken doll Ryan Gosling that reflected the runaway success of the first film. So the negotiations, led by the creative team’s all-powerful CAA agent Bryan Lourd, broke down. The creatives were demanding equal pay, which one person familiar with the deal pegs at around $25 million each for Gerwig, Robbie and Gosling (Baumbach would share in the writing fee with Gerwig, and he conveniently received a new overall deal at Warners while the “Barbie” negotiations were churning). Team “Barbie” also requested increased pieces of the back end, at which point then-WBD CEO David Zaslav balked — shutting down the talks as the studio’s licensing rights to the famous toy faced a year-end deadline for renewal. Ellison, Keisz and Lourd are keen to make the “Barbie 2” deal happen by the end of the year, two sources say, and Kreiz is obviously close to the property as Mattel’s former chief executive. But for a company with an $80 billion debt tab, how does a decreased profit margin make sense? In the view of former Warner Bros. CEO Barry Meyer, the key thing that the new owners need to remember is to invest in creativity. At the end of the day, it’s all about the movies and shows. “Creating value with the content is very, very important. Distribution is usually a lot more commoditized than content,” says Meyer, who spent 41 years at Warner Bros., capped by a 14-year run as CEO. “Content is creative. Content is unique. Streaming is how you get it there, but the content is where the value is.” Todd Spangler and Jennifer Maas contributed to this report. articles.title: Daniel Dae Kim and 3AD Board North Korean Defector Documentary ‘School for Defectors’ (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: × Nov 11, 2026 8:00am PT Daniel Dae Kim and 3AD Board North Korean Defector Documentary ‘School for Defectors’ (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Daniel Dae Kim and 3AD Board North Korean Defector Documentary ‘School for Defectors’ (EXCLUSIVE) 34 minutes ago ‘Train to Busan’ Director Yeon Sang-ho on AI Thriller ‘Paradise Lost’: ‘Something as Mysterious and Unknowable to Us as a Black Hole’ 55 minutes ago ‘Adolescence’ Writer Jack Thorne Adapts Matt Haig’s ‘The Humans’ for London’s West End With ‘House of the Dragon’ Star Matt Smith 7 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Damien Fry/Changho Lim “Lost” and “Hawaii Five-0” star Daniel Dae Kim and his production company 3AD have joined filmmaker Jeremy Workman’s documentary “ School for Defectors ” as executive producers. The film follows a small South Korean school where every student escaped from North Korea. The film is set at Jangdaehyun School, in an industrial part of Busan. The school has just 20 students, and each of them is a defector from the North. Workman was let into a community that had never been filmed before. His film looks at the young people there in terms of both what they have lived through and the lives ahead of them. Related Stories ‘The Cry of Serankwa,’ an Indigenous Eco-Thriller and Triple Sanfic Industria Award Winner, Strikes Distribution Deal for Latin America Cineplex Boards Sanfic Title ‘La Residencia’ From ‘Algo Azul' Director Mariel García Spooner 3AD joins a producing team that also includes Bearing North , WildBrush Media, SonaFilms and Hooligan Films. “3AD and I are really excited to join ‘School for Defectors’ as executive producers. We believe deeply in the power of documentary filmmaking, and in telling the story of this special high school, Jeremy has poignantly revealed a story full of heart, humor and humanity,” Kim said. “School for Defectors” premiered at the True/False Film Festival in March. Since then it has screened at a dozen more festivals, including Florida, RiverRun, DC/DOX, Calgary, Hamptons, Woodstock, Heartland and Vancouver. It has won six awards so far and is set to screen at Doc NYC. “What we think makes ‘School for Defectors’ so special is that it’s not simply a story about North Korea. It’s a story about youth, hope, and the universal desire to belong,” Workman said. “Daniel Dae Kim has built a remarkable career championing stories and communities that deserve greater visibility, and we’re incredibly honored to have him and 3AD help bring this film to an even wider audience.” Workman, who is repped by UTA, makes portraits of unusual and often obsessive people. His credits include “Secret Mall Apartment” (Netflix), “Lily Topples the World” (Max), “Deciding Vote” (The New Yorker), “The World Before Your Feet” (Prime Video) and “Magical Universe” (AMC+). Across close to 200 reviews, his documentaries hold a combined 95% score on Rotten Tomatoes. Kim earned a Tony nomination for his role in “Yellow Face.” He hosts and executive produces “K-Everything,” a four-part CNN travel series about South Korea’s cultural reach around the world, which premiered May 9. In June, he appeared in Season 2 of “Avatar: The Last Airbender.” Off screen, his testimony before Congress helped get the COVID-19 Hate Crimes Act passed. He has worked with a number of AAPI community groups and served as advisory council co-chair of TAAF. He is repped by CAA, Linden, Gang, Tyre, Ramer, Brown & Passman, and Narrative. Kim set up 3AD in 2014 to make work in every medium and genre built around people who have historically been underrepresented on screen. The company’s credits include ABC hit “The Good Doctor,” Amazon Prime thriller “Butterfly” and IFC documentary “Bad Axe,” which made the Oscar shortlist in 2022. Producer John Cheng runs development at 3AD, which is under a first-look TV pact with 20th Century Studios. articles.title: ‘Rings of Power’ Season 3 Premiere: [SPOILER] Dies in Shocking Murder, Sauron Assembles Ringwraiths and Jamie Campbell Bower Is Galadriel’s Lover Celeborn
articles.full_text: × Nov 11, 2026 8:15am PT ‘Rings of Power’ Season 3 Premiere: [SPOILER] Dies in Shocking Murder, Sauron Assembles Ringwraiths and Jamie Campbell Bower Is Galadriel’s Lover Celeborn By Jordan Moreau Plus Icon Jordan Moreau Latest ‘Rings of Power’ Season 3 Premiere: [SPOILER] Dies in Shocking Murder, Sauron Assembles Ringwraiths and Jamie Campbell Bower Is Galadriel’s Lover Celeborn 32 minutes ago Donnie Dunagan, Original Voice of Bambi, Dies at 92 2 days ago James Gunn Speaks Out After Stepping Down at DC, Says It Had ‘Highest of Highs’ but ‘Has Been Trying’: ‘I Dislike the At-Times Corporate Nature of the Job’ 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Ben Rothstein/Prime SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for the four-episode premiere of “ The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power ,” now streaming on Prime Video. After a two-year break, it’s time to return to Middle-earth — and to say goodbye to one major character from “The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power.” Season 3 has dropped its first four episodes on Prime Video, and it’s immediately clear that the show has kicked into high gear. The show jumps ahead five years as Sauron (Charlie Vickers) rises to power, commands a massive orc army and begins assembling the ringwraiths, aka his creepy Nazgûl enforcers. He recruits several men to fight for the honor of being a ringwraith, including one surprise combatant: Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin), who wins. But the season starts out on a tender note, flashing back to the love story between Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) and her long-lost husband Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower). They fell for each other in their youth but have since been separated — for now. In the present, Galadriel and Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova) are met by an orc named Marnûkh (Adam Young), who defects from Sauron’s army and promises to lead them to an imprisoned elven blacksmith who could forge them a ring. In Episode 4, the trio makes their way to Gundabad, a mountainous orc prison, where they learn in a twist that the elven blacksmith had died weeks ago. However, they do rescue Celeborn, who’d been locked up for who knows how long. Galadriel, Arondir, Celeborn and Marnûkh fight their way out of Gundabad, but they’re met by a ringwraith who faces off against Arondir. The shadowy knight removes his mask, and it’s revealed that Theo has joined Sauron’s inner circle. Arondir tries to reason with the young man, but Sauron appears and orders Theo to kill the elf. Theo plunges his sword into Arondir, murdering him in a shocking twist. Elsewhere in Middle-earth, things aren’t going much better. The humans are divided, with Numenor’s King Pharazon (Trystan Gravelle) surviving an assassination attempt from a Faithful follower of the blind, deposed Queen Regent Mirel (Cynthia Addai-Robinson). Earien (Ema Horvath), the daughter of Elendil (Lloyd Owen), has also been working as a spy for the Faithfuls, but she’s found out by Pharazon and killed. Over in the dwarven mountains, King Durin IV (Owain Arthur) is dealing with a succession problem. He’s challenged for his father’s crown by his brother Thrain (Eddie Marsan), who wants to work with the ringwraiths to protect the dwarves. They settle the disagreement with a fight, but Durin is thrown off after he learns that his wife Disa (Sophia Nomvete) previously had a fling with Thrain. Durin loses the showdown, and his right to rule the kingdom. Middle-earth’s saving grace may come on the wizard coattails of Gandalf, who finally dons his famous pointed hat after speaking with the mysterious, all-powerful Secret Fire. Red light therapy has moved well beyond the dermatologist’s office. Once largely reserved for luxe celebrity treatments , the technology is now a popular fixture in at-home wellness routines, with everyone from skincare enthusiasts to fitness devotees investing in LED devices designed to support skin health and post-workout recovery. While LED face masks have dominated much of the conversation, red light therapy panels offer a more versatile alternative. Unlike masks, which are generally designed to target the face, panels can be positioned to deliver light to larger areas of the body, from the neck and shoulders to the back and legs. Many combine red light, commonly studied for its potential skin benefits, with near-infrared wavelengths being investigated for muscle and joint recovery. Some are compact enough to fit on a desk, while others require dedicated floor space and cost well over $1,000. Shoppers should pay attention to the number and type of wavelengths, treatment coverage, adjustable settings and whether a stand is included. It’s also worth distinguishing the science behind red light therapy from the marketing. Research suggests that certain wavelengths may improve skin appearance or help with particular types of pain, but evidence varies by condition, and the benefits of any specific consumer device aren’t guaranteed. Below, we’ve rounded up seven red light therapy panels worth considering — from entry-level investments to more elaborate additions to your wellness routine. Unlike smaller panels that require multiple sessions to cover different areas, the 64-inch Blaze delivers head-to-toe coverage in a single setup, with a motorized, 360-degree rotating stand that makes it easy to use while standing or lying down. It also offers preset modes for skin health, muscle recovery, hair growth and more, plus customizable intensity and pulsing settings for a more tailored experience. articles.full_text: × Nov 11, 2026 8:26am PT Kate Berlant and John Early to Host Film Independent Spirit Awards By Clayton Davis Plus Icon Clayton Davis Chief Awards Editor byClaytonDavis Latest Kate Berlant and John Early to Host Film Independent Spirit Awards 30 minutes ago Is ‘I Play Rocky’ Original or Adapted? Stallone’s ‘Rocky’ Origin Story Faces a ‘Barbie’-Style Oscar Dilemma (EXCLUSIVE) 18 hours ago Oscars: Best Original Score — Could One of Hollywood’s Most Overlooked Composers Finally Get His Moment? 22 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Sela Shiloni Kate Berlant and John Early , two of comedy’s most gloriously unpredictable performers, will co-host the 2027 Film Independent Spirit Awards . The 42nd annual celebration of the best in independent film and television takes place Saturday, March 6, 2027, at the Hollywood Palladium, eight days before the 99th Academy Awards on March 14. The date marks a later slot on the calendar and a return to Saturday after this past year’s Sunday, Feb. 15 ceremony, which was hosted by “Saturday Night Live” alum Ego Nwodim. Related Stories Benjamín Vicuña, Star of Netflix Hit Series 'Envious,' Joins ‘My Last Stand' by Goya-Winner Matías Bize Cineplex Boards Sanfic Title ‘La Residencia’ From ‘Algo Azul' Director Mariel García Spooner “If there’s one thing we don’t need, it’s another predictable awards show,” says Film Independent President Juan Devis. “Kate and John are two of the funniest, strangest and most brilliantly unpredictable performers working today. They embody everything we love about independent storytelling: originality, fearlessness and a healthy disregard for convention. We’re excited to shake things up, break a few rules and have some fun along the way.” The hosts are ready for the assignment. “We’ve always been obsessed with awards shows, and we’re so honored we get to host the coolest one. Tune in to see if we choke under pressure!” Berlant and Early say in a joint statement. Berlant and Early join a roster of past Spirit Awards hosts that includes Nwodim, Aidy Bryant, Hasan Minhaj, Megan Mullally and Nick Offerman, Aubrey Plaza, Nick Kroll and John Mulaney, Kate McKinnon and Kumail Nanjiani, Fred Armisen and Kristen Bell, Andy Samberg and John Waters. Friends and creative collaborators for more than a decade, Berlant and Early have built a devoted following on a distinctive brand of absurdist comedy that blends sharp social satire, improvisation and performances that rarely go where you expect. Their joint work includes the acclaimed sketch series “555” and the Emmy-nominated Peacock comedy special “Would It Kill You to Laugh?,” which took familiar comedic conventions and twisted them into something entirely their own. Individually, both have carved out celebrated careers across film, television and live comedy. Berlant’s film credits include “Sorry to Bother You,” “Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood” and “Don’t Worry Darling,” and she has appeared in FX’s comedy-drama series “The Bear.” She also earned acclaim for her one-woman show “Kate” and her comedy specials “Cinnamon in the Wind” and “Parmesan.” Early is best known for his breakout performance in the dark comedy series “Search Party,” which ran on TBS before moving to HBO Max, as well as his stand-up special “Now More Than Ever.” He recently made his feature directorial debut with “Maddie’s Secret,” which also features Berlant. This year’s ceremony adds two new categories, best international first feature and the Digital Creator Award, expanding the show’s reach across platforms. Filmmaker Roman Coppola will also bring his artistic vision to the show in the newly created role of creative consultant.The Nominee Brunch, the annual gathering that honors all nominees and features the presentation of the Emerging Filmmaker Awards, returns to The London West Hollywood on Saturday, Jan. 9, 2027. articles.title: From a ‘Hell House’ to ‘The Woods,’ Stephen Cognetti Proves His Versatility as a Scary Movie Maestro
articles.full_text: × Nov 11, 2026 8:30am PT From a ‘Hell House’ to ‘The Woods,’ Stephen Cognetti Proves His Versatility as a Scary Movie Maestro By William Earl Plus Icon William Earl @beautifulbill Latest Variety Announces Program for Inaugural Women of Awards Season High Tea 23 hours ago The Team Unveils New Board as Firm Regroups After Rebrand From Wasserman 1 day ago Danielle Fishel Gets Honest About ‘Girl Meets World’ Pay, Says She Knew She Was Disliked on Set for Setting Boundaries (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy photo Stephen Cognetti ’s newest film is a hard pivot from the franchise that made him a household name in horror. Cognetti, who wrote and directed all five chapters in the found footage “ Hell House LLC ” franchise, just finished filming his latest feature, “ A Body in the Woods .” It stars Emma Roberts as Alice Lincoln, a turn-of-the-century woman who lives in a remote cabin in an area of the woods that might be haunted by a witch. Related Stories Benjamín Vicuña, Star of Netflix Hit Series 'Envious,' Joins ‘My Last Stand' by Goya-Winner Matías Bize Invercine, Gema Films and Gaman Cine, Top Producers on Latin America’s Film-TV Scene, Bring to Market New Productions Manifest Pictures is launching international sales for the film at AFM . Cognetti spoke with Variety about his dark new vision, his influences and the future of “Hell House LLC.” How did you come up with the idea for this new film? I actually wrote this right after the fourth “Hell House” movie. I felt like I was in a very good state of mind, scare-wise. It was the quickest first draft of a script I’ve ever written. I got the idea, and it just flowed. What did Emma’s performance bring to the film? She’s not only a wonderful actress, but she’s just so creatively intelligent. She has all of these good instincts. She just gets things better than anyone I’ve ever worked with on screen. Every discussion with her is on another level because she understood everything. From what we were doing behind the camera to what she was doing on screen, she just has a great understanding. Were there any movies you were inspired by for the look of “A Body in the Woods?” There were two films that really inspired me. The first is not horror at all, but it’s “The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford.” When I was writing this, I was not only always thinking about the visuals; I was also listening to the soundtrack the entire time. “Assassination” was always in my head. Also, Robert Eggers’ “The Witch” is a film that I just adore. I love everything he did with the camera. It is a very deliberate movement, slow movement, and the camera takes its time. We take our time story-wise; we take our time with the scares, the story. I wouldn’t call this a slow burn at all, but I just love the style of a well-paced, slower horror film, rather than something like I’m used to in the found footage world, which is very jumpy and we’re hopping around quickly, getting to scare after scare. Here we’re just building a world and building a character who’s mostly isolated. How are you a different director from when you first began? You’ve got to learn to pivot quickly. It has gotten a lot easier with every subsequent film, just because I’ve learned how to strategize better and how to put together a game plan for every day. When something’s not working, that experience helps a lot. Will there eventually be another “Hell House LLC” movie? There is a future story. The fifth one, for better or for worse, ended on a cliffhanger, and that was always the intention. But making those films is impossible for where I’m at right now, for a lot of behind-the-scenes reasons. But I would always love to tell more of the story. I just don’t know how it would ever be able to happen. It might come in other forms. I’ve always said that there might be a novel, a graphic novel, to not only tell the final chapter, but also flesh out more of the story that we’ve seen. articles.full_text: × Nov 11, 2026 8:56am PT Alief Boards ‘Borges and Me,’ Closes Major Market Theatrical Sales (EXCLUSIVE) By John Hopewell Plus Icon John Hopewell Chief International Correspondent john_hopewell Latest ‘Gordon,’ a Big Netflix Series From Argentina, Unpacked by Pablo Trapero and Star Rodrigo de la Serna 2 days ago Sanfic Prizes: ‘Monguen’ and ‘Narciso’ Win at Pared-Back Ceremony Due to Sudden Demise of ‘A Fantastic Woman’ Director Sebastián Lelio 3 days ago Seville European Film Festival Honors Agnieszka Holland, Thierry Frémaux and Cartoon Saloon 5 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source (L-R) Luis Gnecco and Fionn Whitehead in 'Borges and Me' France and U.K.-based Alief has boarded as a sales agent “Borges and Me,” a big scene adaptation of U.S. writer Jay Parini novelized memoir of a life-changing encounter with Argentine literary great Jorge Luis Borges. Directed by Marc Turtletaub (“Jules”) and produced by his label Big Beach (“Miss Sunshine”), “Borges and Me” stars Fionn Whitehead (“Dunkirk”), Luis Gnecco (“Neruda”) and Alan Cumming (“Avengers Doomsday”). Related Stories Sanfic Mórbido Lab Lineup Ranges From an LGBTQ Alien Monster Comedy to a Mapuche Parable, Extreme Horror and Cold War Sci-Fi Alex de la Iglesia on His Upcoming Chilean Shoot ‘The Misunderstanding’: ‘Reality Has Become My Parallel World’ “Delightfully imbued with poetry, magical realism and melancholy, ‘Borges and Me’ is a charming ride with an outstanding British cast. We are delighted to be representing the film,” said Alief President Brett Walker, announcing the pickup. The Edinburgh Festival world premiere has also closed first major market theatrical deals before the AFM with Icon Distribution (U.K. and Ireland), Rialto Distribution (Australia and New Zealand), German-speaking Europe with MFA Film and Spain, bought by Alfa Pictures across what alien describes as “multiple major markets.” Alief is now in conversations with buyers from Central Europe, MENA, Mexico, Cono Sur countries of Argentina, Chile and Uruguay and Asia, it told Variety on the first day of trading at the American Film Market . Written by Oren Moverman (“The Messenger”), working off an earlier adaptation by “Borges and Me” picks up on Parini (Whitehead) in 1971 as young American graduate student at Scotland’s St. Andrews U. desperate to find his voice as a writer, who is persuaded by mentor Scottish poet and Borges translator Alistair Reid, to chauffeur Borges for a week’s road trip in the Scottish Highlands to meet poet George Mackay Brown (Peter Mullan). Their journey—an improbable road trip in an old Morris Minor—transforms from a reluctant obligation into a profound, life-changing experience, Alief noted. In real-life, Argentina’s Jorge Luis Borges was a towering literary presence. Asked to name the greatest works in Latin America literature, Nobel Prize winner Mario Vargas Llosa answered “Borges, everything.” Yet Borges wrote famously in a poem that “I have committed the worst of all sins: I have not been happy.” The Borges Parini encounters in 1971 is a 72-years legend making up for lost time: eager, though blind, to grasp the moment, feel it to its fullest. As played by Gnecco, that drivers moments of comedy, but as the film builds in emotion in his second half, delivers a life changing lesson for Parini. “ Borges has remained with me every day of my life,” he says in his voiceover narrative. “Oren Moverman pivots between moments of graceful poetry and others of simpler feelgood sentiment. The final balance slightly favors the latter,” Guy Lodge wrote in an upbeat Variety review. Peter Mullan (“My Name Is Joe”), Freya Mavor (“My Policeman,” and Morven Christie (“The Bay) also star. “Borges and Me” is a Big Beach presentation of an Ossian International, Big Beach, Lemming Film, and A Private View production. Alex Polunin, Turtletaub, Michael B. Clark, Tim Foley produce; Stephen Burt, Moverman and Parini executive produce. “It is a thrill to work with Big Beach,” added Alief partner Miguel Govea. “Their gorgeously shot ‘Borges And Me brings to life the book, capturing its essence of time, place, and recollection in a strikingly clear and evocative upbeat road movie that audiences and buyers are connecting with.” Director Marc Turtletaub added: “We are thrilled to be working with Alief for international. Their passion for the film was apparent from the first conversations we had with them. And we love the enthusiasm from the distributors who they have partnered with.” “We fell in love with ‘Borges and Me’ for its warmth, gentle wit and endearing charm. It’s a beautiful story about an unlikely friendship between two very different generations, and how much they come to learn from one another,” said Kelly Roger CEO, Rialto Distribution. “We are very excited to be releasing ‘Borges and Me ‘in the U.K. and Ireland next year and can’t wait to share it with audiences everywhere,” said Spencer Pollard, CEO, Icon Film Distribution, a John Gore Studios company “‘Borges and Me’ is a delightful package -– combining the poetic of Borges with the magic of the Highlands. We trust German arthouse audiences will love it,” added Christian Meinke,foinder of MFA Film Distribution. articles.title: Judge Declines To Dismiss Donald Trump’s Defamation Claim Against BBC
articles.full_text: Skip to main content By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted Judge Declines To Dismiss Donald Trump’s Defamation Claim Against BBC House Blocks Effort To Impeach Secretary Of Defense Pete Hegseth Pete Hegseth Defends Tenure, Lavishes Praise On Trump & Calls Impeachment Threat “Sabotage” In Rare Pentagon Press Conference View All November 10, 2026 6:06pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source (L-R) Donald Trump & the BBC headquarters in London Getty A federal judge on Tuesday declined to dismiss Donald Trump ‘s defamation claim against the BBC over edits made to a documentary about January 6th that aired in advance of the 2024 election. U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Kuntz rejected the BBC’s efforts to toss the case, ruling that Trump had sufficiently pleaded actual malice. In his ruling, Kuntz wrote that the BBC confirmed “it had edited a video to make it appear as though President Trump made a statement he never made. And it acknowledged it chose to release the video in a documentary only a week before the 2024 Presidential Election, at the time it would have the most impact. To make sure it was seen in Florida, BBC even emailed U.S. and Florida based commenters with instructions to on how to view the documentary.” Related Stories News Netflix's 'The Perfect Neighbor' Beats 'Mr Nobody Against Putin' To Top Prize At UK Grierson Documentary Awards Legal Hasan Piker's $72.5M Defamation Suit Over Lynching Quotes Should Be Tossed Out, Scott Jennings Says; Statements Are "Literally True," CNN Contributor Claims He added, “Whether President Trump can prove these claims and establish he sustained damages at summary judgment or trial is left for another day.” Watch on Deadline The judge kept alive Trump’s defamation claim but dismissed his claim of violation of Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act. Trump sued the BBC for $10 billion. In the documentary, Trump: A Second Chance? , a clip is shown from his January 6 speech, in which he says, “We’re going to walk down to the Capitol … and I’ll be there with you. And we fight. We fight like hell.” In fact, the remark was an edit of different portions of the speech. Trump claims that the documentary — which was produced by October Films — was streamed on iPlayer by “hundreds of individuals” using a VPN in the U.S., despite it being geoblocked in America. His lawyers have accused the BBC of a “brazen” attempt to interfere in the 2024 U.S. election, which the corporation denies. In the fallout from edited speech, BBC director general Tim Davie and Deborah Turness , who led the news division, stepped down. The BBC apologized, calling it an “error of judgment,” but they did not offer to pay any damages. The judge wrote of the editing, “Trump properly alleges that BBC spliced and edited together a twelve-second segment that resulted in reputational harm based off ‘deceptive and defamatory distortion.'” “On its face, a twelve-second clip seems insignificant, but in the context of the complaint, these twelve seconds are the result of splicing two segments that are separated by nearly fifty-five minutes in the speech from which the segment is sourced.” Among other things, the BBC contended that Trump lacked personal jurisdiction, as the Panorama documentary did not air in Florida, where the case was filed. The judge ruled that Trump had sufficiently claimed jurisdiction. The judge wrote, “Trump has alleged extensive contacts tying BBC to the State of Florida. BBC tries to frame this as an operation entirely disconnected from Florida. That cannot be the case. Trump is a Florida resident, and the Documentary is almost entirely about Trump. Portions were filmed in Florida and BBC identified Florida as an important part of the Documentary. Therefore, ‘it seems disingenuous’ for BBC to argue that they ‘could not have anticipated being haled into court in Florida.'” Kuntz was nominated to the bench by Trump and confirmed by the Senate earlier this year. Trump called the ruling a “huge victory” and called the BBC “a terrible abuser of truth.” He wrote on Truth Social, “We will continue fighting against, and defeating, all of those who try to deceive the American People!” A BBC spokesperson said, “We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court’s authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage. “We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process. It would be inappropriate to comment further while proceedings are ongoing.” Sarandos Faces Unrest From Past & Present Execs Over Netflix’s Direction ‘Mike Hammer’ Star, Film & Stage Actor, Dies At 85; Career In Photos Jason Orley Directing New Take On Rom-Com ‘You’ve Got Mail’ For Warner Bros Leah McKendrick Sets ‘Voicemails From Isabelle’ Follow-Up; Maddie Ziegler Stars Read More About: 7 Comments
