articles.title: Lisa’s ‘Always Lalisa’ Heads to YouTube Premium, Singer to Release New Single “Leave With Me” (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Nicole Fell Plus Icon Nicole Fell Associate Editor nicolemfell Follow Sign Up View All November 10, 2026 7:03am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Lalisa Manobal at the premiere of 'Always Lalisa' during the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Robin Marchant/Getty Images Always Lalisa , director Sue Kim’s behind-the-scenes look at global pop star Lisa , will soon be able to be viewed on YouTube Premium, The Hollywood Reporter has exclusively learned. The documentary, hailing from Sony Music Vision, premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival in September and made a limited-release stop in theaters last month. Lyor Cohen, head of global music at YouTube, told THR that the decision to bring the documentary to the platform was a no-brainer, given the platform’s global-forward focus. “YouTube has been such a big part of my journey from the beginning,” Lisa tells THR . The global superstar, a member of girl group Blackpink, speaks on the phone from rehearsals. Related Stories Music K-pop Star Wonho Announces 2027 Noche World Tour (Exclusive) Music Jisoo to Release Original Song for Upcoming 'The Angry Birds Movie 3' (Exclusive) “From sharing music videos, to my Coachella livestream it has helped me reach fans around the world so it felt right for me to share my documentary on YouTube,” she continues. The film heads to video platform on Nov. 18 and will be exclusive to premium members. The 29-year-old rapper and singer will also release a new single, “Leave With Me,” on Nov. 18. The song was made for and featured in the documentary. “I’m excited,” Lisa tells THR about people being able to watch the film at home. “Me and my mom went to theater to see the movie, but we were also like, ‘Oh, we can’t wait for this movie to come up on YouTube so we can just nonstop watching it.'” The singer says the reception to the documentary from people in her life has been great. Even some of her closest friends told her that the film helped them learn more about her, finding out about some of the struggles she’s had to overcome through the film as she had remained strong to those around her. Lisa recently released an EP Press Play in October, led by the pre-release single “SaWaDiKa.” In the time since that album dropped, the singer’s been busy preparing for her upcoming Las Vegas residency, which kicks off on Thursday (Nov. 12) at The Colosseum at Caesars Palace. The singer exudes excitement, and a little nervousness, about the accomplishment, as she’ll be the first K-pop star to hold a Las Vegas residency. “It’s going to be so much fun,” she says. “Everybody’s going to be there for me, [and] all my fans know every single of my songs, so it’s going to be a fun night.” The venue, which sits at just over a 4,000 cap, is intimate for the singer, who’s used to playing stadiums, arenas and festival crowds. “You can see everyone faces up close,” she says. “I know that they’re going to be so up close to me, so I hope that I can just [get] eye to eye with everyone.” THR

articles.title: Tilly Norwood Creator’s New Project? An AI Talking-Dog Movie With the Co-Director of ‘The Lion King’
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Steven Zeitchik Plus Icon Steven Zeitchik Senior Editor, Technology and Politics View All November 10, 2026 7:15am Add us as a Google Preferred Source A still from 'Storm Dogs.' Particle 6 Tilly Norwood may have divided the town and broke the Internet, but the woman behind it says she thinks AI can be all love, too. So she’s making a talking-dog movie. Eline van der Velden, the Holland-born, London-dwelling producer of Tilly, has been developing Storm Dogs , a hybrid live-animated family film involving a motley crew of pups helping a toddler lost in the woods get home. And she’s hired The Lion King co-director Rob Minkoff to helm it. The film will use AI generations for the child and its wide range of canine breeds (with human voice actors) and adult actors for select live-action scenes. “I wanted to make a film that needed to be made with AI,” van der Velden, whose Particle 6 will produce the movie, tells The Hollywood Reporter . “Dogs are talking so that’s never really been possible [as convincingly] with normal animation or CGI before, and also you never want to shoot with dogs and toddlers. We’re using AI in a whole new way,” she adds. (You can see a teaser below.) Perhaps most notable for the project is the recruitment of Minkoff, the veteran family filmmaker (he also directed the first two Stuart Little films and in 2014 was behind the well-regarded DreamWorks Animation sci-fi adventure Mr. Peabody & Sherman) — and whose involvement can’t but be seen as a coup for the AI upstarts of van der Velden and Particle 6. “Eline pitched the idea to me and I thought ‘this is the best use-case of the technology,’” Minkoff tells THR, hastening to add that he is not involved in any way with nor does he endorse Tilly Norwood. “I’ve worked with animals and I’ve worked with children and I known how difficult it is. With animals in particular it borders on the inhuman to put them through the paces of a movie set. And now we can bring them to life in the way the story needs without any of that.” The film’s use of an AI generation for a two-year-old is also a good use case, Minkoff says; he used human toddlers for Stuart Little and found such an effort wanting at best and often downright unfair, both to crew and child. Getting the animals in Storm Dogs to move congruously and convincingly, Minkoff acknowledged, won’t be in easy. Dogs shot in close up have very specific features of the kind AI can struggle to match, particularly from one scene to the next. van der Velden and her team built the tool using existing models; the group is also using the veteran 3D animation software Blender to create their work. The Particle 6 team — it also includes tech guru Filip Parulski, who says a group of new tools will “help us actually direct rather than spend time in the ‘AI casino'” — aim to show the above 2 1/2 minute proof-of- concept at select public events and to players in the industry. Minkoff estimates that developing the story and creating the right generations as well as script-polishing, editing, shooting live footage and other tasks to complete the film should take about a year — not an overnight process but also not the eons-long effort that animated and hybrid movies often require. (He is pictured below right, working on the movie.) The film is being financed via a private donor who is behind Particle 6 and will be seeking studio distribution deeper into the process. Producers hope that Storm Dogs offers a kind of business disruption as well. Given their costs, animated family films tend to be financed and produced mainly by large studios.But AI can sufficiently reduce costs, van der Velden and Minkoff say, that it could allow for a new indie flowering in the space as well — only with technology instead of private equity and foreign pre-sales. Minkoff says that as much as the movie could serve as a proving ground for AI in family films, he doesn’t want audiences to notice or even know how he made it. “We are all the in the magic business; all of these tools are meant to serve an illusion,” he says. “If people are aware of the magician then they’re paying attention to the wrong thing.” Minkoff is touching on an issue that will only become more prevalent. Hollywood likes to hide the ball under the tophat. But it doesn’t want to be engaging in rampant deepfakes either, and how to use AI without making audiences feel like they’re being misled will be among the challenges filmmakers face as they roll out AI generations more widely. The 40-year animation and family-entertainment veteran says he does find parallels in this regard to CGI animation. “With that tech I thought the early tests were incredibly crude and a computer wasn’t going to revolutionize the animation business; people weren’t going to go for it. And now we see how that’s evolved,” he says. “I think we will see the same thing here.” van der Velden says she’d understand why some might be skeptical of what she’s doing with Storm Dogs given the auspices but feels the finished product will help overcome those reservations. “It’s a fun new way to tell a story that will hopefully bring a lot of joy to people,” she says. “This really is a wholesome family story that could not have been told this way before.” In general, she notes, “My husband says you can’t be doing pioneering work and expect everyone to love you, so you’ve just got to suck it up.” Meanwhile the Tilly train rattles on. van der Velden is producing the AI-generated sci-fi feature Misaligned with the character and rolled out the generation at a press tour in September to a fair amount of attention and nearly as much backlash. The appearance had some high-profile glitches, including an appearance on Piers Morgan’s show in which it spontaneously began speaking Chinese. But van der Velden says all of this is to be expected and furthers what she says is her true cause. “I definitely knew it was controversial when I started making her. But I also always knew my moral compass was in the right place and that she’s not here to replace any actors,” van der Velden says, continuing, “I wanted people to know before it’s here that this is happening, this is coming. I could have written a white paper but they weren’t going to listen to me if I’d done that. So I did it in a form that was a piece of art.” She added, “The result was what I wanted to achieve, which was awareness and people having the conversation. So the end point shows this was the right thing to do.” Rob Minkoff (r.) working on ‘Storm Dogs’ Particle 6 THR

articles.title: Katelin Arizmendi on Bringing a New Perspective to Action With ‘Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All November 10, 2026 7:42am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother,' Katelin Arizmendi Courtesy of Amazon MGM Studios/Theo Wargo In Bassam Tariq ’s Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother , cinematographer Katelin Arizmendi takes on the action genre for the first time, bringing a distinctive visual sensibility to a film that moves between crime thriller, family drama and spiritual meditation. At its center is Latif ( Mahershala Ali ), a devout Muslim and professional assassin whose world is upended by his wife’s death and the demands of caring for their three children, in particular the search for breast milk to feed his newborn daughter. The unusual setup gives Tariq and Arizmendi a new way, within the structure of an action film, to tell a story about masculinity, faith and fatherhood, as concerned with emotional vulnerability as it is with physical violence. Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother premiered in Toronto and was released in the U.S. via Amazon MGM Studios on Sept. 25. Related Stories News David Walliams Revealed as Previously Unnamed Celebrity Alleged to Have "Preyed on Teenage Girls for Sex" Movies 'Aroma' Takes a Sensory Trip Into Loneliness, Fantasy and Forbidden Desire (Exclusive Tallinn Trailer, Chat) Speaking with THR at the TorunCamerimage festival, Arizmendi discussed finding that visual language with Tariq, the practical challenges of shooting the film’s elaborate action sequences and the experience of being a woman cinematographer working in a still very male-dominated field. What was your first conversation with the director about the film? Was it about the visual design, or did you start with the story? It’s always about the story and the characters for every project. I like to at least talk about that first before I start bringing up ideas visually. I told him what I was drawn to in the script, which is that it’s a fresh take on a usually more masculine genre of action movies. It’s about something this man is striving for, which is breast milk, which has no material value to it. But I also had a really strong connection with his daughter, who I pointed out I wanted to share as much weight as him, because she’s sort of the one who always shines a mirror back on him. And then, obviously, there’s the spiritual side of this, his spiritual struggle with his faith. I’m not a Muslim, so I was asking a little bit of questions about his faith. It started to naturally progress into some visual ideas, and then I made a visual deck that I presented, and we went through that. So first conversations are always just about my connection to the project. From left: Adia as Fatiha, Mahershala Ali as Latif and Jahleel Kamara as Qadir in Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother . Jaclyn Martinez/Amazon Content Services When you started talking specifically about the visuals, what were the key points? Were there particular touchstones or references you were looking at? I tend to always choose projects where there’s much more of a first-person perspective. So we knew that this story needed to be told through Latif, and that would guide how we would frame things, where the camera would be, or even whether we’d be focused on the back of his head during a scene, even if someone’s talking to him out of focus. We knew this would be a very subjective film. But progressively, it also becomes more subjective through his daughter, Fatiha [Adia]. By the end, you feel like you’re more with her during this journey. I had never done an action movie before, so I had some ideas, and I knew what I didn’t want to do. I didn’t want to have two films: a film that felt very emotional and grounded in the visuals, and then suddenly you go to an action scene and it’s a different movie. I wanted to make sure those married visually and felt cohesive. But you still have to shoot action in a certain way because you have to cheat some of the punches and the impact of hits and things like that. It’s tricky because I could have done every scene in one shot, like Oldboy or something, and been happy with that. But we also needed to make these action scenes feel very different, so they don’t just end up with the same visual language, and they needed to get more and more elevated, so the end really feels more epic. Ali’s Latif (right) with John Cho as Pastor Hwan in Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother . Jaclyn Martinez/Amazon Content Services We came up with different adjectives to assign to each fight. The first one is really about brutality, precision and calmness. We need to see that he’s a skillful killer. That guided how the camera was locked off and on a long lens, so it felt a little more abstract. I didn’t want to give it all away right away. The second fight scene is the strip club, where he’s mostly thinking about his baby, Aziza. It’s Aziza, Aziza, Aziza. That fight is messy and it’s always moving. That helped guide the camera, which was constantly panning around the room, shooting through reflections on Steadicam, tracking with him. There’s a messiness to the camera work as well. The third fight is the fight in his home, so it’s in his sacred space. There’s an awareness of his family and his kids and his wife. He feels remorseful. By thinking of those things, we knew we should be in a wide shot here. When he kills this man, we’re taking in the entire room and we see his kids’ artwork on the wall and the presence of his family around. The last one was really about being a warrior, revenge and epic scale. We referenced samurai films a little more and wanted that to feel really epic. We tried to do as few shots as possible. We designed a couple of Steadicam shots, and then there’s also what we call the transcendental perspective. Before or after every action scene, there’s a massive high-angle, bird’s-eye shot. It alludes to this higher being that’s watching him and judging him for his actions. Latif and Qadir in Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother . Jaclyn Martinez/Amazon Content Services You’ll see that as he goes into the room where he’s going to have that final fight scene at the mansion. We stitched together the Steadicam shot and a crane shot that goes up overhead. We were also very aware of prayer times because there are very specific times when people pray, and I needed to be very honest about the lighting for that. Even though the apartment was on a stage, I couldn’t just decide that something would look a lot prettier with directional, low golden light coming in if it was really high noon. I had to be very honest about that. The film has the bones of a professional assassin revenge story, but the family and religious elements are quite different in tone. How did you approach those transitions visually? There’s a lot more intimacy and longer lenses in the family scenes, especially with the baby, and that was intentional. We wanted this real closeness with the family. But we also had to check ourselves every now and then because even within those scenes, we had to remember to let things breathe and pull out into wides. At first, we started finding the lenses that we loved, and we found that we were on a really tight shot with a long lens, 100 millimeter. We were like, “Well, the studio is going to say something if we don’t start pulling out into these wides.” For the fight sequences, by the end we ended up on a pretty wide lens for the Steadicam shots. But I tend to prefer shooting with every lens you have in your set and finding a purpose for it and marrying it together. I don’t really love it when you’re not playing enough or experimenting enough with different ways to move the camera or different lens choices. I kind of already work that way, being able to marry scenes shot with really wide lenses with other scenes shot very intimately. So that flow was kind of natural to me already. Ultimately, what grounds each scene, whether we’re shooting an action sequence or an emotional beat, is the emotion of the action sequences. As soon as we grounded it back to that, it felt much more like the same film. The fight scene in his house, for example, we shot over about two and a half days. It was extremely fast, and we didn’t have time to get a shot that I felt was very important: a moment of breath when he falls into his kid’s room. It’s a high-angle, slow-motion shot that pulls up, and you realize he’s just destroyed his sacred space. I fought for us to get that because if it’s just this fight sequence, you start to lose that emotional connection with the characters. Keeping things like that in made it feel more cohesive. Ali in Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother . Jaclyn Martinez/Amazon Content Services Can you give me a technical breakdown of what you shot on, in terms of cameras and lenses? We shot on Alexa 35 with Panavision Variel lenses and Primo zooms, with a little bit of LF (Large Format) sprinkled in for more scale and scope. I had an incredible colorist, Damien Vandercruyssen, who added film texture in post and made it look as close to film as possible. What was it like doing your first action film? Have you developed a taste for it? I shot second unit for Dune , so I had done action, but I wasn’t designing those sequences. My job on Dune was mostly to keep the visual language of the second unit cohesive with the first unit. But I loved it. I love a challenge, and I love trying different genres and different kinds of scripts. I would do it again as long as I felt that, at the core of the story, the script outside of the action was something I cared about. I’ve turned down action movies that just felt like there wasn’t anything there for me to resonate with. Do you have a personal favorite shot in the film? I guess it would be the shot that sort of breaks reality and goes underneath into water, when his daughter is praying for him and she brings him back to life. That shot was actually inspired by a video that our incredible production designer, Akeem McKenzie, sent me. It was of these kids who were shooting with a DSLR through water. We’d been discussing what this moment would look like visually because it needed a really epic moment. Basically, Bassam was like, “The rest of the film’s not going to work unless we can figure out something that’s so exciting for him coming back to life.” I saw this video, and then I had the idea to start on him and make it look like we’re moving through the ground, then coming up underneath him, and it’s water. There’s significance in Islam for water. It signifies mercy, so that made sense. I approached the art director, Shawn [D. Bronson] and asked him to come up with a rig that we could do practically because I felt we needed to see the space practically through the water. It would be very hard to do this on a blue screen, or it would feel different. It’s a platform, and the camera can get below with a Libra head and then end up shooting through the water. The VFX made it look like the platform was still the floor. Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother Courtesy of Amazon MGM Studios Women cinematographers are much more visible in the industry now, including among Oscar winners . But is gender still an issue in the industry? I would say it’s still a problem. I’ve faced a lot of misogyny, even on this movie. Even when you get the job, sometimes you have to really prove yourself. I was basically treated by somebody who needed someone to blame for us not being able to make the schedule, way before we even started shooting. It was like, “Oh, well, she normally takes two hours to get her first shot up,” because he had talked to other ADs I’d worked with. I was like: “You’re comparing it to a movie that was shot in the desert with animals, where it was the director’s first movie, and we were shooting on film.” It was just so obvious that he looked around a room full of men and said, “Oh, well, look at this young female DP, she doesn’t know what she’s doing.” I’ve had experiences where I don’t think about it at all, and it’s not like that. And then there are times when I’m reminded, “Oh yeah, I am a woman, and there is still misogyny out there and judgment.” But I’ve also come up in a time that’s much easier for women than it was even for DPs 10 years older than me, and I’m very grateful for that. In some ways, it’s probably helped my career more than been a hindrance. I’ve come up in a time when people are more excited about hiring a woman. I also realize that by not wanting to talk about the fact that I’m a woman, I’m not really helping anything. I’ve stopped doing that. I’ve accepted the fact that I’m in a proud place in my career, and I have a lot of eyes on me. If I just don’t talk about the fact that I’m a woman, then I’m not helping any of the women who are aspiring to be where I am. You need to see more women in these roles. You have to see that you can do it to be able to want to try to do it. Seeing that there are women shooting action movies may mean there will be more women who want to do it because they know it’s possible. And it doesn’t all have to look a certain way, either. You can bring a sensitivity to it. THR

articles.title: Brandon Sklenar on ‘Iron Jane,’ Body Dysmorphia and His Rapid Hollywood Rise
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content Brandon Sklenar Leo Jacob Brandon Sklenar is taking a moment to catch his breath. Over the past few years, the 36-year-old actor has watched his career explode with co-starring roles in Taylor Sheridan’s Paramount+ series 1923 , the much-discussed Blake Lively drama It Ends With Us , the South by Southwest sensation Drop and The Housemaid , Lionsgate’s $400 million-grossing erotic thriller starring Sydney Sweeney and Amanda Seyfried. And he has four more star vehicles expected next year — Paramount’s contemporary Western The Rescue , Warner Bros.’ special forces thriller F.A.S.T. , scripted by Sheridan; Ramin Bahrani’s romantic thriller Vegas: A Love Story , opposite Maika Monroe; and Lissette Feliciano’s female bodybuilding drama Iron Jane , co-starring Eiza González . Related Stories Movies Katelin Arizmendi on Bringing a New Perspective to Action With 'Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother' News David Walliams Revealed as Previously Unnamed Celebrity Alleged to Have "Preyed on Teenage Girls for Sex" “I’ve pretty much been going nonstop for the last few years, and only just very recently, in the last couple months, have I had a moment of stillness to take stock,” Sklenar says. “And now that I can stop and look around, I’m like, ‘What the fuck? This is crazy.’” He adds: “I mean, I can sort of see the linear progression of my career, but the opportunities that have been afforded to me in the last year or so have made me feel incredibly lucky.” Sklenar grew up in New Jersey, and his journey to Hollywood stardom is the stuff of vintage kid-makes-good stories — the sort of old-school outsider triumph that has grown increasingly rare in the era of nepo babies, influencers and YouTube crossovers. “I was with a girl at the time, and we just put all our shit in garbage bags and didn’t tell anybody,” he says of his move west right after high school. “And we just drove, literally in the middle of the night, like a Bruce Springsteen song. It’s so cliché, but it’s true. We just left.” A month or two after arriving in Los Angeles, Sklenar approached a stranger outside Mel’s Diner on Sunset Boulevard to bum a smoke. The man turned out to be a manager, who told him he “had a great look” and invited him to perform a scene from A Streetcar Named Desire, later helping him find an agent. Years of background work, acting classes, plays and small film roles followed before 1923 gave him his breakthrough as Spencer Dutton, the adventurer at the heart of Sheridan’s Yellowstone prequel. Before his next wave of projects reaches audiences, Sklenar now says he’s taking a moment to focus on his well-being (he just recently kicked smoking). “I’m trying to check in and just see where I’m at — mentally, physically and spiritually — so I’m ready for whatever the next chapter is,” he explains. “I want to try to strengthen my foundation a little before the next train leaves the station, because the last one went like a fucking rocket.” Iron Jane is among the projects Highland Film Group is presenting to buyers at this week’s American Film Market ahead of an expected festival launch next year. Written and directed by Lissette Feliciano ( Women Is Losers ), the film stars Eiza González ( Baby Driver, 3 Body Problem ) as Janie John, a woman who turns to competitive bodybuilding after a childhood marked by neglect. Under the guidance of a former champion played by Sklenar, she embarks on a punishing physical transformation, finding recognition and a sense of control even as her pursuit of perfection threatens to consume her. Sklenar is a first-time producer on the project through his recently launched Vista Lane Pictures banner. CAA Media Finance and WME Independent are handling U.S. rights. The Hollywood Reporter recently caught up with Sklenar by phone from Atlanta to discuss the creation of Iron Jane and why it’s an especially meaningful film for him. Where are you? I understand you were shooting something today. How’d it go? I’m in Atlanta right now. I’m doing additional photography for this movie, The Rescue , I have coming out next year. We’re adding some extra scenes to the movie. I had been off for a bit, doing home stuff and whatnot, and now I’m back on set, and I’ve got a fake mustache on and a wig — and it’s kind of tormenting me! It’s always so funny when you have to put on a fake mustache and have to try not to feel like an idiot. You know what I mean? I’ve never been in that situation, but I can certainly imagine. It just feels so ridiculous. (Laughs.) There’s something about wearing a fake mustache that makes you acutely aware of the fact that you’re wearing a fake mustache. OK, let’s talk about Iron Jane . I think there are no fake mustaches in that one. No fake mustaches. I understand this was a film you were trying to help get made for a long time. Can you take me back to the start of the project for you? So I met Lissette Feliciano a couple years ago at a festival party. Jay Glazer, my partner in my company, Vista Lane, had met her and he introduced us. He mentioned she had this really great script about a female bodybuilder, and he thought I would respond to it. So I met her and we just really got on. She came to Santa Barbara, where I live, and we chatted and got to know each other. And I read her script, and I thought it was a really special story. I just loved the texture and the point of view that she has. The story was really coming from a deep, personal, emotional place for her and I really thought it was something I wanted to see. So I was like, “If I can have any hand in helping this become a reality, then it would be crazy for me not to do that.” And then over the next couple years, I was fortunate enough to step in enough good puddles that I somehow got to the place where I was able to help someone get a movie made. I woke up one day and I was like, “Oh, apparently I am now in that position. So let’s make your movie.” Eiza coming on board was also a huge part of that. So it was a best-case scenario, really. Tell me a little more about the story and your character. You play a former bodybuilder, right? Iron Jane is an inspiring, classic underdog story in a sense, but it’s also very fantastic. It has a very hopeful spirit, and it’s very cinematic, colorful and vibrant — very much like the world of competitive female bodybuilding. There’s a sense of pageantry to the whole piece. There’s the glitter and the lights, and their bodies are just insane, but at the core, it’s a heartfelt story about a woman trying to take control of her life and better herself. I personally was drawn to it because I grew up in northern New Jersey working in an underground bodybuilding gym. When I was 15, I was cleaning the floors, and by 18, I was a trainer, training everybody and running the whole gym. There was an MMA gym upstairs, and I would just train MMA all day and then train other people. I started doing martial arts when I was really little, like six. So I was living in that bubble for years, and I understood this world very specifically. I’ve trained with Mr. Olympias and seen them pose — the diets, the steroids, everything. And there is an element of Iron Jane that really goes into body image and body dysmorphia, which is something that I just really feel needs to be talked about more, especially in this age of social media and fitness influencers. This is something I’ve struggled with, so we really wanted to translate that, and Lissette was really open to working with me on getting across [my character] Josh’s dysmorphia and what he goes through. Josh is a former bodybuilding champion. He was on that path a decade ago, and then he got injured. His body just couldn’t do it. He didn’t have the genetics. Now he trains people and coaches them to be champions and compete on that stage. He meets Jane and takes her under his wing, and he just really puts himself into her entire world — her burning desire to feel better about herself, physically and emotionally. So he trains her to take control of her body and become Iron Jane. Are you comfortable talking about your own experience with body dysmorphia? How do you cope with that? Yeah, for sure. It’s something I’ve had since I was a kid. I was a little kid — short, chunky. I swam in a T-shirt and got made fun of. Then I had a growth spurt and became really lanky, and I got made fun of for that. So I started training a lot and got obsessed with working out, like, “I’ll show them.” And then it became a kind of obsession, and it becomes a very weird thing, where you see yourself completely differently than pretty much anybody else does, and usually in not a good way. It’s very much an ongoing process. Therapy helps for sure. If you look at me now as a 36-year-old man, you’d never guess it, but I still very much feel like that 12-year-old chunky kid — that sense of nothing is ever good enough. You have to find a way to check your self-talk, because that’s really where it begins and ends — but it’s easier said than done. I imagine you and Eiza had to train quite a lot and put on muscle to prepare for the film? I trained in a very specific way for the film, but it wasn’t necessarily about bulking up. I put on a bunch of size for another film I had done earlier in the year. I’m starring in this film Taylor Sheridan wrote called F.A.S.T. for Warners. It’s coming out in May. I played a Delta Force operator, and I got massive. So I was still kind of working with that foundation. For Josh, I wanted it to feel real. He’s a guy who used to be really big, but he’s not broadcasting his body anymore. He’s just a fit guy now. So I didn’t want to overdo the preparation, because you can tell when actors do that. Where there’s a shot of their body, and it’s like, “This was my shirtless day,” and they’ve done the water-dehydration thing, and now they’re unnaturally cut. I wanted Josh to feel much more lived-in and natural. There is a scene where my body is fully on display, and I’m posing, and the camera’s panning up and down — and I was so nervous. I’ve been pretty much naked in a film before, but it’s a whole different thing to literally be posing and have the camera panning up and down your body, detailing everything. When I was shooting that scene, I was so uncomfortable. Dealing with my issues, it was very challenging to work through that. But at the same time, I was thinking about Eiza, because she had to do that the entire fucking film. Every scene is about her body on some level. So, I was like, “Goddamn, if I feel this way, I can’t imagine how she feels.” She trained for I don’t know how many months, but that woman put in serious fucking work. It’s really hard for women to put on that amount of muscle. My partner is a trainer and a nutritionist, and I know how difficult it is. You’ve got to eat so much. But Eiza trained her ass off, and she got in incredible shape for this film. I just have so much respect for her. As you mentioned earlier, you’ve started your own production banner, Vista Lane Pictures. What is the motivation and vision behind that? Well, when I first set out to be involved in film, I always wanted to produce and direct. So the idea that maybe I could help shape the projects I’m involved in was very appealing to me. I’ve been fortunate enough to work with some great producers, who I’ve been able to learn a lot from. The company is still in its infancy. We got this first-look deal from Lionsgate, which we’re incredibly grateful for. I’m just trying to soak up and learn as much as I can. I love acting more than anything in the world and I want to make interesting choices. I want to be involved in films that are purely about the spectacle and taking people on an exciting ride, and also I want to do films that aren’t purely commercial, where we tell a unique, universal story — and maybe I can even change my own life by playing a character that will help me understand how to be a better son, father or husband. Selfishly, I just want to play the widest range of characters I possibly can. So if I’ve hit a point in my career where maybe I can help myself do that by starting my own company, why wouldn’t I, right? THR

articles.title: Christopher Briney and Michelle Randolph Star in Trailer for Prime Video’s Holiday Rom-Com ‘Clashing Through the Snow’
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Nicole Fell Plus Icon Nicole Fell Associate Editor nicolemfell Follow Sign Up View All November 10, 2026 8:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Clashing Through The Snow' Christopher Briney and Michelle Randolph are channeling their best rivals-to-lovers in the newly released trailer for Prime Video’s Clashing Through the Snow . The pair star as rival publishing editors in the film from Carlson Young. The trailer starts with a voiceover introducing the characters Hannah (Randolph) and Ryan (Briney). It cuts to the characters dressed as Santa and Mrs. Claus, with the voiceover explaining that it bets the audience is wondering how they ended up in that situation. Hoping to both score the book that’ll save their job over the others, Briney and Randolph are forced to make a journey to New York together that doesn’t go as planned, all set to Olivia Rodrigo’s new holiday single “Take Me Home (4 Christmas).” When they find Lukas Gage’s character in a seemingly haunted inn, Briney’s Ryan tells Hannah, “If I get murdered in my sleep, I will haunt you, aggressively.” Related Stories Movies Dwayne Johnson and Jack Black Get Flirty in 'Jumanji: Open World' Trailer Movies Nicolas Cage Is Unrecognizable in 'Best Pancakes in the County' Trailer “In this romantic comedy, a holiday snowstorm strands rival publishing editors Ryan Mitchell (Briney) and Hannah Hendricks (Randolph) at the airport, forcing them into a shared rental car for a cross-country race to New York,” the synopsis reads. “With budget cuts threatening to eliminate one of their jobs, both are secretly chasing a career-saving deal, turning every mile into a high-stakes showdown. But between roadside mishaps, unexpected detours and small-town charm, the holiday spirit has a way of melting even the fiercest rivalry into something neither of them saw coming.” Clashing Through the Snow is directed by Young and written by Danny Mackey and Rebecca Ewing. Briney, Randolph and Gage are joined by a supporting cast of Andrew Schulz, Julia Fox and Paris Hilton. McG, Mary Viola, Lena Roklin and Bruce Wayne Gillies produce the film. The holiday rom-com drops on Prime Video on Nov. 23. Watch the trailer below. THR

articles.title: Don’t Have 210 Spare GBs? ‘GTA VI’ Is Coming to Xbox Cloud Gaming (and the Xbox One) at Launch
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All November 10, 2026 8:19am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Grand Theft Auto VI Rockstar Games Grand Theft Auto VI is coming to Xbox Cloud Gaming at launch (Nov. 19), and will be playable on both the current-generation consoles (Xbox Series X|S) and the prior one (Xbox One). You read that right: Xbox One . Xbox said on Tuesday that GTA VI is “the most pre-ordered title of all time on the Microsoft Store.” The console-maker “encourage(s) everyone to begin pre-loading as soon as possible to ensure you’re prepared for launch day.” GTA VI is so massive (210 gbs) that it will take at least 10 hours to download. Many players will have to delete a number of other games from their library just to fit Grand Theft Auto VI . (You don’t lose ownership of the game, but you just have to re-install it to play again.) Or… don’t use a console at all! Grand Theft Auto VI will be playable on day one via Cloud Gaming at 1 a.m. ET. The game uses Xbox Series S graphics settings when cloud-streamed. (So actually downloading the game will still present the best-looking option for those with an Xbox Series X.) To cloud play, which allows for play away from your primary console, one still must purchase the game. PlayStation players do not (currently) have the cloud-play option, though the PlayStation 5 Pro still provides the single-best GTA VI playing experience possible. Win some, lose some. Here is a handy, Xbox-provided guide to how and when you can play Grand Theft Auto VI on or through its consoles: XBOX Series X: Play natively with the best XBOX console experience, available now to pre-install. XBOX Series S: The most affordable way to play GTA VI natively on XBOX, available now to pre-install. XBOX One: Stream Grand Theft Auto VI through XBOX Cloud Gaming on the XBOX One. You’ll need one of those three devices — smart TVs, browsers and devices like Amazon Fire sticks won’t cut it (for now). Other Rockstar Games like Grand Theft Auto V and Red Dead Redemption 2 are coming to Xbox Cloud Gaming “in the coming months,” Xbox said. Additionally, starting Wednesday, players in 29 supported markets can “buy cloud playtime to stream supported games without a Game Pass subscription,” per Xbox. (For 10 hours: $3.99, for 25 hours: $7.99, for 50 hours: $11.99.) THR

articles.title: Jann Arden, Cassandra Naud, Hunter Cardinal Lead ‘Expiry Date’ Dark Dramedy (Exclusive)
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All November 10, 2026 8:25am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jann Arden, Hunter Cardinal, Cassandra Naud, Rylan Oleksyn Fear and Desire Productions Top Canadian singer-songwriter Jann Arden, Influencer star Cassandra Naud and Hunter Cardinal ( BET ) have nabbed lead roles in Expiry Date, a dark cancer dramedy from writer and director Rylan Oleksyn. Naud plays Jessica and Cardinal is Milton, two young people living with terminal cancer. While initially clashing, they eventually find friendship and comic relief as they deal with family tensions and differing attitudes to treatment and possibly dying young. Arden, who along with Naud identifies as a queer artist, plays Jessica’s mother. Related Stories TV 'Nobody Wants This' Star Timothy Simons Reveals Biggest Season 3 Concern and Looks to Season 4: "They Burned One Another -- So They're Even" Movies 'Steps' Review: A Stellar Voice Cast Including Amanda Seyfried, Ali Wong and Bette Midler Gets Stuck in a Tortured Revisionist Fairy Tale “Jessica pushes Milton to take chances, while Milton helps Jessica confront what she has been avoiding. The film finds humor in their disagreements without losing sight of the circumstances that bring them together,” a synopsis from the producers states. The film, director Oleksyn’s first feature that expands on an earlier short film of the same name, draws on the filmmaker’s experience in losing family members to a deadly disease. “Cancer has ripped holes in my family multiple times,” Oleksyn said in a statement. “With this film, I wanted to explore what these brave people can teach everyone who is lucky enough to stay healthy. I hope people will laugh, I hope people will cry, and I hope people will take it as a reminder of how quickly everything can go away, so go live.” Arden, a multi-platinum recording artist and entertainer, as an actor co-created, executive produced and starred in the comedy Jann picked up by Hulu. Naud stars in Shudder ’s Influencer and the sequel Influencers , also appeared in Mike Flanagan’s Carrie series for Prime Video and has film and TV credits that include It’s a Wonderful Knife , opposite Joel McHale, and the series Tracker and Loudermilk. Cardinal plays Michael in Netflix ’s BET live action TV adaptation of the hit Japanese manga thriller Kakegurui and has appeared in CBS’s Sheriff Country. He is also an indigenous artist and a veteran stage actor. Expiry Date is shooting in Tisdale, Saskatchewan and is produced by Ryan Reaney and Kurtis Burke. Steven Gary Banks is executive producing. “Working on Expiry Date is pretty kick ass. The entire town of Tisdale, Saskatchewan is behind Rylan and his crew. Great script, great actors, all coming together to make something wonderful,” Arden, a veteran of 16 studio albums and concert touring, said in a statement. THR

articles.title: Alexander Skarsgard to Narrate Quinn Audio Erotica Original Set in World of ‘Wicker’
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Lexy Perez Plus Icon Lexy Perez Senior Digital Editor and Producer View All November 10, 2026 8:29am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Alexander Skarsgard Quinn The Wicker phenomenon is now venturing into audio erotica. Wicker star Alexander Skarsgard will narrate Felled , the winning entry in a fan-fiction contest inspired by the world of Black Bear’s hit film, for audio erotica app Quinn , it was announced Tuesday. Last month, ahead of the film’s theatrical release, Quinn partnered with Wicker to launch a fan-fiction contest inviting fans to create original stories set in the world of the film. With hundreds of submissions from around the world, Emma Parkinson’s Felled was selected as the winning entry. Related Stories Movies 'Godzilla Minus Zero' Powers $31M in Historic Box Office Launch Against Subdued 'Cat in the Hat' Movies 'You Can See Everything,' 'Clayface' Fighting for No. 1 in Quiet Halloween Weekend The story follows a willow tree that forms a deep attachment to a farmer’s daughter before being cut down. When they reunite years later, they discover that their bond has endured. “I haven’t really experienced this before, where I’ve been part of a project that has taken on a life of its own like this,“ Skarsgard said in a statement. “It’s also been really fun and inspiring to see how creative people are.” When asked what drew him to collaborate with Quinn, Skarsgard said, “It was quite refreshing to have something sensual and erotic that wasn’t androcentric for a change!” “ Wicker fans have been so passionate about the film since day one, so partnering was a no-brainer,” says Caroline Spiegel, founder and CEO of Quinn. “There were hundreds of incredible, creative stories about mermen, porcelain men, witches and more. Felled stood out, and we knew our users had to hear Alexander narrate it.” From directors, co-writers and real-life married couple Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer, Black Bear’s Wicker has taken on a life of its own, going viral on social media and becoming an erotic, meme-making phenomenon. The film, released on Oct. 23 and based on author Ursula Wills-Jones’s short story The Wicker Husband , follows “an ostracized fisherwoman ( Olivia Colman ) who commissions a husband made of wicker (Skarsgard) from the local basketmaker (Peter Dinklage). When her new husband awakens her desires and captures the village’s attention, jealousy, fascination and chaos follow, challenging the conventions of marriage, sex and the rules that bind them.“ “We always thought of the sex scenes as the comedy of the film, too,“ Wilson told THR . “They were supposed to be played for laughs, and they are. But I think once we actually had Alexander in costume, Olivia and Ita O’Brien, our intimacy coordinator, working together on these scenes — that’s when they did become surprisingly more sexy than we thought they would.“ The film even features a full frontal look but only when the Colman’s fisherwoman is looking at the nude wicker man off in the distance in the water. Felled is the latest Quinn original series to be added to the company’s growing catalog of produced romances that have enlisted Hollywood talent. Other stars who have lent their voices to Quinn originals include Wilson Bethel, Chris Briney , Andrew Scott, Manny Jacinto, Tom Blyth , Jamie Campbell Bower, Victoria Pedretti, Jesse Williams, Lucien Laviscount, Thomas Doherty, Katherine Moennig, Costa D’Angelo , Tyriq Withers, Shawn Hatosy , Sam Heughan and Matt Smith. Stars who have teamed for Quinn duet productions include Love Hypothesis stars Tom Bateman and Lili Reinhart ( Olympus U) , Heated Rivalry stars Hudson Williams and Connor Storrie ( Ember & Ice ) and Off Campus stars Mika Abdalla and Stephen Kalyn ( Rent Free ). Felled by Emma Parkinson, narrated by Skarsgard, is available now on Quinn. Alexander Skarsgard for Quinn x Wicker ‘s Felled Quinn THR

articles.title: R.J. Mitte’s Final Director Dedicates Film to Late Actor: “I Can’t Believe He’s Not Here to See It”
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Jeffrey Levine, as Told to Jackie Strause Plus Icon Jeffrey Levine, as Told to Jackie Strause View All November 10, 2026 8:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source RJ Mitte at a screening of 'Talking To Strangers' on Sept. 30 in Beverly Hills, California. Unique Nicole/Getty Images Jeffrey Levine is executive producer of Morph Media , and producer/writer/director on R.J. Mitte ’s final movie, SNAFU: Situation Normal All F’d Up (working title). *** This is the beginning of a beautiful friendship. That was how I felt the last time I saw R.J. Mitte. Several weeks before his death, I drove R.J. to the airport. We had just finished filming for our movie that R.J. was featured in. R.J. was leaving Los Angeles and was heading back home for a quick turnaround to London for a convention. Related Stories Movies Giancarlo Esposito and John Turturro Hated Each Other on 'Do the Right Thing.' Now They Break Character to Cry Mid-Scene News R.J. Mitte's Mother Shares Tribute After His Death: "We Are Lost Without Him" The ride took about two hours, and when we arrived at LAX, I got out of the car and I hugged him. I said, “I’ll see you soon.” And he said what he always said, “Let me know if you need anything.” That’s just who R.J. was. My experience with R.J. was over a shorter period of time than many of the people who have been speaking out since his unexpected death. There are a lot of people who knew R.J. better than me. But he was the type of person where it didn’t matter how long or how short you knew him. Once you did, you knew the real him. He wasn’t an actor who just did a scene and left. He was bigger than that, a positive force, and we were just starting our friendship. I first met R.J. in May of this year, when our executive producer, Bradford Rand, cast him in our movie, SNAFU: Situation Normal All F’d Up (working title). We had our first conversation over Zoom, the three of us, about him playing an AI executive in our social impact film. It began as a smaller part. And from the second Bradford put me on the phone with R.J. and he heard that our mission for the film was to impact the lives of kids, he said, “I’m in.” That was my experience with him from that day on. We would talk about the character and the story, because R.J. really cared about this movie, and his role evolved as we produced the film. It became very important for me to have an impactful character arc for him. In the story — after criminals exploit the protagonist’s teenage son — R.J.’s character, an AI developer, is asked to help, and he begins to reflect on the far-reaching negative impact of AI. R.J.’s character uses his position for good and, in the end, he faces a pivotal decision on whether or not to walk away from his high-paying executive job to create what I am hoping someone with influence will one day execute: a global AI regulation company. R.J. Mitte and Jeffrey Lewis on set. Courtesy The film will inform parents about the dangers of social media and AI, but in a commercial and entertaining way. The objective is for parents to be able to start a dialogue with their kids about the far-reaching effects of AI, social media and our changing media landscape. And it’s R.J.’s character who says, “Enough. We have to do something.” It’s such an impactful character, and I just can’t believe he’s not here today to see it. Our independent film deals with mental health, which isn’t lost on me now. We wrapped filming not too long ago. We’re currently in post-production. We are in talks on distribution and hope to get the film in front of as many people as possible. But as I’m watching assemblies now, it’s emotionally wrenching. And then there’s R.J.’s extensive behind-the-scenes video addressing AI, and I can’t bring myself to watch that right now. R.J.’s scenes were so good. It’s crazy how his authenticity carries on screen through the character. Pure talent. Being a part of our project, for R.J., was always about the impact. It was never about money or fame. He wanted the character to be as true, real and impactful as he could be. And he delivered in spades. This film is the first in a slate for our social impact feature division. I couldn’t imagine a better person to carry this torch. I find myself thinking about R.J. and all the things we talked about, and all the things he truly cared about — his mom and his sister and his fiancé and his work with the Mitte Foundation . R.J. was pure good. It’s a level of human being you don’t see very often. During our two-hour drive to the airport, he spoke about his foundation and what he wanted to do. He truly wanted to make a difference. He felt like he had a deeper purpose. I asked, “How can we help?” And we talked details, and I’m confident that we will. We’ve been working with the Sentinel Foundation, which deals with the exploitation of kids, and its Clinical Director, Dr. Ashley Poklar, who flew out to be on set during filming. The end of our movie will include a QR code that will direct viewers to resources, both for parents to be able to talk to their children, and for teens who may be going through something and need to know where to go for help. When I would finish directing a scene with R.J., he’d say, “Are you happy, Jeff? Because if you’re happy, I’m happy.” I am so sad that he suffered and that this happened. What we can do for R.J. now is to keep our promise. Honor what we set out to do, and why he signed up to make our film in the first place. Create awareness, dialogue and impact as many people as we can. Our film is dedicated to R.J., and for anybody who is going through something. We want our message to reach anyone who needs to hear it. You are never alone. I didn’t know R.J. for a very long time. But the time I knew him, I’ll never forget. THR

articles.title: Is the Hope at AFM Real?
articles.full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All November 10, 2026 8:55am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Elizabeth Holmes in You Can See Everything Courtesy of A24 Film execs heading to L.A. for the American Film Market may be feeling something they haven’t in a while: hope. Disruption still reigns, but independent and specialty fare has had a run of breakouts at the North American box office, topped by this weekend’s launch of Godzilla Minus Zero . The sequel from GKIDS and Toho opened to an estimated $32 million, well above the distributor’s mid-$20 millions projection. Takashi Yamazaki’s follow-up to the Oscar-winning Godzilla Minus One (2023) reportedly cost in the mid-teens and is being touted as the biggest live-action foreign-language opening since 2004’s Hero , which bowed with $17.8 million. Related Stories Movies Brandon Sklenar on 'Iron Jane,' Body Dysmorphia and His Rapid Hollywood Rise Movies Claes Bang, Valerie Pachner Drama 'I Is Another' Sells Wide Ahead of AFM It isn’t the only surprise. A24’s You Can See Everything , the Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, is entering blockbuster territory, having grossed almost $80 million domestically. That’s a rare result for nonfiction in a theatrical market that has been unkind to documentaries, and the film is only beginning to roll out internationally. Niche programming is delivering, too. Angel Studios’ faith-based Drummer Boy , from directors Ben and Joel David Smallbone, opened to around $9 million. Nitesh Tiwari’s Indian epic Ramayana: Rise of a Legend , handled in the U.S. by Sony, grossed an estimated $8.6 million in its first weekend, on the widest domestic launch ever for an Indian film. Add this year’s indie horror run, from Obsession ($500 million worldwide and counting) to Backrooms ($400 million-plus) and the self-distributed Iron Lung ($50 million-plus), and the makings of a good-vibes AFM are in place. For sellers, the biggest takeaway is that audiences are showing up, and that they are young. Sarah Lebutsch, head of sales at U.K. group Protagonist Pictures, points to You Can See Everything as proof that a smart campaign and the right timing can still produce a hit. “Look at what You Can See Everything is doing at the moment in the U.S. It’s incredible,” she says. She is equally encouraged by who is buying tickets. “It’s great to see those sorts of box office results, and the fact that Gen Z are going, and Gen Alpha are going and seeing films together in cinemas,” Lebutsch says. “There is a big resurgence of that, which I think we should all be very, very encouraged by.” Policy may help, too. California Gov. Gavin Newsom is pushing a major expansion of the state’s film and TV tax credit program, proposing to raise the annual credit from $750 million to $1 billion. The incentive has been crucial for keeping projects in the state. Newsom is also backing the bipartisan effort in Congress, championed by President Trump, to create a national film and TV tax incentive that would stack with each state’s own credits. For indie producers piecing together financing, having a federal layer on top of state incentives would be a significant and much-needed change. The presale market, long AFM’s foundation, also appears to be holding up. “At Protagonist, we’ve always done very well out of the AFM,” Lebutsch says. “Presales have always worked really well for us there. The big buyers from across the world, they’ll all be there to pick up packages.” Protagonist will be shopping It’s All Right , with Paul Bettany as an aging rock star and Asha Banks as a rising singer who, unbeknownst to her, is his forgotten daughter from a one-night stand. The online creator-to-director pipeline will be a major talking point at this year’s AFM. Seemingly all the hot young horror directors honed their craft, and built their respective fan bases, online before their theatrical breakouts. “The film industry can certainly learn from creators that storytelling doesn’t need to be limited necessarily to strict forms,” says veteran horror producer Steven Schneider ( Paranormal Activity , Insidious ), whose Spooky Pictures recently scored a hit with Hokum , which has grossed $25 million worldwide on a $5 million budget. “Stories can begin online, narratives can be told, shared and expanded through shortform videos and parsed out over time in a way that builds awareness and excitement. Creators have shown incredible prowess in meeting their audiences where they’re at.” But Schneider cautions that success online does not always translate to cinemas. “Traditional storytelling conventions and techniques are established for good reason,” he says. “We want to innovate and bridge the gap between an online audience and a theatrical one, but it’s important to respect the differences in the form.” Traditional filmmaking, he argues, can “connect more deeply and profoundly with an audience through intricate storytelling,” and that craft “shouldn’t be dismissed in favor of virality or easy dopamine hits.” Not every indie package at AFM will become the next Obsession or You Can See Everything . But audiences are returning, U.S. tax incentives are on the horizon and a new generation of filmmakers is packing theaters with younger fans. For a market that for years felt like it was in terminal decline, that’s reason enough to cheer. THR

articles.title: David Walliams Shows, Including ‘Little Britain,’ Removed From BBC Streaming Platform
articles.full_text: × Nov 10, 2026 8:02am PT David Walliams Shows, Including ‘Little Britain,’ Removed From BBC Streaming Platform By Leo Barraclough Plus Icon Leo Barraclough International Features Editor LeoBarraclough Latest David Walliams Shows, Including ‘Little Britain,’ Removed From BBC Streaming Platform 32 minutes ago David Walliams Speaks Out on Allegations: ‘I Am Not a Sexual Predator’ 1 hour ago Fantastic Fest Award Winner ‘Bloody Tennis,’ Starring Sandra Guldberg Kampp and Helena Zengel, Sells to Further Territories (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Matt Lucas (left) and David Walliams in "Little Britain" (Courtesy of BBC/Everett Collection) The BBC has said it will remove from its streaming platform those shows, including “Little Britain,” that star or were written by British comedian, author and former “Britain’s Got Talent” judge David Walliams , after allegations that he was a sexual predator were published on Tuesday by the Guardian. The newspaper alleged that Walliams “groomed fans he met when they were as young as 15 and harassed women in the workplace over a number of years.” He denies the allegations. Related Stories Olivia Rodrigo, Katseye and Sienna Spiro to Be Honored at Variety’s 10th Annual Hitmakers Event Raye Wins Mercury Prize for Album of the Year Among the allegations, which were made during a joint investigation by the Guardian and ITN, is that Walliams was “predatory” and “pushy,” repeatedly contacting young women either via social media or modelling agencies, inviting them to his home or his dressing room at “Britain’s Got Talent.” One woman, who became friendly with the comedian after he contacted her, said he would “constantly pester her for sex.” A spokesperson for the BBC said: “These are serious allegations. As such, the BBC is looking carefully at all material featuring and written by David Walliams on our platforms. “We are in the process of removing some programs, including ‘Little Britain,’ whilst this review is underway.” Walliams was a judge on “Britain’s Got Talent” for 10 seasons, but his offer to appear in the 2023 season of the ITV show was withdrawn after the Guardian alleged he made sexually explicit remarks about two performers.
