articles.full_text: × Nov 10, 2026 8:11am PT Sofia Franklyn on ‘Call Her Daddy,’ Alex Cooper and Hopes for a Scripted Adaptation of Her Memoir: ‘I Spent the First Few Years Very Scared. Now I’m Good’ Franklyn's memoir "Daddy Issues" hits shelves Nov. 10. By Anna Tingley Plus Icon Anna Tingley Latest Sofia Franklyn on ‘Call Her Daddy,’ Alex Cooper and Hopes for a Scripted Adaptation of Her Memoir: ‘I Spent the First Few Years Very Scared. Now I’m Good’ 34 minutes ago Hollywood Is Obsessed With a Cheeky Slogan Tee 24 hours ago David Schwimmer Reunites With His Famous Red Sweater From ‘Friends’ in Nostalgic Quince Campaign 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source It’s a week before Sofia Franklyn ’s memoir, “Daddy Issues,” officially releases, and for the most part, her nerves have settled. “It depends on the day,” she says over Zoom from a hotel room in New York City, one of her two home bases. Franklyn, who splits her time between New York and Italy with her husband, is back in town for a packed month of press. “I would say 90% of the time I’m incredibly excited.” Related Stories Olivia Rodrigo, Katseye and Sienna Spiro to Be Honored at Variety’s 10th Annual Hitmakers Event Raye Named Variety’s 2026 Hitmaker of the Year But the road to telling her side of the explosive “ Call Her Daddy ” breakup with Alex Cooper has hardly been smooth. When Franklyn first announced the book in February, her agent received a phone call from Matt Kaplan, Cooper’s husband and business partner, allegedly screaming on the other end, as Franklyn recounts in the book’s foreword. Anticipating the backlash, Franklyn had already booked an island getaway to escape the noise. This time, though, she has no plans to disappear. “I don’t feel a need to,” she says. “I’m in such a different place than I was six years ago.” The 240-page memoir, which hits shelves Nov. 10, is split into three parts: her childhood and upbringing in Salt Lake City, Utah, with her single mom, who had her at 20 years old after a one-night stand; her post-college move to New York City, where she met and moved in with Cooper and launched the “Call Her Daddy” podcast; and, perhaps the meatiest section, her side of their dramatic breakup and the experience of watching the podcast she helped create become a multimillion-dollar media empire — without her. She now has the Unwell Network, a name she says she came up with herself for merch years earlier, blocked on social media. “I found myself sobbing at parts that I thought I was so completely healed over,” she says of revisiting these moments over the past year. Many of the details she shares in the book are already out there (that Cooper was being paid more without Franklyn knowing; that Cooper secretly met with Barstool Sports founder Dave Portnoy to negotiate a deal without Franklyn). But the memoir also reveals new details about the behind-the-scenes operations of “Call Her Daddy,” including the involvement of Cooper’s childhood friend Muji Fricke, who, according to Franklyn, was on the podcast’s payroll for a short time before Cooper fired him without warning. “She’s gonna fuck you,” Franklyn remembers Muji telling her. According to Franklyn, Muji was an integral part of the “Call Her Daddy” podcast, even feeding Cooper some of her most memorable bits, including the viral “Gluck Gluck 3000” joke. “I realize it’s one of several jokes – like saying her favorite porn star is Lisa Ann on an IG Q&A – Alex has made that could not have come from the mind of a white, blond college athlete,” Franklyn writes in the book. She continues: “Muji’s ideas become central to the show, and especially to Alex’s persona: an overtly sexual, clout-chasing WAG wannabe. Off-camera, Alex and I don’t even find a lot of Muji’s sexual humor funny. But we take his knowledge – the good, the bad and the ugly of sports and dudes – and put it on Alex, a dabbing hardo white girl in a push-up bra…Comedy gold.” His involvement was largely unknown until now. “This is how the show was put together,” Franklyn says, “and I don’t think people actually know.” As a childhood friend of Cooper’s, Muji also had firsthand knowledge of her personality before the fame. “Cooper doesn’t have friends,” Franklyn remembers him telling her. “I’ve watched it happen since high school.” He was also one of the few people Cooper confided in during the early stages of “Call Her Daddy” — and, according to Franklyn, warned her that even then, Cooper didn’t have her back. “Even at the beginning she would take the lines I wrote for you, or just cut all of yours,” he allegedly told Franklyn. She remembers clocking those early warnings but still feeling an inherent sense of trust. She couldn’t imagine that her best friend and roommate, with whom she spent nearly every waking hour, could be capable of that level of betrayal. “I clocked it, but I think my knee-jerk reaction was to just run over to Alex. I was so close with her that I thought, there’s a reason that he’s saying that, and she’s gonna explain it to me.” “But I did clock it,” she says. “And I did start to wonder about how she functions in her friendships.” By now, the general story of their breakup is largely known. It dates back to 2020 when Cooper and Franklyn, then two years into their wildly successful podcast, sought to renegotiate their three-year contract with Barstool Sports, which owned the show’s IP. Portnoy offered the co-hosts a deal that included $500,000 annual salaries, a larger cut of merchandise revenue and full ownership of the podcast’s IP after one more year at Barstool. Cooper wanted to accept; Franklyn did not, maintaining that the terms were still unfavorable. Cooper eventually went behind Franklyn’s back to negotiate a separate deal with Portnoy, returning to the podcast as its sole host in May 2020. Cooper went on to secure a reported $60 million Spotify deal in 2021, followed by a $125 million deal with SiriusXM in 2024, while Franklyn launched her own podcast, “Sofia With an F.” Unsurprisingly, this period felt like rock bottom for Franklyn. She turned to alcohol, drugs and nicotine, moved back in with her mom and experienced intense paranoia. “I get fucked up to remove myself from the vortex of pain, of betrayal, and loss,” she writes. At one point, she snaps when her mom takes out her phone, paranoid that even she might be secretly recording her to sell the footage online. With the power of Barstool behind Cooper, the public largely believed her side of the story and painted Franklyn as a villain. Over time, that narrative has shifted. “The audience is smarter now, they understand media a bit better,” Franklyn says, marveling that TikTok didn’t even exist when they first started “Call Her Daddy.” “Now they understand how things work.” It helped when, earlier this year, influencer Alix Earle had her own highly publicized falling-out with Cooper after parting ways with her Unwell Network in 2025. Earle, who launched her “Hot Mess” podcast under the network in 2023, later accused Cooper of being “manipulative and toxic,” claiming she received little production support and learned of her departure through the press. Cooper has disputed Earle’s account, with the feud drawing renewed scrutiny of her business dealings. “Alix and I have obviously shown each other public support,” Franklyn says. “There was, and I hope this doesn’t come out the wrong way, some validation in seeing that.” “I remember my mom and I were both kind of emotional about it because we had been put in this world where you didn’t know what was real and why that happened to me,” she continues. “And so to see it play out in a very different way, but in a very similar way…there was some validation in that. But I obviously felt terrible for Alix.” Others have confided in Franklyn about their own experiences with Cooper. But sparingly, she says. “People are very scared.” It’s a feeling she can empathize with. “I did spend the first few years very scared, and sometimes I will catch myself being a bit guarded or a bit paranoid, but it’s very rare,” she says. “Now I’m good. I’m back to normal, back to how I…” she trails off. “Even better than I was before “Call Her Daddy.'” While she’s ready to put this phase of her life behind her, she’s also not totally done telling her side of the story. She’s hoping for a scripted adaptation of her memoir sometime down the line. “Nothing’s confirmed,” she clarifies. “I’m just hoping to put that out in the universe.” She’s learned many lessons over the past six years. The biggest takeaway? “Some people you meet don’t turn out to be what you thought.” “But you can’t live your life keeping yourself protected,” she concludes. “If you’re doing that, you’re not living your life.” Julia Garner Says Madonna Biopic Status Changes ‘Every Hour,’ But She’d ‘Love for the Movie to Get Made’ Fantastic Fest Award Winner ‘Bloody Tennis,’ Starring Sandra Guldberg Kampp and Helena Zengel, Sells to Further Territories (EXCLUSIVE) Phil Rosenthal’s ‘Somebody Feeds Phil’ Flies to YouTube From Netflix, With Lift From United DC Studios’ New Boss Jeremy Latcham Has a ‘Guiding Light’ for Superhero Movies: Would My Grandma Like It? ‘You Have to Make Them for Everybody’ Nurse John Sets 2027 Tour (EXCLUSIVE) Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Designates the Troubadour as a Landmark Venue; Going Forward, L.A. Will Host Hall’s Induction Ceremony ‘At Least Every Other Year’ (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments...

articles.title: AFM 2026: Indie Film Faces a Tougher Market — But Theatrical Breakouts Offer Hope
articles.full_text: × Nov 10, 2026 8:15am PT AFM 2026: Indie Film Faces a Tougher Market — But Theatrical Breakouts Offer Hope By Elsa Keslassy Plus Icon Elsa Keslassy International Correspondent @elsakeslassy Latest AFM 2026: Indie Film Faces a Tougher Market — But Theatrical Breakouts Offer Hope 31 minutes ago How the American French Film Festival Is Bringing French Cinema to 3,000 Los Angeles High School Students With Packed Screenings of ‘In Waves’ 15 hours ago French Judo Legend Teddy Riner Announces 2027 Presidential Bid, Drawing Praise From Emmanuel Macron 15 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source River courtesy TIFF The indie film biz head into this year’s American Film Market amid one of the industry’s most tumultuous periods in recent memory. The completion of Paramount Skydance’s merger with Warner Bros. Discovery and Netflix’s leadership shake-up have triggered a wave of layoffs and cuts within the last month, while streamers across the board are becoming much more selective about acquisitions. For indie producers, sales agents and distributors, the upheaval means fewer buyers and projects, and an increasingly competitive marketplace. Yet the business has also been reshaped in ways that give reason for optimism. Theatrical is once again the engine of the indie economy, and Gen Z audiences are driving some of the year’s surprise hits, from “Obsession” to “Backrooms,” and, most recently, the nearly three-hour doc “You Can See Everything.” “We’re going to see so many more of these stories dominating in the box office. It’s what audiences want to see. If you look at the data and you look at what’s happening in the industry, the strongest, the best-positioned players in this sector are the independents,” says Jackie Brenneman, a former top executive at the National Assn. of Theatre Owners, who in January was appointed president and CEO of the Independent Film & Television Alliance, which organizes the American Film Market. Related Stories Olivia Rodrigo, Katseye and Sienna Spiro to Be Honored at Variety’s 10th Annual Hitmakers Event Raye to Headline BST Hyde Park With Sienna Spiro Opening AFM runs Nov. 10-15. Brenneman is preparing to oversee her first AFM with an expanded program aimed at attracting more filmmakers, financiers, exhibitors and technology companies to “show the broader industry why independent films are incredibly investable and why you should be bullish on independent film.” AFM also faces fresh competition from Toronto’s new market, but accreditation numbers for the L.A.-set event are on par with last year, with more than 80 countries represented among registered buyers. The U.S. leads, followed by Germany, the U.K., South Korea, Spain and France. China is also returning after several years of limited turnout. Heading into AFM, the mood among buyers and sellers is hopeful but cautious, with several predicting a busy market. “There are a lot of people crossing their fingers that it’s a strong market and there’s a lot of stuff there. I think the appetite is there for movies, especially after Toronto. The projects just need to be there,” says Scott Shooman, head of IFC Entertainment Group. Fabien Westerhoff, CEO of London-based European sales outfit Film Constellation, describes the current mood as a “dual, conflicting emotional state.” On one hand, he points to over-indexing specialty titles such as his company’s queer adult animation “Jim Queen,” which grossed $3 million at the French box office, and the doc feature “The History of Concrete,” which just passed $2.5 million in the U.S. Such hits, he says, have reinvigorated specialty distributors after years of “streaming hegemony.” On the other hand, Westerhoff says the “box office is extremely polarized around a handful of films, which isn’t healthy.” Domestic box office reached $8.28 billion from Jan. 1 through Oct. 28, up 20.8% from the same period in 2025, according to Box Office Mojo, but at the same time, fewer films are getting a real shot, as only 68 features had wide releases through summer 2026, down 14% from the same period in 2019, according to Rentrak. For David Atlan-Jackson, chief operating officer of European distribution group Vuelta, the business has narrowed to a single question: Does the film work in cinemas? “We’ve entered an increasingly binary, black-and-white market. Either a film gets a theatrical release or it essentially disappears. Television broadcasters have pulled back considerably, and everything now depends on theatrical success,” says the executive, whose banner is behind Bertrand Bonello’s next film “Santo Subito!,” starring Mark Ruffalo and Charlotte Rampling, which is in post-production and has yet to land a U.S. deal. “Every other revenue stream has become a multiplier of theatrical performance. If your film doesn’t succeed theatrically, you’re facing a real commercial failure. There’s very little middle ground anymore,” says Atlan-Jackson. A soft opening in theaters isn’t always fatal, though, points out Nick Shumaker, head of AC Independent, the sales and finance arm of Anonymous Content. “Look at the success of ‘The Apprentice’ on VOD: It got released, but it certainly didn’t solicit the theatrical numbers that I think some people would have really wanted it to, but it over-indexed on VOD in a huge way without ever finding a streaming home for obvious reasons,” he says. He hopes the same will be true for Alex Gibney’s “Musk,” which has struggled in theaters but is he says “is second only to ‘The Odyssey’ in VOD preorders on Apple. … We’re already seeing the Elon Musk film over-index on VOD pre-orders and it’s a four-hour film,” he says. Shooman agrees, pointing to three IFC releases this year, “Forbidden Fruits,” “Over Your Dead Body” and “Motor City,” which didn’t turn out to be box office hits but went on to perform well on VOD. The films that do break through are also proving harder to predict. A24’s “You Can See Everything” has become one of the year’s most improbable B.O. sensations, bolstered by social media buzz. It grossed $15.6 million during its opening weekend and has since climbed to more than $45 million domestically. Creator-driven films such as “Obsession” and “Backrooms” have also shown the appeal of projects built around online audiences. “What’s exciting is knowing success can come from anywhere: a found-footage horror, a politically socially relevant documentary, or a classic historical melodrama that moves you to tears,” says Westerhoff. Buyers, he says, “want films that can be eventized, generate word-of-mouth and fandom.” Shooman says the year’s surprises haven’t changed his thinking. “Does it make me rethink what’s a commercially viable film? No. I think the same holds true in that if you have a unique perspective, great access, a filmmaking talent, a story that people want to talk about, that still is, I think, at the core of moviegoing,” he says. “And when you look at the box office this year, three independent films had a bigger second weekend off of the semi-wide first weekend, being ‘Buddy,’ ‘You Can See Everything’ and ‘Obsession.’ So I think there is an appetite for audiences to come back. They want something that they can talk about.” The breakouts of “Backrooms” and “Obsession” have also sent buyers scrambling for the next creator-filmmaker. “I think everyone this summer suddenly said, ‘Oh, we have to scrub the internet for YouTubers because of ‘Backrooms’ and ‘Obsession.’ But the reality is the younger audience is a lot more welcoming to genre films, and YouTube is just where a new generation of filmmakers who have a phone and a laptop and can create content on their own are exhibiting their art,” says Shooman, who also notes that the biggest deals at major festivals consistently are genre films, citing “River,” “Leviticus,” “Talk to Me” and “Obsession.” Brenneman is looking to bring digital creators into the AFM fold with the launch of the Global Screen Economy Summit, which will feature a dedicated creator-economy discussion with executives from Spotter, Kynetic Media Ventures and Bamboo Bridge, along with creator entrepreneur Tyler Chou. “Some creator filmmakers are going to just be filmmakers, and some of them are going to want to become studios and sales agents. And those are the ones I need to ensure are part of IFTA. They are not a threat, they’re more people making and selling content across borders,” she says. “So anyone who is in that business belongs at AFM, belongs in our tent, and belongs on our stages.” Financing is getting more complicated and with pre-sales harder to come by, the money behind independent films is also changing. “Equity has stepped in,” says Westerhoff. He adds that equity brings “downward pressure” on budgets and more reliance on soft money to limit commercial exposure. “That’s why we structure our projects around European shoots, leveraging equity against international and U.S. rights.” Pre-sales remain essential above a certain budget, says Shumaker. “You just have to be really specific about the films and realistic about what the expectations are in terms of the necessity of presales to greenlight certain types of films. We’ve been happy on Mia Hansen-Løve’s new film [‘If Love Should Die’] in terms of the presales on that. So again, it really just depends on the film. If you’ve got a $50 million or $60 million action film, you need to pre-sell a whole bunch to greenlight that film.” In Europe, ambitious projects increasingly get financed through multi-territory co-productions, with the budget raised from several countries and production spending allocated accordingly. That’s the case with “Santo Subito!,” which is produced by Mandarin in France, with Vuelta co-producing in Italy, where much of the film is being shot. While the U.S. box office rebound is good news for international players, they’re lamenting the scarcity of buzzy American projects available for indie buyers and the growing difficulty of securing domestic distribution. If a film doesn’t get a U.S. theatrical release or ends up going directly to a streaming platform, “it becomes much harder for us to establish it in our territories,” says Atlan-Jackson. Shumaker points out it’s always been hard to find distribution in the U.S. “There’s a paradigmatic shift that has been happening for quite some time where a lot of distributors either want to be involved in third-party films earlier, or they are developing their own material. So as a result, they’re not buying as much at the completed film stage, with exceptions,” says Shumaker, citing Netflix’s acquisitions of “La Bola Negra” and “Gentle Monster,” which were unveiled at Cannes. Powerhouse indies, such as A24 and Neon, are in the position to not only acquire worldwide rights and but also handle international sales themselves. “I consider them studios. They’re not just producing their own films. They’re also acquiring films and controlling their international distribution, and when they resell the film internationally, they charge significantly more than the original sales agent would have,” says Atlan-Jackson. He uses “Club Kid,” Jordan Firstman’s Cannes breakout, as an example: A24 bought worldwide rights for $17 million from UTA and Charades at the festival after a bidding war. “‘Club Kid’ became much more expensive for independent distributors through A24 than it had been through Charades,” says Atlan-Jackson, noting that “they handle the marketing, the awards campaigns, the theatrical release — everything. They give the film real value. And naturally, they want to capitalize on the value they’ve created. That’s why they can resell a film for three, four or five times the original price.” Yet for international buyers balking at pricey U.S. packages, Shooman has a ready answer. “International buyers tend to complain all the time, and all it takes is them having pre-bought an ‘Obsession’ or a ‘River’ or a ‘Backrooms’ or a ‘You Can See Everything’ for that thing they felt like maybe they paid too much for to end up being a fantastic deal,” says Shooman. Alex Ritman contributed to this report. articles.title: From a Mockbuster Version of ‘The Odyssey’ to a ‘Jiu-Jitsu Nun’: How Producers Are Keeping the Low-Budget Film Market Alive Via Streaming and FAST Channels (and Even Lower Budgets)
articles.full_text: × Nov 10, 2026 8:15am PT From a Mockbuster Version of ‘The Odyssey’ to a ‘Jiu-Jitsu Nun’: How Producers Are Keeping the Low-Budget Film Market Alive Via Streaming and FAST Channels (and Even Lower Budgets) By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest From a Mockbuster Version of ‘The Odyssey’ to a ‘Jiu-Jitsu Nun’: How Producers Are Keeping the Low-Budget Film Market Alive Via Streaming and FAST Channels (and Even Lower Budgets) 31 minutes ago Kiah Roache-Turner Reunites With ‘Furiosa’ Star Alyla Browne on ‘Horrifically Creepy’ Road Movie Horror ‘Don’t Look’: ‘There Are Scenes That Are Going to Traumatize People’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Former Hello Sunshine and AGC Studios Execs Wifreddy Chiang and Anant Tamirisa Launch Baseline Media 24 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy The Asylum “Our journey begins with the Cyclops,” says a ginger-bearded and bald Odysseus somewhat nonchalantly in the trailer for “ The Odyssey ,” moments before a giant one-eyed AI-generated monster bursts onto the screens. The film, based — rather loosely — on Homer’s epic poem, released this summer and was met with mostly comic derision and a flurry of one-star reviews. “Dumb, ridiculous, embarrassing, nonsensical,” wrote one online critic. “Not a single redeeming feature,” bellowed another. But this “Odyssey” was not Christopher Nolan’s $250 million “Odyssey,” the epic from Universal, something many online said they’d discovered only after buying the film online. Nor was this the “historical accurate” retelling touted by Elon Musk and made using Grok. This was the $250,000 version from the Asylum , the B-movie icons and American Film Market stalwarts both loved and loathed for its vast number of so-called “mockbuster” rip-offs, its cult “Sharknado” franchise and an array of ludicrous film posters often involving multiple-headed monsters. In fairness, “The Odyssey” — thanks to being in the public domain for roughly 2,500 years — isn’t strictly a mockbuster. The title didn’t need to be tweaked for copyright reasons, like the Asylum did with other self-aware cash-ins “Top Gunner,” “The Da Vinci Treasure,” “Jurassic Domination,” “Alien Disclosure Day,” “Immortal Combat” and many more. But the film was absolutely made and timed to ride on the $125 million M&A coattails of Universal’s pic and, the company claims, succeeded. “It performed very well,” says David Rimawi, CEO and co-founder of the Asylum. “We’ve said this before, but we’ve found there’s a direct correlation between how well the studio film does and how well ours does. If it’s a hit, ours is generally a hit as well.” Related Stories Raye Wins Mercury Prize for Album of the Year Raye Named Variety’s 2026 Hitmaker of the Year “The Odyssey” Courtesy of The Asylum Other recent Asylum mockbuster hits include “The Last Hail M.A.R.Y.,” a sci-fi with a similar Earth-saving theme to Amazon MGM’s “Project Hail Mary” (but, instead of a CGI alien rock creature, it’s “a dude with some prosthetics,” says the Asylum co-founder David Latt); “The Mummy,” a totally different horror story to “Lee Cronin’s The Mummy” yet released around the same time; and, more recently, zombie copycat “Resident Dead.” (The company notes that it chose not to make a low-budget version of “Digger”). But success today is markedly different to how it was two decades ago. Back in 2005, the Asylum shocked itself by selling around 100,000 DVDs of its $500,000 “War of the Worlds,” its first — and, it claims, mostly coincidental — mockbuster, released just a day before Paramount’s Tom Cruise-led behemoth. In the years that followed, its DVDs — often cunningly designed to look like a major Hollywood release or with outlandish graphics that disguised the tiny budget — would line the shelves at Walmart, ready to lure in either the comically aware, cinematically curious, foolishly unsuspecting or just plain short-sighted. (The latter is something the Asylum tipped a meta and tongue-in-cheek hat at in its 25th anniversary title “2025 Armageddon,” featuring a scene in which a grandmother mistakenly buys one of its DVDs rather than a studio film.) But that highly-profitable physical market has long since come crashing down and, with it, the spoils. For its slate of mockbusters, monster thrillers and disaster movies, the Asylum now operates in what Rimawi describes as the “tiny margin world” of digital, mostly reliant on volume and the occasional breakout to lift the overall tide. “We actually have to make more to make a little,” notes Latt. There is still business to be made, however, with ad-based streaming platforms, such as Tubi, Roku and Pluto TV having come to the rescue in recent years. “This is where our customers and the Asylum found each other again, and if you’re watching the wrong movie, you can gloriously just jump to the next,” he says. “It’s the core of our business model now.” There’s also the ad-based FAST channel (the Asylum has its own), plus cable-based rental and purchasing transactions, although Rimawi says this business has largely shifted to Amazon, where “some films can do nothing, but some can be massive hits — that’s where our big performances come.” Curiously, the Asylum also still shifts around 10,000-20,000 DVDs a year at Walmart. “It’s baffling to us,” notes Rimawi. “I think people just use it like a rental store.” The Asylum may be keeping itself afloat in its own shark-infested waters, but lurking further into the independent film depths, for fellow makers of wild genre titles, the challenges of today’s world seem even greater. ITN Studios has spent years churning out scores of low-budget horror and action-thriller titles about clowns, dolls, dinosaurs, scarecrows, sharks and other classic baddies. This year it comes to AFM with a slate including the wonderfully named “Mary Magnum: Jiu-Jitsu Nun” (a thriller about a former military sharpshooter who breaks out of a convent to rescue her former lesbian lover). The film isn’t its first featuring a woman of the cloth. Its “Bad Nun” franchise launched in 2018 (the same year Corin Hardy’s supernatural horror “The Nun” stormed the box office). With the DVD market gone, ITN is also plying its trade across platforms like Amazon, Roku, Xumo, Pluto, Peacock, Tubi and YouTube, many of them with revenue share agreements. “But it’s definitely a lot harder now,” says ITN CEO Stuart Alson, who says operating as a volume business is the only way to survive. “If you’re trying to make it or break it on one film at a time, that’s what can be challenging. But if you have a slate of films and you’re constantly putting films out, some win, some lose.” Thanks to ITN’s impressive library of more than 1,000 titles (just a few years ago it was releasing almost 100 a year), many of its older films have long since broken even — meaning any new earnings, however minuscule, help to keep the lights on. Courtesy of ITN Studios But for others, due to a growing oversaturation in low-budget genre, both the opportunities to grab money-generating eyeballs and the budgets to make these films have been dramatically squeezed. About five years ago, Alson says he was financing films in the $30,000 and under range, but even this microbudget has now more than halved. “You’ve got people making movies for $5,000,” he says. Brit duo Scott Champer and Rhys Frake-Waterfield were among those making scores of cheap-as-chips horrors for ITN, but thanks to their slasher smash hit “Winnie-the-Pooh: Blood and Honey” (ITN’s biggest success to date), they are now focused on their own “Poohniverse” of murderous children’s characters (the third “Winnie” film is currently in post). But they assert that the low-budget genre arena where they once thrived is dying out. With films, and so many of them, now battling for attention on VOD platforms, the pair claim that where DVDs in the past could effectively fool people into thinking a movie is a higher-budget production, online you simply can’t hide. “Often the trailer appears instantly, and straight away you can tell,” says Chambers, adding that the immediate availability of online reviews and IMDb ratings also plays into it. “People are just becoming more savvy,” adds Frake-Waterfield. “If it looks too low budget, why would you invest $5 when you could rent, I don’t know, ‘John Wick’?” While many in the industry might turn their noses up at this schlocky corner of low-budget filmmaking, there’ll be little to celebrate were it to actually vanish. As Chambers and Frake-Waterfield note, it’s an area where emerging filmmakers can learn their craft, as they did. But there are also many who love it for what it is. For all the angry reactions to the Asylum’s “The Odyssey” knock-off, there were plenty rejoicing in the audacity of the film’s existence and its unashamedly cheap, so-bad-its-good quality. “I’ve never laughed so hard,” said one, cheering at a supposed Greek warship that was “nothing more than a little rowboat.” It’s too early to know the exact financials of the film — the figures from the various online platforms and the splits from the complex rent-sharing agreements can take months to come in. But with the $250 million blockbuster original having topped $1.6 billion at the box office, the Asylum is confident its version — coming in at a thousandth of the budget — can make at least more than $250,000 back. “We’re very happy with how it turned out,” says Latt. “So we’re now looking forward to Christopher Nolan’s ‘Iliad.’” ‘GTA 6’ Presales ‘Far in Excess’ of Expectations Ahead of Next Week’s Launch, Take-Two CEO Says Indian Paranormal Horror ‘Numinous’ Wraps, Fearfolks Takes First Look to AFM (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Heated Rivalry’ Final Episodes to Release in 4DX at Regal Theaters Kiah Roache-Turner Reunites With ‘Furiosa’ Star Alyla Browne on ‘Horrifically Creepy’ Road Movie Horror ‘Don’t Look’: ‘There Are Scenes That Are Going to Traumatize People’ (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Chasing Summer’ Director Josephine Decker Says That ‘Filmmaking Is Lonelier Than Ever,’ So It’s Time to Build a Community ‘De Gaulle,’ ‘La Gradiva’ and ‘Alice: Pioneer Of Cinema’ Among American French Film Fest Winners- Film News in Brief Loading comments...

articles.title: David Walliams Dropped by Agency Following ‘Grooming’ Allegations
articles.full_text: × Nov 10, 2026 8:21am PT David Walliams Dropped by Agency Following ‘Grooming’ Allegations By K.J. Yossman Plus Icon K.J. Yossman @KJYossman Latest As Russell Brand’s Begins a 10-Year Prison Sentence, Why Celebrities Fear the Power of an Expose 10 minutes ago David Walliams Dropped by Agency Following ‘Grooming’ Allegations 31 minutes ago David Walliams, Former ‘Britain’s Got Talent’ Judge, Accused of ‘Grooming Fans’ as Young as 15 After Failing to Get Injunction 4 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Tim Whitby Former “Britain’s Got Talent” star David Walliams has been dropped by Independent Talent Group following allegations of “grooming” and “harassment.” “ITG is deeply disturbed by the allegations concerning David Walliams,” said a spokesperson for the agency. “Our thoughts are with anyone who has been affected. We are no longer representing him in any capacity.” Walliams has been accused of grooming fans as young as 15 in a joint investigation by the Guardian and ITV News, who allege the comedian invited teenage girls over to his house, where they stayed over, and to his dressing rooms. They also allege he would “pester” and “pressure” young women, including models and an employee at his publisher HarperCollins, to go out with him and in some cases even take part in sexual activity. Related Stories Raye to Headline BST Hyde Park With Sienna Spiro Opening Raye Named Variety’s 2026 Hitmaker of the Year One alleged victim, who claims Walliams drove her to his house when she was 15 where he attempted to engage in sexual behavior, said she now regards the interaction as sexual assault. Walliams has denied all the allegations , saying: “I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me.” Last month Walliams attempted to obtain a High Court injunction to prevent ITV and the Guardian from publishing the allegations, although this was denied. Walliams rose to prominence for his comedy show “Little Britain” before becoming a judge on “Britain’s Got Talent.” He was dropped in 2022 after audio was leaked in which he made derogatory comments about some of the contestants. articles.title: AI Takes Center Stage at Tech-Forward AFM With Innovation Hub and AFM House Expansion
articles.full_text: × Nov 10, 2026 8:23am PT AI Takes Center Stage at Tech-Forward AFM With Innovation Hub and AFM House Expansion By Corbin Bolies Plus Icon Corbin Bolies Latest Elvis Music Owners, Eminem Publisher File Sprawling New Lawsuits Against AI Music Generator Suno: ‘The Next Elvis Won’t Pick Up a Guitar’ 3 days ago Netflix Names Mattel Executive Roberto Stanichi as VP of Consumer Products and Experiences 5 days ago How Grimes’ Cameo in Theater-Bound AI Film ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Came Together (EXCLUSIVE) 5 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy IFTA First it came for the films, then the film festivals. Now, AI has taken hold of this year’s American Film Market. The five-day independent film marketplace in Los Angeles, produced by the Independent Film and Television Alliance, already has a splashy year planned, with pic packages on offer, including a new Armando Iannucci film and A24’s expensive “Elden Ring” adaptation. But as producers and distributors go about buying and selling movies, they’ll do so as the film industry’s third rail — artificial intelligence — takes center stage. The 2026 edition will see the market’s Innovation Hub, a space where exhibitors showcase new technologies gripping Hollywood, expand into its inaugural “ AFM House,” a 15,000-square-foot space across from the AFM HQ at the Fairmont Century Plaza. The list of companies participating has also expanded, with nearly 20 firms eager to highlight their own technology and a suite of new panels discussing AI’s impact. The Hub launched last year in collaboration with the Marché du Film, the Cannes Film Festival’s cinema marketplace that proved to be very AI-friendly this year. But this year’s extensive expansion of the Hub, and the prominence of AI, represents the latest example of Hollywood’s growing tolerance for the technology in how films are produced, sold and distributed — all tenets of AFM. “Technology is going to be a key driver, no matter where you sit on kind of AI,” says Jackie Brenneman, who is shepherding her first AFM after taking the reins as IFTA president in January. “AI as a creative tool — there’s a lot more debate on that than AI as a really great way to analyze data and make predictions. That’s what AI has been doing for a long time, and so AI serves lots of different roles. At AFM, we’re not here to make a judgment call, but I do think that a lot of the tools … are much more in the latter [category], in using AI and data to help people make better decisions or do things better, faster, cheaper, and less on just AI as the next full-scale studio. But of course, we have room for all.” Such an expansion in space for the Innovation Hub means an expansion of the companies set to populate it. Returning to AFM is Largo.ai, a Sylvester Stallone-backed Swiss firm that uses AI to help brands, studios and creatives determine whether their idea is producible. The company was founded in 2018 as an offshoot of the Swiss university EPFL, back when AI was simply “machine learning” and the AI agents we’ve come to know and somewhat fear were merely the product of science fiction. Its collection of tools includes simulated focus groups and projections to see which actors could best fit a character, providing independent filmmakers with the tools usually reserved for the deep-pocketed Hollywood studios. Largo’s chief panel at AFM includes a “Shark Tank”-style pitch presentation, where producers working with the firm will showcase for distributors and financiers how Largo’s platform can help analyze the commercial viability of their projects. Sami Arpa, the firm’s CEO, says Largo is mindful of fears that film production can be too data-driven and argues the company is more “data-assisted” than eager to infuse AI into the creative process. “In the tools specifically, we never tell people what to do,” he says. “There are tools a bit going beyond that,” he admits. “They are replacing full human creativity. Obviously, people are feeling danger from that, and I think they have the right to feel that danger. But with our experience, we don’t think the audience is welcoming full AI-generated content if a human still is not at the center of the creativity.” For those in Hollywood who do want to create fully AI-generated content, enter Oxen.ai. The company, founded in 2022 by IBM veteran Greg Schoeninger, works as both a platform for creators to build AI shots with a selection of AI models and as a studio to produce AI shots for vendors. Some of the creatives who’ve used its tools come from Disney, Google and Live Nation. The platform differentiates itself from other similar all-in-one model aggregators such as Higgsfield and OpenArt by publicly outlining the token cost for each model it offers before anyone pays a cent, including the pennies it costs to use Black Forest Labs’ FLUX models and the $55-per-million tokens Claude’s Fable model requires. It adds a layer of transparency to the use of AI that’s often obscured by monthly subscription costs offered by competing platforms, a fact Schoeninger takes great pride in. “It’s a subtle thing, but it’s a huge reason people switch,” he says. Schoeninger says AFM approached the company about appearing in the new AFM House after the startup’s “Cmd+Shift+Create” summit in September. At that event, professionals across the AI and creative landscape met and showcased how they’re weaving the technology into their work. He says the market’s expanded embrace of the technology reflects the “tipping point” the industry has reached, one where more Hollywood luminaries and executives are willing to go public about how they’re using AI despite the fear expressed by some of their peers over its impact on human jobs and creativity. “‘Jurassic Park’ is one of the first movies to do full visual effects,” he says, noting the few minutes in the 1993 film that contained computer-generated imagery. “It just felt like there was way more because of how Steven Spielberg used it in the film. I feel like we’re kind of in that era right now where, yeah, you might get ripped on if you’re doing a whole film in AI, but if you just use it for those shots that you need it, it seamlessly fades into the background or helps bring the film to life.” AI is also a focal point of some of AFM’s panels, such as the Producers Guild of America’s panel on “the AI Decisions Facing Film and TV Leaders” on the market’s main stage. The Cine Group, a Paris-based company that works with cinema operators, is bringing its Marché du Film-backed Cinemas Club to the AFM House and hosting a panel on how non-generative AI in the industry is a “utility rather than Tilly” — as in Norwood, the AI actress rankling Hollywood’s creatives. Patrick von Sychowski, the Cine Group’s international editor-in-chief and moderator of the panel, says the discussion is meant to reflect how AI already has a stronghold across film, and “sticking your head in the sand is not a solution.” AFM is representative of that ethos in its willingness to showcase the technology, he adds. “AFM under IFTA is not just moving with the times, but trying to stay a step or two ahead of the times in terms of what is required at these kinds of get-togethers,” von Sychowski says. “It’s such a unique opportunity to get together in person and bring together the right people for discussions, for deals, everything.” Being so public about embracing the technology does harbor some risk. Take the case of Urbanworld, the BIPOC-focused film festival that lost a yearslong sponsor in the AI-averse Writers Guild of America over its decision to host an AI program for its 30th edition last month. Big A-list festivals, such as Cannes, exclude AI-generated films from their official lineups. But Brenneman, while sensitive to people’s fears over the technology, says the purpose of the marketplace is to allow producers and financiers to determine what types of films emerge for public consumption. If they decide it’s AI films, then so be it. “We’re not a festival,” she says. “We are not making selections. We do not make judgment calls. That’s for the buyers. You know, the buyers are the ones who get to decide who it is that they want to support, what art it is that they think is commercial. Our job is just to make sure that there’s a forum to enable that to happen.” Related Stories Raye Wins Mercury Prize for Album of the Year Raye Named Variety’s 2026 Hitmaker of the Year ‘Heated Rivalry’ Final Episodes to Release in 4DX at Regal Theaters Indian Paranormal Horror ‘Numinous’ Wraps, Fearfolks Takes First Look to AFM (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Ramayana’ Makes History as First Indian Film to Top U.K., Ireland Box Office as ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Debuts in Third ‘The ‘Burbs’ Ups RJ Cyler to Series Regular For Season 2; Daniel Ezra, Retta, Vincent Kartheiser Set as Recurring Guest Stars (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Overcompensating’ Season 2 Release Date: Benito Skinner Returns for a Steamy Spring Semester (TV News Roundup) CNN Sees Some Staff Buyouts Under Skydance Merger Plan Loading comments...

articles.title: Josh Van Valkenburg Named President of Universal Publishing Nashville, Troy Tomlinson Moves to Exclusive Advisor
articles.full_text: × Nov 10, 2026 8:36am PT Josh Van Valkenburg Named President of Universal Publishing Nashville, Troy Tomlinson Moves to Exclusive Advisor By Jem Aswad Plus Icon Jem Aswad Executive Editor, Music jemaswad Latest Raye Named Variety’s 2026 Hitmaker of the Year 37 minutes ago Kanye West Breaks His Own Record for Biggest Rap Concert in U.S. History — Again — With 83,132 Fans 24 hours ago Richard Lloyd, Television’s Fiery and Fluent Guitarist, Dies at 75 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Josh Van Valkenburg has been named president of Universal Music Publishing Group Nashville, it was announced by UMPG chairman & CEO Jody Gerson. Van Valkenburg will report to Gerson, be based in Nashville and assume his position on January 4, 2027, as longtime UMPG Nashville chairman & CEO Troy Tomlinson transitions to an exclusive advisory role, according to the announcement. Related Stories Raye Wins Mercury Prize for Album of the Year Raye to Headline BST Hyde Park With Sienna Spiro Opening In his new position, Van Valkenburg will oversee the management and creative direction of UMPG Nashville, leading the team in identifying, signing and developing emerging talent and supporting its acclaimed roster of songwriters, artists and producers. Van Valkenburg was most recently executive VP of creative at Sony Music Publishing Nashville, promoted to that role in 2021 after joining the company in 2015. Over the years he has worked closely with such talents as ASCAP Songwriter of the Year Josh Osborne, four-time BMI Songwriter of the Year Ross Copperman and SESAC Songwriter of the Year Jon Nite. He launched his music publishing career at EMI in 2006. In making the announcement, Gerson said, “Country music is more global today than at any time in its history, and the opportunities for Nashville’s songwriters have never been greater. Josh brings the vision, ambition and leadership skills to build on that momentum, along with deep relationships throughout the creative community and a gift for identifying and developing exceptional songwriters. I’m thrilled to welcome him to UMPG and look forward to all he and our Nashville team will accomplish together.” Van Valkenburg added, “Jody Gerson is an exceptional leader who remains steadfastly passionate about fighting for creatives and their art. I’m grateful for her trust and the opportunity to lead UMPG Nashville into its next chapter. I want to honor Troy Tomlinson for his genuine love of songwriters, his willingness to share his wisdom and experience with the many of us who look up to him, and his long-standing leadership within UMPG and the greater Nashville creative community.” Tomlinson has served as chairman and CEO of UMPG Nashville since 2019. Over more than four decades, he has worked closely with such artists as Taylor Swift, Kenny Chesney, Megan Moroney, Keith Urban, Luke Bryan, Brooks & Dunn and Kelsea Ballerini; and writers including Chase McGill, Tom Douglas, Tony Lane, Jim Beavers, Rodney Crowell, Dean Dillon and Casey Beathard. He previously served as President and CEO of Sony/ATV Nashville from 2005 to 2019, having joined the company in 2002. Before Sony/ATV, he spent 15 years at Acuff-Rose Music Publishing. He previously led the Nashville division of Fame Music Publishing. Of Tomlinson, Gerson said, “Having worked with Troy for nearly 15 years, first at Sony and then at UMPG, has been a gift, and I’m deeply grateful for his leadership and friendship. He is loved and respected throughout Nashville by the songwriters and artists he’s championed and, equally, by his countless colleagues across the industry. Troy is an icon in the Nashville and publishing communities, and I’m thrilled that, as he eases into retirement after such an illustrious career, he’s agreed to stay on as an advisor and continue sharing his wisdom and experience with us.” Tomlinson said, “Reuniting with Jody, an extraordinary leader and dear friend, has been deeply rewarding, and I’m proud of what we’ve built together. I’m also grateful to our Nashville team for their never-ending passion and commitment to songwriters. Having brought Josh onto our creative team at Sony/ATV many years back, I know firsthand his ear for songs, eye for talent and deep understanding of music publishing. I’m thrilled Josh will lead UMPG Nashville and confident he’ll take this team to new heights. After more than four decades in music publishing, I’m looking forward to more time with my family, especially spoiling my grandsons, and I’m deeply grateful to my wife for the love and care she’s given us all.” British Horror ‘Rise of the Rats,’ Dark-Web Chess Thriller ‘The Rules of the Game’ Head to AFM With Black Mandala, Red Owl (EXCLUSIVE) Jennifer Hudson Will Headline Vatican’s ‘Concert With the Poor,’ With Pope Leo Scheduled to Attend Julia Garner Says Madonna Biopic Status Changes ‘Every Hour,’ But She’d ‘Love for the Movie to Get Made’ ‘Ramayana’ Makes History as First Indian Film to Top U.K., Ireland Box Office as ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Debuts in Third ‘Heated Rivalry’ Final Episodes to Release in 4DX at Regal Theaters David Walliams, Former ‘Britain’s Got Talent’ Judge, Accused of ‘Grooming Fans’ as Young as 15 After Failing to Get Injunction Loading comments...

articles.title: Jordan Fisher to Star as the Kid in Broadway’s ‘Purple Rain’
articles.full_text: × Nov 10, 2026 8:37am PT Jordan Fisher to Star as the Kid in Broadway’s ‘Purple Rain’ By Rebecca Rubin Plus Icon Rebecca Rubin Senior Film and Media Reporter rebeccaarubin Latest Jordan Fisher to Star as the Kid in Broadway’s ‘Purple Rain’ 11 minutes ago David Ellison on DC Shakeup: Jeremy Latcham Will ‘Build the Future of DC,’ Praises James Gunn and Peter Safran’s ‘Passion’ 22 hours ago Box Office: ‘Heated Rivalry’ Fans Drive Show’s Theatrical Release to $1.4 Million 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jordan Fisher will portray “The Kid,” the iconic role made famous by Prince, in Broadway ‘s “ Purple Rain .” Fisher is a theater veteran, having appeared in musicals like “Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street,” “Moulin Rouge! The Musical,” “Dear Evan Hansen” and “Hamilton,” but this marks the first time he’s originating a role on Broadway. “We know that Jordan Fisher is an extraordinary talent, but what’s been thrilling about watching him inhabit ‘The Kid’ is discovering the fire beneath the surface: the swagger, vulnerability and restless creative spirit we recognize in Prince,” said director Saheem Ali. “Jordan brings all of that to the role, along with an infectious generosity that makes everyone around him better. He’s finding something raw, surprising, and deeply human in this iconic character, and I can’t wait for Broadway audiences to experience it.” Related Stories Raye to Headline BST Hyde Park With Sienna Spiro Opening Raye Wins Mercury Prize for Album of the Year An alternate performer will play the role of “The Kid” on Tuesday evenings and Wednesday matinees. Additional casting will be announced at a later date. “Purple Rain” will premiere next spring at the Majestic Theatre, with previews beginning on March 12 ahead of opening night on April 12. The show is based on the 1984 classic, which became a box office hit with nearly $100 million worldwide and inspired the mega-selling album of the same name. Here’s the show’s official logline: “Minneapolis, 1984. A new era of music television is creating overnight stars. A magnetic young performer known as ‘The Kid’ seems like the perfect frontman to lead his bandmates to stardom. But when his past threatens everything he’s built, he’ll have to sing his way out of the darkness and into the spotlight where he belongs.” The stage adaptation features over 20 of Prince’s iconic hits, including “When Doves Cry,” “I Would Die 4 U,” “Take Me With You” and “The Beautiful Ones.” Peter Duchan (“Dogfight”) wrote the musical’s book, while Jason Michael Webb (“MJ the Musical) is leading the music team. Bobby Z and Morris Hayes, both of whom worked with Prince for years as bandmates and musical collaborators, serve the production as music advisers. The musical was first staged in 2025 at Hennepin Theatre Trust’s historic State Theatre in Minneapolis, where Prince was born. articles.title: As Russell Brand’s Begins a 10-Year Prison Sentence, Why Celebrities Fear the Power of an Expose
articles.full_text: × Nov 10, 2026 8:42am PT As Russell Brand’s Begins a 10-Year Prison Sentence, Why Celebrities Fear the Power of an Expose By K.J. Yossman Plus Icon K.J. Yossman @KJYossman Latest As Russell Brand’s Begins a 10-Year Prison Sentence, Why Celebrities Fear the Power of an Expose 13 minutes ago David Walliams Dropped by Agency Following ‘Grooming’ Allegations 34 minutes ago David Walliams, Former ‘Britain’s Got Talent’ Judge, Accused of ‘Grooming Fans’ as Young as 15 After Failing to Get Injunction 4 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source LEON NEAL Standing in the glass dock at Southwark Crown Court in London, awaiting his sentence for one rape and three sexual assaults to be handed down, Russell Brand was addressed directly by the judge. “No doubt your companions thought it was outrageous laddish behaviour that only you could get away with,” Justice Bennathan said, referencing an incident in which Brand had launched himself on an unknown woman in the middle of a studio corridor as his entourage looked on. “It was outrageous and possibly laddish, but also a criminal sexual offence. And as it turns out, you haven’t got away with it.” Related Stories Olivia Rodrigo, Katseye and Sienna Spiro to Be Honored at Variety’s 10th Annual Hitmakers Event Raye to Headline BST Hyde Park With Sienna Spiro Opening Brand may well have gotten away with it had it not been for a joint investigation by Channel 4 documentary strand “Dispatches” and The Sunday Times of London. Their reporting, published in Sept. 2023, contained numerous serious allegations, including that the former comedian had sexually assaulted four women between 2006 and 2013. Brand denied any wrongdoing (none of the women who made the allegations in the documentary were involved in the recent criminal trial although it is understood the Met Police are now investigating at least one of those complaints and Brand may face yet more charges). The former comedian, who’d appeared in Hollywood movies and had a short-lived marriage to Katy Perry at the height of her success, had long cultivated an air of degeneracy as part of his persona, enabling him to operate in plain sight. Yet it wasn’t until the Channel 4/Sunday Times investigation was published that police opened an investigation. Whether it’s because the reporting had prompted more women to come forward – as Brand’s lawyer in the trial, Ian Winter, repeatedly argued — or because the media spotlight gave the authorities the resolution they needed to investigate a celebrity will probably never be known. But Brand is not the only celebrity to have found themselves in the dock after being accused of wrongdoing in the media. In 2023 news anchor Huw Edwards , once the best-known and highest paid journalist at the BBC, was the subject of an expose by The Sun, who revealed he had been in an inappropriate text-based relationship with a teenager during which he’d paid for nude photographs. Although he had not acted unlawfully in that instance, Edwards was arrested less than a year later and eventually convicted of making indecent images after police found videos of children as young as seven being abused on Edwards’ phone. It emerged he had been sent them by a pedophile to whom he’d, apparently unrelatedly, gifted numerous instalments of cash. Kevin Spacey has also faced an endless series of legal battles – both criminal and civil on both sides of the Atlantic – after he was accused of sexually assaulting a 14-year-old boy in a 2017 Buzzfeed interview. None have resulted in any finding of liability or criminality and Spacey has always denied any allegations of sexual misconduct but his career has never recovered. In the U.K. Spacey was, like Brand, tried at Southwark Crown Court, where he was on trial for nine charges of sexual assault against four separate men. He was acquitted on all counts . After the trial, some of the jurors asked to meet the Oscar-winner and shake his hand. So it’s unsurprising that David Walliams, a comedian, bestselling children’s author and former “Britain’s Got Talent” judge, sought an injunction last month to prevent the same newspaper from publishing an investigation into his alleged sexual misconduct. Lawyers for Walliams told London’s High Court he would be likely to commit suicide if the story was published. The judge held that suicidal ideation is not a ground on which to prevent the publication of an article potentially in the public interest, although he noted his decision to dismiss the injunction does not mean the allegations are true. Published today, the Guardian’s report accuses Walliams of grooming young fans and harassment. One woman told the newspaper she was 15 when she alleges Walliams drove her to his house and engaged in behavior that she now considers to be sexual assault. Walliams has denied all the allegations. There is no police investigation into Walliams nor any suggestion he may face charges, but, like Spacey, his career now lies in ruins. (Walliams has been dropped by his agent and his books will no longer be published). Brand’s celebrity loomed large throughout his trial: some of his victims were fans who were initially thrilled to meet him, others were vulnerable because of his disproportionate power over them. In his sentencing remarks, Justice Bennathan accepted the former comedian’s fame was “an intrinsic part of each offence” as it allowed him to carry out his crimes. But, he noted, “I also need to be careful I am not punishing you more because you are famous.” Coddled by their managers, obeyed by their assistants and adored by their fans, some celebrities have been able to abuse their exalted status. But when an intrepid journalist turns that spotlight to expose alleged misconduct, whether criminal or otherwise, fame can also be their undoing. ‘De Gaulle’ Wins Top Prize at American French Film Festival as 30th Anniversary Edition Draws 18,000 Attendees DC Studios’ New Boss Jeremy Latcham Has a ‘Guiding Light’ for Superhero Movies: Would My Grandma Like It? ‘You Have to Make Them for Everybody’ Prime Video, Scanbox Entertainment Team on New ‘Hamilton’ Films and TV Series Based on Bestselling Swedish Spy Franchise (EXCLUSIVE) Raye Named Variety’s 2026 Hitmaker of the Year ‘GTA 6’ Presales ‘Far in Excess’ of Expectations Ahead of Next Week’s Launch, Take-Two CEO Says Jennifer Hudson Will Headline Vatican’s ‘Concert With the Poor,’ With Pope Leo Scheduled to Attend Loading comments...

articles.title: BMG’s Concord Originals Preps Supernatural Gothic Horror Pic ‘Wolf at the Door’ (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.full_text: × Nov 10, 2026 8:45am PT BMG’s Concord Originals Preps Supernatural Gothic Horror Pic ‘Wolf at the Door’ (EXCLUSIVE) The five-year-old division is taking a 360-degree approach to an expanded portfolio following Concord's merger with music and theater powerhouse BMG and acquisition of RKO's classic film library By Anna Marie de la Fuente Plus Icon Anna Marie de la Fuente @adelafuente1 Latest Disney+ and ‘The House of Flowers’ Director Manolo Caro Prep Series Adaptation of ‘Blood Wedding’ by Federico García Lorca (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago ‘Longlegs’ Star Alicia Witt Toplines Colombian Horror Thriller ‘Incuba Project,’ Directed by Chile’s Juan Pablo Arias (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago ‘The Cry of Serankwa,’ an Indigenous Eco-Thriller and Triple Sanfic Industria Award Winner, Strikes Distribution Deal for Latin America 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Sophia Dilley, Charles Hopkins Courtesy of Concord Originals The full moon is out at Concord Originals , the film and TV arm of music and theater powerhouse BMG , where it is developing and producing supernatural gothic horror feature “Wolf at the Door.” Based on the eponymous play from Concord Theatricals, the genre pic will be helmed by Argentina’s Agustina San Martín, who recently directed the psychological horror feature “Psyche,” starring Noah Jupe (“A Quiet Place”) and Isabela Merced (“The Last of Us”), currently in post. Related Stories Raye to Headline BST Hyde Park With Sienna Spiro Opening Raye Named Variety’s 2026 Hitmaker of the Year The adaptation is written by playwright, poet and screenwriter Marisela Treviño Orta, based on her play “Wolf at the Door,” part of a trilogy of theatrical productions inspired by Latinx mythology and the Brothers Grimm fairy tales. ‘Wolf at the Door’ Credit: Liz Lauren Set in 19th century New Mexico, it centers on a young woman, close to giving birth to her first child, who foretells the return of a malevolent half-man half-wolf creature, only to discover that another predator has already entrenched itself in her hacienda. Casting is underway. “Wolf at the Door” is produced by Concord Originals’ Emmy-nominated exec VP Sophia Dilley (HBO’s “Stax: Soulsville, USA”) and VP of development Charles Hopkins (“Billy Preston: That’s the Way God Planned It”). Concord Originals’ Quíle Miguel Gomez, Victor Zaraya and Bob Valentine executive produce. “We’re film executives within a music and theater company, and this is the first play we’ve commissioned and developed entirely in-house. I’m really excited about what this represents and how it demonstrates our team’s ability to go beyond simply packaging and building projects,” said Dilley. Hopkins concurred: “This project encapsulates exactly what Concord Originals is all about: identifying world-class IP under the BMG roof and reimagining it for screen.” The eight-person team of this r elatively young division, founded in 2021, has its work cut out for it, given the deep vaults of BMG’s catalog plus those of Concord Theatricals (18,000+) and the recent acquisition of RKO, which adds another 5,000+ IP assets, including such classic cinema titles as Alfred Hitchcock’s “Suspicion” and Fritz Lang’s “The Woman in the Window.” “RKO has such a rich history and so much of it hasn’t been oversaturated, which makes it ripe for reinvention and a chance to reach new generations. It also feels like a deep well of stories that’s particularly timely for where the industry is today. Historically, RKO was interesting in how it made films on contained budgets, and I’m excited to explore what that approach could look like today,” Dilley remarked. Concord Originals’ scripted slate also includes “Bleeding Love,” an original movie musical featuring hits from multi Grammy-winner Ryan Tedder, a limited series adaptation of Rodgers & Hammerstein’s “Cinderella” with Skydance TV and projects with Jennifer Lopez ’s Nuyorican Prods. for Disney+. Reflecting on the fact that “Wolf” director San Martin is a protégé of BMG client Lin-Manuel Miranda for the Rolex Mentor and Protégé Arts Initiative, Hopkins said: “That is the advantage we now have in this bigger organization, is that there are these connecting dots between all of the talent that we work with on the filmmaking side as well as the music and theater side. So I think we’ll encounter more and more of those common connections among the artists we work with in the future.” Dilley pointed out that a single property could generate a film, stage production, album and other associated content. “We cover so many different areas, so the exciting part is bringing them together. Our ambition is to take a 360 approach to projects wherever we can, connecting film and TV with music and theater … bringing artists into a series, playwrights into the writing process, or developing a film that also has a stage production and an accompanying album,” said Dilley. “We have the opportunity to be involved in the life cycle of these copyrights, from beginning to end. Ultimately, it’s about keeping artists, iconic legacies and great IP in the zeitgeist, championing them and giving them the biggest cultural impact possible. articles.title: Jon Stewart Praises ‘60 Minutes’ & Ross Douthat For Donald Trump Interview: “I Think I’m Going To Enjoy This”
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Armando Tinoco Armando Tinoco Staff Writer @armietinoco More Stories By Armando Jon Stewart Praises ‘60 Minutes’ & Ross Douthat For Donald Trump Interview: “I Think I’m Going To Enjoy This” Julia Garner Shares Madonna Biopic Update: “Every Hour It Changes” Keira Knightley On Fans Quoting ‘Love Actually’ To Her: “It Means Nothing To Me” View All November 9, 2026 9:22pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jon Stewart hosts 'The Daily Show' Comedy Central Following the 2026 midterm elections and the blue wave, Jon Stewart returned to The Daily Show . After gloating over all the Republican seats that flipped to Democrats, the Comedy Central host took time to react to Donald Trump’s 60 Minutes interview. Related Stories News Donald Trump’s ‘60 Minutes’ Interview Was A Mixture Of Denial, Reflection And Contradiction Following Midterm Drubbing News Trump Admits He Was “Only Kidding” About UFC’s Dana White Becoming White House Press Secretary On Sunday night, Trump sat down with Ross Douthat for an interview that left many pleasantly surprised. CBS has undergone many changes over the last year following Bari Weiss’ takeover, with many long-time journalists leaving amid allegations that they were being mandated to give Trump favorable coverage. Stewart aired a clip where Trump says his administration has “created wealth at a level that our country has never seen,” with Douthat adding, “including for yourself.” Watch on Deadline “Young man, was that sass?” Stewart said. “Did the new magnified CBS 60 Minutes just deliver sass to Donald Trump?” When Douthat pointed out that Trump’s personal wealth went up by $3 billion, Stewart said, “I think I’m going to enjoy this. I did not come into this interview thinking I’m going to enjoy this, but now, as I am watching this, I am thinking to myself, ‘I am going to enjoy this.'” Stewart also praised Douthat after he pointed out that Trump is a co-owner of a company with investors connected to the United Arab Emirates government. The 60 Minutes journalist noted that if he had told Trump that the Biden family had a similar situation, he would have called it corrupt. “I’ll have what he’s having,” Stewart said, nodding to Meg Ryan on When Harry Met Sally . Stewart continued to praise Douthat for continuing to press Trump, adding, “My God, Ross, you beautiful bearded bastard. Do you know what you’ve just done here? Do you have any idea what you just did here? You have made Donald Trump admit that the difference between him and Joe Biden is that Joe Biden is more aware of his surroundings.” The comedian also gave props to 60 Minutes for the timing of their commercial breaks during pivotal moments of the interview “for maximum dramatic impact.” Trump was asked if he would forgive any of his enemies in order to go to Heaven, to which he said, “Can I be honest? I probably cannot do that now because I do hate some of my enemies, and I always will.” The iconic 60 Minutes tick-tock then starts playing, with Stewart adding, “Oh shit! No, they didn’t. Oh shit! That is some Ebenezer Scrooge bullshit on that.” Stewart continued, “ 60 Minutes directed by [Ingmar] Bergman, now? Is there a sound that is any more of an ominous portent of the fate that awaits Donald Trump?” Watch Jon Stewart’s talk about the midterms and Trump on The Daily Show below. articles.title: Richard Schiff Among Cast Added To Broadway’s ‘Awake And Sing!’ Revival
articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg ‘Purple Rain’ Musical: Jordan Fisher Is New Prince Of Broadway ‘Here There Are Blueberries’ Broadway Review: Evil As Banal As A Bowl Of Fruit ‘Wanted’ Broadway Review: Historical Musical Plays With Gospel Truth View All November 10, 2026 7:23am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Richard Schiff Stephen Lovekin/Deadline/Penske Media via Getty Images UPDATE, Nov. 10: Additional cast has been announced for Manhattan Theatre Club ‘s upcoming Broadway production of Clifford Odets’ Awake and Sing! New to the revival are: Michael Aronov as Moe Axelrod; Benjamin Pelteson as Sam Feinschreiber; The West Wing ‘s Richard Schiff; and Stephen Schnetzer. PREVIOUS, July 30: Micaela Diamond (Broadway’s Parade , TV’s Grotesquerie ) and Will Pullen (Broadway’s To Kill a Mockingbird , Netflix’s The Unforgivable ) have been added to the cast of Manhattan Theatre Club’s upcoming Broadway revival of Clifford Odets’ landmark 1935 American drama Awake and Sing! Related Stories News 'Purple Rain' Musical: Jordan Fisher Is New Prince Of Broadway News 'Here There Are Blueberries' Broadway Review: Evil As Banal As A Bowl Of Fruit Diamond and Pullen join the previously announced Danny Burstein, Jessica Hecht and Jeremy Shamos. Additional casting will be announced later. Watch on Deadline The new production, directed by Tyne Rafaeli, will begin previews on Tuesday, December 15, at MTC’s Samuel J. Friedman Theatre, with opening night on Thursday, January 7, 2027. MTC announced the new cast members today. The synopsis: “It’s the 1930s, and the Bronx is a furnace. New ideas clash with the old amidst the poverty and shattered promises of the Great Depression. And three generations of the Berger family, trapped inside their cramped tenement, struggle to hold different visions of an American dream.” MTC describes the play as a “classic battle between hope and disillusionment.” Diamond will play Hennie Berger, the family’s young daughter, and Pullen will play Ralph Berger, Hennie’s younger brother. Diamond is a Tony and Grammy Award nominated actor for her star turn as Lucille Frank in Parade on Broadway. She made her Broadway debut as Babe, the youngest Cher, in The Cher Show . Most recently, she appeared in the The Seat of Our Pants , at the Public Theater, a musical based on Thornton Wilder’s The Skin of Our Teeth . On TV she most recently appeared as series regular Sister Megan Duval in Ryan Murphy’s Grotesquerie . Pullen can next be seen reprising his role in the sequel to Aaron Schneider’s feature Greyhound , opposite Tom Hanks for Apple, and can currently be seen in Ridley Scott and Peter Craig’s Apple limited series Dope Thief . He recently starred in Angus MacLachlan’s feature A Little Prayer and Nora Fingscheidt’s Netflix feature The Unforgivable . He had a recurring role in the Apple series Dickinson , an on Broadway he starred as Jem in Aaron Sorkin’s To Kill a Mockingbird. He recently appeared in Adam Bock’s play The Receptionist at Second Stage, and additional stage credits include his Broadway debut in Lynn Nottage’s Sweat . Other screen credits include a FX’s The Americans and Jenji Kohan’s HBO pilot The Devil You Know. Awake and Sing! originally premiered on Broadway in 1935, produced by the legendary Group Theatre, and helped establish Odets as a major voice in American theater. Subsequent Broadway stagings opened in 1939, 1984 and, most recently, 2006 with a cast that included Mark Ruffalo, Ben Gazzara and, in the roles of Hennie and Ralph, Lauren Ambrose and Pablo Schreiber. The MTC production will feature scenic and costume design by David Zinn, lighting design by Isabella Byrd, and original music and sound design by Daniel Kluger. Awake and Sing! is produced in association with Brian and Dayna Lee, and Nicole and Stephanie Kramer. articles.full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz Asian World Film Festival Reveals Asian Vision & Focus On Sections ‘Somewhere In The South’ Takes Top Award At TCCF Pitching; ‘Reunion Dinner’ Scoops Three Prizes ‘The Hit List’ From ‘Gangs Of London’ Director Kim Hong-sun Boarded By Finecut For Sales View All November 10, 2026 8:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source A Little Dream Of Me 30 Pictures EXCLUSIVE: Reel Citrus has acquired North American rights to Vietnamese musical A Little Dream Of Me and is lining up a theatrical release on December 4. Directed by Chung Chí Công, the film features an 18-track original soundtrack from music producer Phạm Hải Âu and was shot in Vietnam , South Korea and New York. Kaycee, Trần Doãn Hoàng and Hữu Châu head the cast of the film about a pair of young dreamers who chase music from Hội An and Saigon to Busan and New York. Veteran actor Hữu Châu plays the hearing impaired father of the female protagonist, which has drawn praise in Vietnam for representation. Related Stories News Vietnam's Mockingbird Launches Horror Duo & Comedy Drama 'The Happiest Cell' At Busan's ACFM News Streaming & Local Film Propel Major Asian Markets To $15B Content Spend This Year - MPA Produced through Chung’s Saigon-based 30 Pictures , the film grossed around $2M (VND44BN) in Vietnam, making it the highest-grossing musical ever, in a market where the genre is rare, and the box office is dominated by horror and family drama. Watch on Deadline Opening on February 27, 2026, with around 400 screenings, the film benefitted from strong word-of-mouth and within three days was extended to more than 1,200 screenings. It held the number two spot at the box office through its opening week. With four days, the title and theme song were trending on TikTok, YouTube and through Google Search and were generating more than 11,500 social conversations. The theme song passed 13 million YouTube views and peaked at number two on the IFPI Official Vietnam Singles Chart. The film also became the first Vietnamese release to host sing-along screenings, with eight sold-out sessions drawing more than 1,500 fans. A live soundtrack concert, another first for a Vietnamese film, drew 700 people. “This is a different kind of Vietnamese film – it’s a full musical, it is joyful, and it is a story about family,” said Reel Citrus founder and executive director Brittany Tran. “Audiences in Vietnam made it a hit by sharing the songs and singing along in theaters. We want to bring that same experience to audiences here. The Vietnamese title [ Cảm Ơn Người Đã Thức Cùng Tôi ] means ‘thank you for staying up with me’, and December is the perfect time to say it with your family in a movie theater.” The film recently made its North American debut as the opening night film of Viet Film Fest in October. Byrne) who has to make some cuts because “publishing isn’t what it used to be.” “Nobody reads your book selections anyway,” Briney’s Ryan tells Randolph’s Hannah in a parking garage.
